Early Childhood
Jenkins Family 1.0
The Jenkins family consisted of Marvin (1937), Gloria (1939), Marvin (Buddy) (1961), Lynne (1964), and Julie (1966).  From the pictures I have seen, it was a typical 1970s family, where everything appeared to be great.  I think we have all found that pictures are definitely worth a 1000 words, and not always good.
Apparently it was a well-known fact that my dad ran around on my mom.  No one really knew why, but there were reasons not many new about.  Within the first 6 months of marriage to my Dad was overseas, Mom’s mother Dorothy, arranged a dinner with another man for my mom where one thing led to another.  Dorothy always hated my Dad and she treated him as such.  My Dad never forgave my mother for that and thus figured what was good for the goose is good for the gander.  Horrible way to look at it, but nonetheless, it happened that way.  I don’t say these things to make my Mom look bad, but to make sure that my Dad, was not viewed as a horrible person who was unfaithful for no reason and was just a bad person.  Again, not justifying any of this.  I am married now and realize that how I treat my wife is not dependent on how she treats me, but how I can glorify her.

Affair
For those that don’t know, I am the product of an affair my father had with Barbara Jean Dorff.  I have heard that my parents were separated at the time and I have heard that my dad cheated on my mom.  Regardless, it is 51 years later and it doesn’t really matter to me because although it was not a good situation at the time, I am happy to be here.
Being in construction, my dad worked extremely hard days, often from dark to dark.  From what I hear, he played just as hard.  Some of the guys he ran around with or at least knew from construction would hang out at a familiar bar.  This is where my biological mom worked at the time.  Apparently, Dad and she enjoyed each other’s company.
Going to Dad:
Dad had been seeing me on a weekly basis the first year of my life and giving my biological mother money to take care of me.  Often being taken care of by my sister Sharron.  Although overall a good person, I have heard that Barbara Jean was not the best mother.  She was the life of the party as I have heard.  Everyone liked her, fun loving, open spirit kind of woman, but not one to stay home and take care of her family.  
It turns out that my sister Sharron was actually taking better care of me at 17 as my biological mother had many “friends” and was still working at the bar.  My dad had repeatedly been asking her to give me to him and let him have me.  He had a good, stable life, able to care for me in ways she couldn’t.  It sounds like it got pretty ugly between them about my custody until one day she showed up at my dad’s house where his wife opens the door and she hands me to her saying, “here, he belongs to your husband”, then turning and walking away.  You can imagine the look and shock that must have been to my mom.  My dad told her to hold me and he would be right back, follows her down the sidewalk basically telling her that was a “shitty” way to do that, but he is happy to have me.  Because the way it all went down, he basically told her to stay away and she would never get me back.
My Dad, now realizing he has to come in and face his wife about a baby she didn’t know existed (I was approximately 11 months old).  I didn’t get all the details, but basically my Mom had to decide if she was going to stay and raise 4 children or leave and possibly support 3 on her own.  
My mom told me about this interaction that basically made up her mind to stay!  About 2-3 weeks later, my biological Mom showed back up while my Dad was at work to take me back.  My Mom had strict orders from my Dad to now allow her to take me under any circumstances and to call him immediately if she showed up.  While they waited for him to get there, they were sitting in the kitchen booth, L-shaped, with each of my moms on the other corner.  I was in the booth between them.  At one point, my biological mom reached out and said come to mommy and I turned from her and went to Gloria.  She stated that is when I knew I wasn’t leaving your father.  Any baby that won’t go to his own mother shouldn’t be sent back there.  She wasn’t sure how this was going to pan out, but she knew she was going to become my mom.  Long story short, my dad arrived, not happy at all, and proceeded to cuss Barbara Jean out and sent her on her way.  I am pretty sure there were some harsh words and threats made at that time that told her my dad meant business and not to come back ever again.

Childhood 
My childhood memories are all good ones.  I was raised by two loving parents, didn’t want for anything I truly needed.  Always had bikes, skateboards, sports, etc.  My extended family in Tennessee never made a lot of sense to me.  Back when I grew up, you talked to Granny maybe 1-2 times a year on the phone and that was it.  I remember going back to TN when I was like 7, but to be honest, my biggest memory there was when I spent the night with my Aunt Linda and my cousin Jeremy.  Of course, Kelly was there, but Jeremy and I were the same age and I wanted to be with him.  My own personal memory is the smell of their basement.  I had never been in a basement before and it had a unique musty smell.  Funny how that is a good memory for me because Jeremy and I played down there and I remember having a lot of fun.  I also remember playing outside and not having any sidewalks.  To a little California boy, that was really weird to me.  There we acres of woods behind the house and to a 7-year-old, that was huge!  One of Aunt Linda’s favorite stories to tell on me is about her garden.  They happen to be digging up potatoes and I was so amazed that people in Tennessee got their potatoes from the ground.  My Aunt laughed at my amaizment and she asked where I got mine from and I said my mom gets them from the store in a bag.  To a little California boy, gardens were not something I was familiar with.  I was clueless about gardens.
The family I had in California consisted of my Mom’s mom (Dorothy), my mom’s sister, Aunt Janice, and her three children, my cousins, Chris, Jon, and Sara.  Chris and Jon are identical twins and were probably the two I was closest with growing up.  I didn’t get to see them a ton, but man, when I did, I loved spending time with them.  They were both good athletes and whenever they were around, I remember heading up to the elementary school, Sea Side, and playing basketball.  Growing up they were always taller than me, just a little bit better, but close enough I still remember doing well against them.  Funny the things you remember.
Teens
My teens consisted of a few major points.  My mom leaving, sports, girls, and starting college.
Mom Leaving
My teen years are a little bit of a blur.  My mom left my dad when I was 14.  I was a typical teenage who though he knew more than his parents. Why are you not fighting for me?  Don’t you want me?  Of course, I had no knowledge of my biological mom, how I was not her biological child, how I was not adopted, etc.  So, to a 14-year-old boy, that was devastating. Moving to Tennessee
Once my parents separated and then divorce, my dad had to sell the house after I graduated high school per the agreement. This is when my dad decided he wanted to move back home to Tennessee, sorry Daisy to be specific. My dad was born and raised in Daisy Tennessee the town next to Soddy Tennessee which eventually grew together to become Soddy Daisy Tennessee. Both are small one light town that have a lot of history. Once the house sold my dad gave me the option to either stay or move back to Tennessee with him. I had only been to Tennessee one time, back when I was seven years old.  What I remember about Tennessee was very limited but I remember the smell in my aunt Linda’s basement where I spent several days hanging out with my cousin playing games. It was kind of like the kid’s playroom at the time.
College
Arriving At Alabama
January of 1992.  New to the University of Alabama, I arrive in Tuscaloosa to find my new apartment on 15th Street at University Downs.  Fairly new apartment complex, nice, pool, up on the second story.  Several other players live in the same apartment complex, but I was rooming with two guys I had never met.  Pete and Jerry.  Jerry was the first to arrive, green, just out of PA and never been away from home.  That was good, because I had never been out on my own either and both dealing with the same thing was good.  Jerry and I hit it off right away.
Memories
Train
I can still remember one of our first nights.  We had baseballs sitting on top of our dresser and all of a sudden in the middle of the night, we hear a train whistle way off in the distance.  Then all of sudden we can feel the train going by us, like it was outside of our window.  Then, one by one, the baseballs start to roll of the dresser and hit the floor, thunk, thunk...  Jerry and I started laughing aloud and end up staying up for a while just talking.  Funny what stands out in your mind huh?
Remember, as I write this, Jerry and I were in college, young, stupid, and did not know better.  That is my story and I am sticking to it.
Locking the sliding glass door 
I remember Jerry and I having to call the apartment office and ask someone to come fix the door lock on our sliding door out to the balcony.  Come to find out we just did not know how to lock the door.  Maintenance man just walked up and flipped the lock and said, all fixed.  We all just laughed and he left.  
Snowball fight
Lucky to be alive.  My Dad should have killed me.  Blizzard of 1992 in Tuscaloosa.  It was probably the biggest snow I have been in that I did not travel to on purpose.  My Dad and Rhonda were there visiting, me and a bunch of the baseball players were outside having a snowball fight.  My Dad came out to take some pictures with his good camera out on the third floor balcony.  Jerry dared me to see if I could hit him.  It was going to be darn near impossible to hit him.  From our distance and him being up on the third floor.  Well, being a baseball player in this situation was a good thing; I reared back and threw it as hard as I could (after packing that snowball into an ice ball).  As it traveled towards my Dad, I grew with excitement, it had a chance, then as it got closer, I started to get nervous, then I yelled, “Look out!”  Too late, the near impossible target took it right in the lens of the camera that make the ice ball explode into the face of my father.  I swear to this day had Rhonda not laughed so hard, I would be dead.  My Dad would not have thought that was funny.  Jerry was laughing so hard, he could not even stand up, just fell to the ground.  Fun memory and happy to still be here.
Hole in the wall
When we got board of playing darts, we thought it would be cool if we threw them up to the ceiling and see if we could jump up and get them.  We had a vaulted ceiling that had an angle with about a 30-40 degree angle.  We threw it to about 9 feet, that was too easy, then 9 and half feet, that was easy.  I thought it would be good to make it challenging, so I put it about 11 feet in the air.  Jerry took a running jump, missed, and when he landed, he lost his balance and backpedaled into the wall where he raised his foot up to stop his momentum.  His foot went right through the wall.  Jerry wore at least a size 12 shoe, big hole.  Good think Dad was a builder, I was able to patch that wall, sand it, and paint it so no one noticed.  At least we don’t think anyone noticed. 
Dishwasher overflowing
So, it’s been said, that Jerry and I have never lived on around in the dishwasher proves it. We decided it was time to clean up the kitchen and we loaded the dishwasher the best we knew Hal. When it came to putting soap in it, we were not sure what to do. I grabbed the dish washing soap and said I think there is a special detergent were supposed to use and Jerry said don’t worry about it just put in a couple of small drops. I forget how long past, but I remember Jerry going into the kitchen and then all of a sudden yelling hey DJ come here. Pizza box stack
For some reason guys do not like to do their own cleaning, at least by themselves. So we would order pizza quite often and when we were done we just set it on the counter in the kitchen.  After about a week we have 45 pizza boxes stacked up on the counter and no one would do anything with it. I’m not sure if you got the bright idea if it was Jerry or me, but one of us took the boxes and stacked in the corner outside our front door. Over the next several weeks we had ordered plenty of pizza and the stack just kept getting bigger and bigger and bigger to the point where we were throwing the boxes up on top of one another and then taking a broom handle to straighten the stack up. After a while it started to smell as we have left pizza crust in the boxes when we were done. I remember my dad coming to visit us and wanting to know what the hell we were doing out there with the pizza boxes. I think that was the motivation to tear down the stack of boxes and go throw them away.
Dishes...  General apartment clean up

Meeting Heather
Through a mutual friend, Vance Traffanstedt, Heather and I met in class.  She was different, I immediately knew it.  Not meaning her, but the way I perceived her.  I had “dated” several girls in college, but I could tell from the moment I met her, she was not going to be one of those girls…  Vance was a typical guy when you talked about girls. We were shallow, talked a big game, but in the end we were just young guys that didn’t know how to be around girls very well. I had earned a certain reputation about girls in college. I didn’t stay in a relationship very long and move from one girl to another pretty quick. Vance knew this and was afraid that I might treat Heather like I had other girls in school. Behind my back he had told Heather about my reputation and to not go out with me, but from what I hear Heather had interest but was definitely apprehensive about going out with me. I knew I had to take it slow with Heather or I would lose her. I remember having a study date with her at her apartment and if I had treated her like any other girl, I would’ve made a move on her expecting more than I should have. Instead, as I left standing at her doorway I asked if it was OK if I gave her a hug. Totally not what she was expecting and as I got the hug and surprised her, I knew I was on the right path.

Early Adulthood
Getting my degree was the start of adulthood for me.  It was the first step in landing my job with the Pinnacle Group right out of college and going on the road for my job.  Heather moved to Atlanta and took a job with Hewitt Associates, typical M-F 8-5:00pm job.  Mine on the other hand was Sunday – Thursday, with long days in between.  As a consultant, you were paid a salary and then bonus based on the number of billable hours you worked.  It was in my best interest to work as many hours as possible to increase my pay by the end of the year.
Shortly after getting my job, I asked Heather to marry me.  It was in November right before we were leaving to head out on a cruise to the Bahamas with my company.  People started coming up and congratulating us before I had actually popped the question.  I hadn’t planned on it until we were on the ship and out at sea.  Instead, I had to take her out to the gardens of the hotel and ask her there.  One of the happiest days of my life was when she said yes.

Being a Dad
October 5, 2002.  Quite frankly, the best/scariest day of my life.  My daughter Haley Nicole Jenkins was born.  In once sense, I can remember it like it was yesterday and, in another sense, it was a life time ago.  Heather was not dilating as needed and Dr. Wakefield said we couldn’t wait any longer.  A cesarean section was performed.  At the end, there were complications and upon delivery, Haley was not breathing.  The doctor spanked her, smacked her feet, anything to get her to blow out her lungs.  Nothing.  The doctor took her and ran down the hall with the nurses telling me I had to go and be with Haley, while leaving Heather in the delivery room to be stitched up without knowing what was going on with the Haley.  Long story short, Haley finally starting breathing, but had to stay in NICU for close monitoring as well as jaundice.  
Hearing Haley cry was one of the happies sounds I could have heard in that moment and time.  From that point and time, one of the worse sounds I could hear.  
Dad’s Stroke
June 21st, 2001, one of the worse days of my life and I am sure my Dad’s.  Around 11:00 pm that night, I received a call from my dad’s neighbor telling us that they found my dad on the bathroom floor and they did not know if we was going to make it.
See, my dad, although not a fan of big gatherings, loved to visit with people.  I had loaned my dad one of my four wheelers and he used that to go through his neighborhood and visit with people each night. That particular night, dad did not show up to Andy and Lisa’s house so they sent their son Kevin over to house to check on him.  It was obvious my dad was home, but he did not answer the door.  Keven called his folks and asked what to do.  They said see if the door was open and to go inside the house and check on him.  Well, that is when they found him on the phone.  After calling 911, they called me and stayed there with him and waited.  
I was packed and on the road with Heather 5 months pregnant.  Looking back, I was not in a good place.  I was speeding in excess of 110 MPH at times, eyes blurry from crying, while Heather sat next to me scared to death for all of us, including baby Haley.
Once the ambulance got there, they called for air transportation.  Come to find out, they had to resuscitate my father twice to keep him from dying.  Final result, Dad’s arteries in his neck were clogged and caused a massive stroke.  Since dad lived alone, he laid there for over 11 hours until Kevin found him.  Lucky to even be alive, he laid there in the hospital bed unable to communicate to anyone, paralyzed below his eyes.  He had no movement anywhere except his eyes.  
When I got there, I think it was Aunt Pat and Carol met me at the door.  Telling me, they had not heard anything and had not seen him yet.  I went to the counter and asked for my Dad.  Luckily, they took me back to him where he was just lying there, staring at me.  I grabbed his hand, not knowing he could not feel it, and just squeezed it.  My Dad, my rock, the one constant in my life since I was old enough to remember, lying there, helpless, now knowing what life would be like, if any at all.
The paralysis would prove to be temporary as time went on.  He spent two weeks in the hospital and another 5 weeks in Siskin Rehabilitation Hospital.  The entire time with me by his side.  I quit my job the day after explaining to my boss that I did not know what was going to happen, but I was not going to leave him until he could take care of himself or I moved him in with us.  Well, we ended moving him in with us down in Alabama.


 
Ancestry Website
I had wondered ever since I heard from my dad that Gloria was not my biological mother, who was it.  I had a birth certificate with her name on it, her husbands for that matter, but didn’t know anything else about her.  
Back before Ancestry.com was well know, I decided to enter some information on myself.  It was really weird, it asked for my parent’s information and I found myself wanting to enter Gloria’s information for my mother.  Having to type in Barbara Jean was weird.  For those of you that haven’t used Ancestry before, if you enter someone’s information and the site thinks it knows something about them, a little tree leaf appears and you can click on it to see a “hint”.  Well, it didn’t take long before there was a little leaf attached to Barbara Jean.  She appeared on someone else’s tree and I sent a quick note to the owner of the tree explaining who Barbara was to me.  I believe that was on a Friday and then I left for the weekend.  Returned home that Sunday to an email from a woman named Karen, claiming to be my sister and told me about my other brothers and sisters.  She left her phone number and asked me to call her.  Of course, I was skeptical, but at the same time was intrigued.  After talking to Heather about it before calling, I decided to pick up the phone.  

Meeting my Family
After receiving the email from Karen, I decided to call her.  A woman answered the phone sobbing, could not even come up with a word that I could understand.  After a few moments, she managed to get out, “Hi Danny”.  We spent about 3 hours on the phone that night.  Very unemotional for me as I did not know if this woman was who she said she was.  I remember feeling bad, because she was so full of emotion, crying, laughing, and sadness.  Basically, any emotional possible.  At the end of the conversation, she gave me my Uncle Danny’s number and said for me to call him.  He knew my dad and knew me when I was a baby.
Talking to Uncle Danny was very interesting.  I had more emotion at this point.  Danny was great, very informative, straightforward, and best of all, supplied me with some pictures.  We were talking about Barbara Jean and he said something about her being very pretty.  I said “really?”  He was like yeah, haven’t you seen pictures of her?  I had not.  Very quickly, he asked if I had an email address and then told me he would send me pictures of Barbara Jean and all her brothers and sisters.  It was cool to see.  Made it more real for me.  I remember still being skeptical of the information and the people I was talking to, so I printed out the family photo and took it to my dad to have him verify it.  
That was a hard moment for both of us.  Dad had not given me much information regarding Barbara, I think from feeling ashamed.  When I showed him the picture, he just started crying.  I knew then it was real.  Remember, at this point, dad could not talk because of his stroke.  While talking to uncle Dan, he did tell me that my dad would probably not know aunt Betty. She was not like the rest of the brothers and sisters that ran around and hit bars, she was a very Christian-based woman who didn’t agree with that lifestyle. That proved to be true as I showed my dad the picture, he pointed at each of the brothers and sister shaking his head yes yet when he got to her, he shook his head no. I told him that my uncle Danny said and he kind of smiled. This is where it all got real for me knowing that I had an entirely different family out there that I knew nothing about. I did learn that my biological mother, Barbara Jean had passed away in 1991. Just a year or so before I found out about her. 
So I ended up having several more conversations with my sister Karen and then ultimately reaching out and talking to my sister Rachelle. We ended up planning a family get-together that consisted of Rachelle, Vickie, Sharron, and her family. I flew out to Los Angeles to see my mom (the one who raised me) and brought Heather and Haley. I then took a flight to Sacramento by myself to meet my sisters. When I arrived at the airport Rachelle was there waiting on me and she was so sweet and so nice and welcoming that it really helped ease my feelings. I spent a day or two at her house before we drove up to my sister Sharron‘s place. Sharron owned and operated a bar at that time and then she just lived a short ways away.  I remember that all the family was really nice and open except for my sister Sharron, she stayed distant and had this really weird look on her face. In preparation for this get-together, I put together a small photo album for each sister that started with pictures of me when I was really little on the way to present with my wife and daughter. As I handed these out to each of them, I noticed Sharron was looking through the pictures and all of a sudden got up and walked away into the kitchen. I was urged by one of the other sisters to follow her. I went into the kitchen making small talk and all of a sudden Sharron turned to me and planted a big kiss on me and started crying. Prior to seeing the pictures in the photo album, she did not believe I was truly her lost brother. For Sharron, this was much more emotional because she cared for me not only the first year of my life but continue to come around the next couple of years when I want to live with my dad. It wasn’t until I started asking questions about where Sharon was that she decided it would be best for me if she disappeared from the picture.  She knew I was going to have a good life with my dad and unfortunately her and the other kids were not exposed to the same level of care and love as I was going to receive. That was a huge sacrifice on her part so when I came back into the picture it was really hard for her to believe that I was there and this was real. She recognized pictures of me and my dad in the photo album and that’s when it really hit home that it was all real. The plan was for me to go back to my sister Rachel‘s house and spend the night and visit with her and her family, but Sharron stepped in and said he staying with me tonight and she and I stayed up talking all night, she shared pictures and stories about each other and we really got to know each other really fast in a short amount time. Sharron had experienced a lot of negative times in her life that has caused her to put up a shield from getting too close to people. She basically told me that she would open up and talk with me all I wanted that night about family and questions about grandparents and everything but after that, she would have to put that box back in its place because she cannot deal with all the negative emotion that might come with it again. She had pretty much convinced herself she would never see me again and although that isn't what she wanted, the emotion that came with seeing me was pretty strong. We had a great night together, something I will never forget, but will miss not being able to have that time with her again. Sharron will always hold a special place in my heart because over the years what little information I did find out about Barbara and her family, Sharon was always the staple point and what a wonderful person she was to me and raising me and loving me. For that I am very grateful.

 
Baseball
Baseball was my safe place.  It is where I went to be safe physically, mentally, and overall just where I felt good.  Growing up in Southern California was a blessing, if for no other reason, I could basically play baseball year around.  Who knew at the time that it would be one of the most important things in my life. 
I started playing when I was 7 years old at Torrance American Boys Baseball (TABB).
1989 Baseball Draft (Drafted in the 35 round as the 905th pick overall)
https://www.mlb.com/draft/tracker/1989/all/round/35

My senior year was a good year for me with baseball. I was co-captain of the team with our shortstop Andy McTaggart. We had grown up together playing baseball for tab and we’re always one of the top 3 to 4 players in the area. Rarely did we get to play on the same team because when teams were picked, we were always one of the first couple to go and that was never on the same team.

Andy grew into maturity early and as a freshman played for varsity, leaving me to play shortstop my freshman year. The summer between my freshman and sophomore year I grew about 7 inches. That’s a lot in a very short amount of time. I remember multiple nights me lying in bed crying because my muscles are so sore from growing and my mom just lying there beside me rubbing my legs for hours. It’s moments like those that reminds you with a great mom she really was.

Anyway, my sophomore year I came back and ran out to shortstop only to realize I had lost most of my coordination, I remember one time stepping on my glove with my hand still in it causing me to fall forward and land right on my face. At my expense, that was one of the funniest moments on the baseball field I think my team ever experienced. How do you not laugh at yourself, that was so unlike me thought it was funny? Anyway, after a few crazy throws and a few missed ground balls, my coach very quickly told me to get my ass over to third base. From that point forward I never played shortstop again. In hindsight, that was a true blessing because although I was never really smart, I knew when a ball was hit hard at me that it was going to hurt. At shortstop, you had time to contemplate whether or not you wanted to get in front of the ball, more often than not I decided it was smarter to play the ball on the side of me so in case it took about hop it wouldn’t hit me. At third base, you don’t have time to think, you just react. My reaction skills were fantastic, you hit a ball at me, I catch it. I didn’t have to think it came very naturally which made me very good. Throughout the year my arm became extremely strong and even more accurate as I threw over the first base. I’ve always had a strong arm and after my growth spurt it got even stronger. I don’t remember what I threw in high school, but I know in college they clocked me at 93 miles an hour. Although not the hardest on the team, 93 was still hard. The problem is, my ball didn’t move much so the higher I got in sports, the more like batting practice it became. Most of the fields we played on in high school did not have fences. Although I was a great third baseman and had an exceptionally strong arm, I was not known for being fast, quick maybe, fast I was not. I would hit the ball a country mile and then would run it out . After about the third time getting thrown out at home plate, my coach vowed never to send me for an inside the park home run again, he was stopping me at third base. There was something about the last 90 feet that I just slow down tremendously,  in hindsight I was out of shape and just tired by the time I got closer to home. However, what does that do is give the perception I was very fast because I like the league and triples that year. This Got the eyes of the scout from the San Francisco Giants . Jack french, one of the true old-timers that grew up playing ball, loved the sport, loved being around the game, and loved looking for a new talent. He found me, the same night I had a double and a triple. He was very impressed as I made several plays third base and he asked me to come out and play with the Giants semi pro team out in the valley. This is where I met George Genovese, the head scout for the San Francisco Giants in the Los Angeles area. I played with the semi pro team and although had many tools  that made me a viable draft pick, I wasn’t a stand out stud like some others I played with. I ended up getting drafted in the 32nd round of the 1989 major-league baseball draft. Not the highest pick in the world, but definitely a complement that they thought enough of me to offer me a contract . The sign in bonus was not very much, but yet to an 18-year-old kid, $10,000 sounded like a lot of money. My dad said that wouldn’t even Carla cover college and that $40,000 would be enough for me to give up my collegiate eligibility and go professional. George did not have the authority to give me that type of money, but he did call the general manager of the San Francisco Giants who flew down and watched me take batting practice and infield practice. He managed to stay for my first at bat where I struck out and then proceeded to leave. Never saying a word to me or my father when he left, but did tell George that they would give me $20,000, but not the 40,000. This put my dad in a bit of a pickle, I was old enough to make my own decisions, but he knew I relied on his advice a lot. He wanted me to follow my dreams, but he also knew $20,000 was not very much money  overall and if I didn’t make it it would not pay for college. Dad gave me the choice but he also gave me some real worldly advice about the statistics of those that go into the minor leagues and those that actually make it. I had the opportunity to go play college baseball  and that would help secure my future, but I had to be good with that choice, not every kid gets an opportunity to play in the minor leagues and if I were to regret that decision it would hurt me for a very long time.

Ultimately, I turn down the contract and enrolled in junior college at El Camino College in Gardena, California . I played one season for them before my Dad and I moved to TN.  

Learning about Mom(s)
It’s hard to pinpoint the exact date I found out that I was not the child of my Mom and Dad (kind of).  I had come home one weekend from college and had gone out for a couple of beers with my Dad’s brother, Charles.  When I got home, my Dad greeted me and expressed he was upset because I had been out “drinking”.  I would hardly call it drinking, but yes, I had had a couple of beers.  Funny coming from someone that had a drinking problem and owned a bar!
He had been telling me for years there was something I didn’t know and “one day” he would tell me.  I was 22, attending the University of Alabama, at what point would I be old enough to know the “one day” information.  Tonight, would be that night.  I don’t remember the exact words I used, but I am pretty sure I was disrespectful, but basically said I was old enough to know anything that had to do with my life and if he wasn’t willing to share it with me now, then he could take it and put it where the sun don’t shine.  OK, maybe I had been out “drinking”.  I didn’t normally talk to my father that way.
Well, he said, you know Gloria, your mom, she’s not who you think she is.  She is not your biological mother.  He said a few things after that, but to be honest, I don’t remember exactly what he said.  Those words have played through my head for years, never getting any easier to hear.  Once I comprehended what he was saying, I started asking questions.  First, what the hell does that have to do with anything regarding me going out drinking with your brother?  He proceeded to tell me that my biological mother abused alcohol and drugs and I had to be “dried out” when I was born.  The doctors told them both then that I would be susceptible to alcoholism and drug addiction when I got older and to keep an eye out for it.  CONNECTION!  OK, makes a little more sense how this conversation came about, but…WHAT?  Go back, what do you mean Mom is not my biological mother?  I am 22 years old, have three older siblings and have never heard about this.  I have been through grades 1-12, 2 years of college, little league, football, basketball, and too many things to count.

What I have come to learn
Matthew McConaughey speech really spoke to me.  It put into words that I have often thought about and even thought was too outlandish to implement.  Starting 9/21/2018, I am going to start putting these joys into place in my life by doing just this.

Matthew McConaughey to Grads: Always Play Like an Underdog
The sooner we become LESS IMPRESSED — with our life, our accomplishments, our career, the prospect in front of us. As soon as we become LESS IMPRESSED — and MORE INVOLVED with these things, the sooner we get a whole lot better at doing them.
So, I’m going to talk to you about some things I’ve learned along my journey — most from experience, some I heard in passing, many I’m still practicing, but ALL of them, true.
Yes, they may be truths to me, but don’t think that that makes them MINE… because you can’t own a truth. Think of these as signposts, approaches, paradigms, that give some science to satisfaction. They are yours to steal, to share, to liken to your own lives, and to personally apply in your OWN lives, in your own way, should you choose to.
1. Life is not easy…
NUMBER 1, LIFE’S NOT EASY…don’t try and make it that way. It’s not fair, it never was, it isn’t now, it won’t ever be. Do not fall into the entitlement trap of feeling you are a victim, you are not. Get over it and get on with it. And yes, most things are more rewarding when you break a sweat to get em.
2. “Unbelievable” is the stupidest word in the dictionary
It shouldn’t ever come out of our mouths.
To say, “What an unbelievable play!” It was an unbelievable book, film, act of courage…really?
It may be spectacular, phenomenal, most excellent and outstanding… but unbelievable? NO. Give others and yourself more credit. It just happened, you witnessed it, you just did it, believe it.
How about the other side of unbelievable? When we humans “under perform” or act OUT of character? — “man flies a suicide jet into the World Trade Center, millions die from diseases that we have cures for, Bob the builder swears he’ll have your house built by Thanksgiving and you can’t move in ’til Christmas, THE NEXT YEAR…” Our best friend lies to us, and WE, lie to our self, all the time…unbelievable? I don’t think so.. Again, it just happened, and it happens everyday …
NOTHING we homosapien earthlings do is unbelievable — one thing you can depend on people being…is people. So we shouldn’t be surprised, we are the trickiest mammal walking the planet!! (It ain’t the monkeys I’m worried about, it’s you and me.)
Acknowledge acts of greatness as real, and do NOT be naive about mankind’s capacity for evil nor be in denial of our own shortcomings.
NOTHING we do is unbelievable. Stupid word. Un-be-lievably stupid word.
3. Happiness is different than Joy
“I just want to be happy.” I hear that all the time. But what IS happiness? Happiness is an emotional response to an outcome — If I win I will be happy, if I don’t I won’t. An if-then, cause and effect, quid pro quo standard that we cannot sustain because we immediately raise it every time we attain it. You see, happiness demands a certain outcome, it is result reliant.
If happiness is what you’re after, then you are going to be let down frequently and be unhappy much of your time. Joy, though, is something else. It’s not a choice, not a response to some result, it is a constant. Joy is “the feeling we have from doing what we are fashioned to do,” no matter the outcome.
Personally, as an actor, I started enjoying my work and literally being happier when I stopped trying to make the daily labor a means to a certain end — I need this film to be a box office success, I need my performance to be acknowledged, I need the respect of my peers.
All reasonable aspirations but truth is, as soon as the WORK, the MAKING of the movie, the DOING of the deed became the reward in itself — I got more box-office, more accolades and respect than I’d ever had before. See, JOY is always in process, under construction — it’s in the constant approach, alive and well —in the DOING of what we are fashioned to do… and enJOYing doing it.
4. Define Success For Yourself
I went to a voodoo shop south of New Orleans a few years back — they had vials of “magic” potions stacked in columns with headings above each defining what they would give you — Fertility, Health, Family, Legal Help, Energy, Forgiveness, Money.
Guess which column was empty? Money. Let’s admit it, “money” is king today, makes the world go round. Money is SUCCESS, the more we have, the more “successful” we are, right?
I’d argue that our cultural values have even been financialized — humility is not in vogue anymore, it’s too passive. It’s a get rich quick on the internet, 15 minutes of fame world we live in. See it every day.
But, we all want to succeed right? Question we have to ask ourselves is, what success is to us, what success is to YOU. More money? OK, I got nothing against money. But maybe it’s a healthy family? A happy marriage? To help others? To be famous? To be spiritually sound? To leave the world a little bit better place than you found it?
Continue to ask yourself that question. Your answer may change over time and that’s fine, but do yourself this favor:
WHATEVER your answer is, DON’T CHOOSE ANYTHING THAT WILL JEOPARDIZE YOUR SOUL. PRIORITIZE WHO YOU ARE, WHO YOU WANT TO BE, AND DON’T SPEND TIME WITH ANYTHING THAT ANTAGONIZES YOUR CHARACTER. DON’T DRINK THE KOOL AID!! It tastes sweet today but it will give you cavities tomorrow. Life is not a popularity contest. Be brave, take the hill but first, answer the question, “What is my hill?”
How do I define success? For me, it’s a measurement of five things — fatherhood, being a good husband, health, career, friendships. These are what’s important to me in my life.
So, I try to measure these five each day, check in with them, see whether or not I’m in the debit or the credit section with each one. Am I in the red or in the black with each of them?
For instance, sometimes my career is rolling (in the black) but I see how my relationship with my wife could use a little more attention. I gotta pick up the slack on being a better husband, get that one out of the red. Or say my spiritual health could use some maintenance (red) but hey, my friendships and social life are in high gear (black)… I gotta recalibrate, checks and balances, go to church, remember to say thank you more often. I gotta take the tally. Because I want to keep ALL 5 in healthy shape, and I know that if I DON’T take care of them, if I don’t keep up maintenance on them, ONE of them is going to get weak, dip too deep into the debit section, go bankrupt, get sick… die even.
So first, we have to DEFINE success for ourselves, then we have to put in the work to MAINTAIN it — take our daily tally, tend our garden, keep the things that are important to us in good shape.
Let’s admit it, we all got two wolves in us, a good one and a bad one, you know what I’m talking about — and they BOTH wanna eat… We just gotta feed that good wolf a little more than the other one.
5. Process of elimination is the first step to our identity
(a.k.a where you are NOT is as important as where you are)
In 1992, I got my first job as an actor. Three lines, three days work, in a film called Dazed and Confused. Alright.
Alright, Alright, Alright.
The director, Richard Linklater, kept inviting me back to set each night, putting me in more scenes which led to more lines all of which I happily said YES to. I was having a blast. People said I was good at it, they were writing me a check for $325 a day. I mean hell yeah, give me more scenes, I love this!! And by the end of the shoot those 3 lines had turned into over 3 weeks work and “it was Wooderson’s ’70 Chevelle we went to get Aerosmith tickets in.” Bad ass.
Well, a few years ago I was watching the film again and I noticed two scenes that I really shouldn’t have been in. In one of the scenes, I exited screen left to head somewhere, then re-entered the screen to “double check” if any of the other characters wanted to go with me. Now, in rewatching the film, (and you’ll agree if you know Wooderson), he was not a guy who would ever say, “later,” and then COME BACK to “see if you were sure you didn’t wanna come with him..” No, when Wooderson leaves, Wooderson’s gone, he doesn’t stutter step, flinch, rewind, ask twice, or solicit, right? He just “likes those high school girls cus he gets older and they stay the same age.”
My point is, I should NOT have been in THAT scene, I should have exited screen left and never come back.
But back then, making my first film, getting invited back to set, cashing that check and having a ball, I WANTED more screen time, I WANTED to be in the scene longer and more, and come back into the scene right?
I shouldn’t have been there. Wooderson shouldn’t have been there.
It’s just as important where we are not as it is where we are.
The first step that leads to our identity in life is usually NOT “I know who I am,” but rather “I know who I AM NOT.” Process of elimination.
Defining ourselves by what we are NOT is the first step that leads us to really KNOWING WHO WE ARE.
You know that group of friends you hang out with that really don’t bring out your best? They gossip too much, or they’re kind of shady, and they really aren’t gonna be there for you in a pinch? Or how about that bar we keep going to that we always seem to have the worst hangover from? Or that computer screen that keeps giving us an excuse not to get out of the house and engage with the world and get some HUMAN interaction? Or how about that food we keep eating? Tastes so good going down but makes us feel like crap the next week when we feel lethargic and keep putting on weight?
Those people, those places, those things — STOP giving them your TIME and ENERGY. Don’t GO there, put them DOWN — and when you DO quit giving them your time, you inadvertently find yourself spending MORE time and in more PLACES that are more healthy for YOU, that bring YOU more joy — WHY?
Because you just eliminated the who’s, the where’s, the what’s and the when’s that were keeping you from your identity. Trust me, too many options makes a tyrants of us all. So get rid of the excess, the wasted time, decrease your options… and you will have accidentally, almost innocently, put in front of you, what is important to you by process of elimination.
Knowing who we ARE is hard. Give yourself a break. Eliminate who you are NOT first, and you’ll find yourself where you need to be.
6. DON’T LEAVE CRUMBS — and the beauty of delayed gratification
What are crumbs? The crumbs I’m talking about are the choice we make that make us have to look over our shoulder in the future.
You didn’t pay that guy back the money you owed him and tonight you just saw him sitting 3 rows behind you…shit…You slept around on your spouse and you just found out that tomorrow, she and the lady you’re having an affair with, are going to be at the same PTA meeting…shit again… You drank too much last night and you’re too hungover to drive your son to his 8 a.m. Saturday morning baseball practice. THESE ARE CRUMBS! They come in the form of regret, guilt, and remorse — you leave em today, they will cause you more stress tomorrow, and they DISALLOW you from creating a customized future in which you DO NOT have to look over your shoulder.
So…let’s flip the script. Instead of creating outcomes that take FROM us, let’s create MORE outcomes that pay us BACK, fill us up, keep your fire lit, turn you ON, for the most amount of TIME in your future.
These are the choices I speak of and this is the beauty of delayed gratification.
Tee yourself up. Do yourself a favor. Make the choices, the purchase TODAY that PAYS you back TOMORROW. RESIDUALS. In my business, it’s called “mailbox money.” I do my job well today, I get checks in the mailbox five years from now — heck of a deal.
So, whether its prepping the coffee maker the night before so all you gotta do is press the button in the morning, or getting ready for the job interview early so you don’t have to cram the night before, or choosing not to hook up with that married woman because you know you’ll feel horrible about it tomorrow (and her husband carries a gun), or paying your debts on time so when you do see that guy three rows back tonight — you don’t have to hunker down in your seat hoping he don’t see you. Get some R.O.I — RETURN ON INVESTMENT — Your investment. You. You customize your future.
DON’T LEAVE CRUMBS.
7. DISSECT YOUR SUCCESSES (and the reciprocity of gratitude)
We so often focus on our FAILURES. We study them. We obsess on them. We DISSECT them. We end up intoxicated with them to the point of disillusion.
When do we write in our diary? When we’re depressed. What do we gossip about? Other people’s flaws and limitations. We can dissect ourselves into self loathing if we’re not careful — and I find that most of the times our obsession with what is wrong just breeds more wrong and more failure.
The easiest way to dissect success is though gratitude. Giving thanks for that which we do have, for what is working, appreciating the simple things we sometimes take for granted. We give thanks for these things and that gratitude reciprocates, creating more to be thankful for. It’s simple, and it works.
I’m not saying be in denial of your failures. No, we can learn from them too, but only if we look at them constructively. As a means to reveal what we are good at, what we can get better at, what we do succeed at.
I’ve read a lot of my bad reviews, and the good “bad reviews,” written by the more talented critics, are constructive. They reveal to me what did translate in my work, what came across, what was seen, or what wasn’t. I don’t obsess on the unfavorable aspect of their review, but I do seek what I can learn from it — Because their displeasure actually uncovers and makes more apparent what I do do well, what I am successful at… and then I dissect that.
Life is a verb. We try our best. We don’t always do our best. Well, architecture is a verb as well. And since we are the architects of our lives, lets study the habits, the practices, the routines we have that lead to and feed our success… our joy, our honest pain, our laughter, our earned tears…Let’s Dissect THAT and give thanks for THOSE things… and when we do that what happens? We get better at them…and have more to dissect.
8. MAKE VOLUNTARY OBLIGATIONS
Mom and dad teach us things as children. Teachers, mentors, the government and laws all give us guidelines to navigate life, rules to abide by in the name of accountability.
I’m not talking about those obligations. I’m talking about the ones we make with ourselves, with our God, with our own consciousness. I’m talking about the YOU versus YOU obligations. We have to have them. Again, these are not societal laws and expectations that we acknowledge and endow for anyone other than ourselves. These are FAITH based OBLIGATIONS that we make on our own.
Not the lowered insurance rate for a good driving record, you will not be fined or put in jail if you do not gratify the obligations I speak of — no one else governs these but you.
They’re secrets with yourself, private council, personal protocols, and while nobody throws you a party when you abide by them, no one will arrest you when you break them either. Except yourself. Or, some cops who got a “disturbing the peace” call at 2:30 in the morning because you were playing bongos in your birthday suit.
An honest man’s pillow is his peace of mind, and when you lay down on the pillow at night, no matter who’s in our bed we ALL sleep alone. — These are your personal jiminy crickets. And there are not enough cops in the entire world to police them — It’s on YOU.
9. From can to want
1995. I got my first big paycheck as an actor. I think it was 150 grand. The film was Boys on the Side and we’re shooting in Tucson, AZ and I have this sweet little adobe guest house on the edge of the Saguaro National Park. The house came with a maid. My first maid. It was awesome. So, I’ve got a friend over one Friday night and we’re having a good time and I’m telling her about how happy I am with my set up . The house. The maid. Especially, the maid. I’m telling her, “she cleans the place after I go to work, washes my clothes, the dishes, puts fresh water by my bed, leaves me cooked meals sometimes, and SHE EVEN PRESSES MY JEANS!” My friend, she smiles at me, happy for my genuine excitement over this “luxury service” I’m getting, and she says, “Well…that’s great…if you like your jeans pressed.”
I kind of looked at her, kind of stuttered without saying anything, you know, that dumb ass look you can get, and it hit me…
I hate that line going down my jeans! And it was then, for the first time, that I noticed…I’ve never thought about NOT liking that starched line down the front of my jeans!! Because I’d never had a maid to iron my jeans before!! And since she did, now, for the first time in my life, I just liked it because I could get it, I never thought about if I really wanted it there. Well, I did NOT want it there. That line… and that night I learned something.
Just because you CAN?… Nah… It’s not a good enough reason to do something. Even when it means having more, be discerning, choose it, because you WANT it, DO IT because you WANT to.
I’ve never had my jeans pressed since.
10. A roof is a man made thing
January 3, 1993. NFL playoffs. Your Houston Oilers vs. Buffalo Bills. Oilers up 28–3 at halftime, 35–3 early in the 3rd. Frank Reich and the Bills come back to win 41–38 in overtime for one of the greatest comebacks in NFL history. Yeah, the Bills won, but they didn’t really beat the Oilers. The Oilers lost that game, they beat themselves.
Why? Because at halftime they put a ceiling, a roof, a limit on their belief in themselves, a.k.a the “prevent defense.” Maybe they started thinking about the next opponent at halftime, played on their heels, lost the mental edge the entire 2nd half and voila, they lost. In a mere 2 quarters defensive coordinator Jim Eddy went from being called DC OF THE YEAR and “the man first in line to be a HC next year” to a man without a job in the NFL.
You ever choked? You know what I mean, fumbled at the goal line, stuck your foot in your mouth once you got the microphone, had a brain freeze on the exam you were totally prepared for, forgot the punch line to a joke in front of four thousand graduating students at a University of Houston Commencement speech? Or maybe you’ve had that feeling of “Oh my God, life can’t get any better, do I deserve this?”
What happens when we get that feeling? We tense up, we have this outer body experience where we are literally seeing our self in the third person. We realize that the moment just got bigger than us. You ever felt that way? I have.
It’s because we have created a fictitious ceiling, a roof, to our expectations of ourselves, a limit — where we think it’s all too good to be true. BUT IT ISN’T. AND IT’S NOT OUR RIGHT TO SAY OR BELIEVE IT IS.
We shouldn’t create these restrictions on ourselves. A blue ribbon, a statue, a score, a great idea, the love of our life, a euphoric bliss. Who are we to think we don’t deserve or haven’t earned these gifts when we get them?
Not our right.
But if we stay in process, within ourselves, in the joy of the doing, we will never choke at the finish line. Why? Because we aren’t thinking of the finish line, we’re not looking at the clock, we’re not watching ourselves on the Jumbotron performing the very act we are in the middle of. No, we’re in process, the APPROACH IS THE DESTINATION… and we are NEVER finished.
Bo Jackson ran over the goal line, through the end zone and up the tunnel — the greatest snipers and marksmen in the world don’t aim at the target, they aim on the other side of it.
We do our best when our destinations are beyond the “measurement,” when our reach continually exceeds our grasp, when we have immortal finish lines.
When we do this, the race is never over. The journey has no port. The adventure never ends because we are always on our way. Do this, and let them tap us on the shoulder and say, “hey, you scored.” Let them tell you “You won.” Let them come tell you, “you can go home now.” Let them say “I love you too.” Let them say “thank you.”
TAKE THE LID OFF THE MAN MADE ROOFS WE PUT ABOVE OURSELVES AND ALWAYS PLAY LIKE AN UNDERDOG.
11. Turn the page
The late and great University of Texas football coach Daryl Royal was a friend of mine and a good friend to many. A lot of people looked up to him. One was a musician named “Larry.” Now at this time in his life Larry was in the prime of his country music career, had #1 hits and his life was rollin’. He had picked up a habit snortin’ “the white stuff” somewhere along the line and at one particular party after a “bathroom break,” Larry went confidently up to his mentor Daryl and he started telling Coach a story. Coach listened as he always had and when Larry finished his story and was about to walk away, Coach Royal put a gentle hand on his shoulder and very discreetly said, “Larry, you got something on your nose there bud.” Larry immediately hurried to the bathroom mirror where he saw some white powder he hadn’t cleaned off his nose. He was ashamed. He was embarrassed. As much because he felt so disrespectful to Coach Royal, and as much because he’d obviously gotten too comfortable with the drug to even hide as well as he should.
Well, the next day Larry went to coach’s house, rang the doorbell, Coach answered and he said, “Coach, I need to talk to you.” Daryl said, “sure, c’mon in.”
Larry confessed. He purged his sins to Coach. He told him how embarrassed he was, and how he’s “lost his way” in the midst of all the fame and fortune and towards the end of an hour, Larry, in tears, asked Coach, “What do you think I should do?” Now, Coach, being a man of few words, just looked at him and calmly confessed himself. He said, “Larry, I have never had any trouble turning the page in the book of my life.” Larry got sober that day and he has been for the last 40 years.
You ever get in a rut? Stuck on the merry-go-round of a bad habit? I have. You are going to make mistakes — own them, make amends, and move on. Guilt and regret kills many a man before their time. Turn the page, get off the ride. YOU are the author of the book of your life. Turn the page.
12. Give your obstacles credit
You know these No Fear t-shirts? I don’t get em. Hell, I try to scare myself at least once a day. I get butterflies every morning before I go to work. I was nervous before I got here to speak tonight. I think fear is a good thing. Why? Because it increases our NEED to overcome that fear.
Say your obstacle is fear of rejection. You want to ask her out but you fear she may say “no.” You want to ask for that promotion but you’re scared your boss will think you’re overstepping your bounds.
Well, instead of denying these fears, declare them, say them out loud, admit them, give them the credit they deserve. Don’t get all macho and act like they’re no big deal, and don’t get paralyzed by denying they exist and therefore abandoning your need to overcome them. I mean, I’d subscribe to the belief that we’re all destined to have to do the thing we fear the most anyway.
So, you give your obstacles credit and you will one. Find the courage to overcome them or see clearly that they are not really worth prevailing over.
BE BRAVE, HAVE COURAGE. WHEN YOU DO YOU GET STRONGER, MORE AWARE, AND MORE RESPECTFUL — OF YOURSELF, AND THAT WHICH YOU FEAR.
13. So how do we know when we cross the truth?
13. Why 13? Unlucky # right?
Well, when did 13 get the bad rap and become the mongrel of numerology? Thirteen’s never done me wrong. In fact, 13 has been a pretty lucky number for me, lemme tell you how:
I’ve always taken these 21 day trips by myself to far off places where I usually don’t know the language and nobody knows my name. They’re adventures and they’re a purge, a cleanse for me. Like a 21 day fast from attention, from all the things I have in my well appointed life. They’re a check OUT, so I can check IN with myself.
See how I’m doing, be forced to be my own and only company, to have a look in MY mirror. And you know what can happen when we do THAT — sometimes we don’t like what we see.
In 1996, right after I got “famous” from a film called A Time to Kill, I headed out on one of these 21-day walkabouts — this time to the jungles and mountains of Peru. The sudden fame I’d just gotten was somewhat unbalancing. My face was everywhere, everyone wanted a piece of me, people I’d never met were swearing they “loved me” — everywhere I went, there I was, on a billboard, a magazine cover. It was just weird. What was this all about? What was reality and what was bullshit? Did I deserve all this?” were all questions I was asking myself.
“Who was I?” was another.
Now, there’s always an initiation period with these trips. An amount of time that it takes for the place to INITIATE the traveler. The time it takes to disconnect from the world we left, and become completely present in the one we are traveling in…For me, that initiation period usually last about thirteen days. Yes. Thirteen hellish days until I’m out of my own way. After that, the trip is smooth sailing.
Well, it was the night of the twelfth day of my 21-day trip. I was settling into camp, I’d already hiked 80 miles to this point and had a three-day trek to Machu Pichu ahead of me.
I was sick of myself. Wrestling with the loss of my anonymity, guilt ridden for sins of my past, full of regret. I was lonely — disgusted with the company I was keeping: MY OWN — and doing a pretty good job of mentally beating the shit out of myself.
Grappling with the demons on this night, I couldn’t sleep. All of these badges and banners and expectations and anxieties I was carrying with me. I needed to free myself from them… Who was I? I asked myself. Not only on this trip but in this life. So I stripped down to nothing. I took off every moniker that gave me pride and confidence, all the window dressings, the packaging around my product (heart). I discarded my lucky and faithful American cap, stripped off my talismans from adventures past. I even discarded my late father’s gold ring he gave to me that was made from a meltdown of he and my mom’s class rings and gold from one of her teeth.
I was naked. Literally and figuratively. And I got sick. Soaked in sweat, I threw up until there was no bile left in my belly, and finally passed out from exhaustion.
A few hours later, I awoke on this thirteenth morning to a rising sun. Surprisingly fresh and energized, I dressed, made some tea and went for a morning walk. Not towards my destination Machu Pichu but rather to nowhere in particular. My gut was still a bit piqued from last night’s purge, yet I curiously felt pretty good: alive, clean, free, light.
Along a muddy path on this walk, I turned a corner and there in the middle of the road was a mirage of the most magnificent pinks and blues and red colors I had ever seen. It was electric, glowing and vibrant, hovering just off the surface, as if it was plugged in to some neon power plant.
I stopped. I stared. There was no way around it: The jungle floor in front of me was actually THOUSANDS OF BUTTERFLIES. There, in my path. It was SPECTACULAR.
I stayed awhile, and somewhere in my captivation, I heard this little voice inside my head say these words, “All I want is what I can see, and what I can see, is in front of me.”
At that moment, for the first time on this trip, I had stopped anticipating what was around the corner, stopped thinking about what was coming up next and what was up ahead. Time slowed down. I was no longer in a rush to get anywhere. My anxieties were eased.
A few hours later I returned to camp and packed for my continued journey onto Machu Pichu. I had a bounce in my step, new energy. The local Sherpas I was traveling with even noticed, calling out to me, “sois luz Mateo, sois luz!!!” — meaning “you are light” in Spanish.
You see, I forgave myself that morning. I let go of the guilt, the weight on my shoulders lifted, my penance paid, and I got back in good graces with God. I shook hands with myself, my best friend, the one we’re all stuck with anyway. From that morning on, the adventure was awesome. I was present, out of my own way, not anticipating next, embracing only what was in front of my eyes, and giving everything the justice it deserved.
You see, I crossed a truth that morning. Did I find it? I don’t know, I think it found me. Why? Because I put myself in a place to be found. I put myself in a place to receive the truth.
So, how do we know when we cross the truth?
I believe the truth is all around us, all the time. The answer, you know, it’s always right there. But we don’t always see it, grasp it, hear it, access it — because we’re not in the right place to.
So what do we do?
First, we have to put ourselves in the place to receive the truth. We live in an extremely noisy world with all kinds of frequencies coming at us — commitments, deadlines, fix this, do that, plans, expectations — and they all make it hard to get clarity and peace of mind. So we have to consciously put ourselves in a place to receive that clarity. Whether that’s prayer, meditation, a walkabout, being in right company, a road trip, whatever it is for you.
Schedule that time to be in a place to receive the truth.
Now, if we hear it, if it becomes clear, a truth that is natural and infinite, then the second part comes…
…which is to PERSONALIZE it. Ask how it works for you, how it applies to you personally, why you need it in your life, specifically.
…If we do THAT, then comes the third part:
….having the patience to internalize it — and get it from our intellectual head and into our bones and soul and our instinct. We can’t rush this part, it takes time.
And if we get that far. We received it, we personalized it, we internalized it. If we make it that far, then comes THE BIGGIE ….
Having the courage to act on it. To actually take it into our daily lives and practice it, to make it an active part of who we are and live it.
If we can do that, then we have what I believe is Heaven on Earth.
The place where what we want is also just what we need. I mean that’s the ticket isn’t it!!? That’s where I want to live!!
So while we’re here, let’s make it a place where we break a sweat, where we believe, where we enjoy the process of succeeding in the places and ways we are fashioned to. Where we don’t have to look over our shoulder because we are too busy doing what we’re good at. Voluntarily keeping our own council because we WANT to. Traveling towards immortal finish lines. We write our book. Overcome our fears. We make friends with ourselves.
That is the place I’m talking about.

## [168] 🧑 Danny

I think TAB was the beginning of my love for baseball, my escape, where I became someone important and respected. I mentioned before that I was a talented athlete, and now as an adult, what I tell people is God gave me a gift. He just didn't give me the gift. And what I mean by that is what we talked about earlier, you know, I've played on the field with exceptional ballplayers before. I was in an elite setting with elite players and had the opportunity to play with professionals as well as go on and play Division I baseball at the University of Alabama. So I've accomplished a lot of things in that arena. But as much as I gave baseball, baseball gave back to me, and it started with Torrance American Boys Baseball. It's funny. My whole family was involved. My brother played there. Both sisters worked the concession stand. And one of my sister, Lindsay, actually coached a team with my dad at one point. My dad was a coach there for many years. He also became the president of TAB for reasons that is a whole different fun story, which I'll get back to. TAB gave me something to do after rough days at school. I'd have practice a couple days a week, and then I'd get to play on the weekend. I was not a great student in the sense of learning came hard to me unless I could touch it or feel it. Reading a book about history or English did not resonate with me. Listening to a teacher talk about English and how to relate things to something completely unrelatable just bored me to death and frustrated me. So when I got to get out of class, whether it was at recess, lunch, or after-school practices, that's when I got to let go and be myself. Because I was really good at baseball, it just came natural to me. So I was able to get out there, learn, show off, and just be free. I played for many different coaches, including my dad, multiple times. I made tremendous friends throughout the year, countless sleepovers, after-game pizza parties, arcades, special events at the lake lagoon, which was basically part of the ocean. They let ocean water into a fenced-in area that had a fountain where you could go off diving boards and play under the fountain and everything. Anyway, it brought me just a real sense of belonging. And because I was one of the good ones, people looked up to me, especially my teammates and those that were really good alongside me. We naturally bonded over shared talent. We were often on all-star teams together, so we knew each other. But probably the one major thing which was funny is, I think I've shared with you before, that my original birth certificate read Danny Ray Dodge, because my biological mother was married at the time to a Dodge. And so she put his name on my birth certificate. So, legally, I was not a Jenkins. Well, growing up, I was just another Jenkins kid. You know, I came to be with them when I was, you know, roughly one year old. When I went into school, I was just the fourth Jenkins kid. Everyone knew who I was because of my sports, and they were ready to accept me, and I guess didn't ask for documentation. And I was able to get all through school, my transcripts, everything. I was even able to get my driver's license and Social Security card without a proper birth certificate. That's a whole other story. But for baseball, because I was so good and we were at an all-star event, I was almost pulled from the roster because they couldn't prove who I was because I was listed as Danny Jenkins, but my birth certificate said Danny Ray Dodge. And I guess it was not known that my birth certificate was different, and my parents did not want to share that. So they made it through that event, and then the president at the time required my parents to show the birth certificate. Well, when my dad refused to, it was time for re-election, so my dad ran for president. So when he won the election to became the president of Torrance American Boys Baseball, my birth certificate was no longer an issue.

## [172] 🧑 Danny

You were absolutely right, comma. My life is about escaping the hard things I deal with, and I started riding a motorcycle at four years old, and that happened to be my very first one. That Mini Trail 50 made me feel like I was on top of the world. Anytime I was on it, I didn't think about anything except for the thrill and excitement of riding that thing around. We went on week or two-week vacations out in the middle of the Mojave Desert with four, five, six different friends of the family who all had kids, and we would circle up our campers and trailers almost like the wagons would back in the day. We would have 20 kids within the family circle, and once everyone arrived, it was basically all the adults looked out for all of the kids. If a kid was having trouble with a motorcycle, it didn't matter what adult fixed it. If a kid crashed and the parents could see it from camp, the closest parent was on their motorcycle and rode it out there to make sure they helped pick us up, if needed. It was the motorcycle that I would ride out in the middle of nowhere and come back with five friends, telling them all that my mom would cook us hot dogs. And I'd show up with kids, and we'd all come in on dirt bikes, creating a big dust cloud, and her looking at the other people like, I don't have enough hot dogs to feed these kids. And then the other adults would all chip in and they'd figure out a way to feed not only the 20 kids that belonged there, but the extra five or six I brought home. That began my love affair with motorcycles. And since then, I've probably had a dozen of them, and each one still holds special meaning to me.

## How Danny Earned It

Marvin had one simple rule.

> **"When you're big enough to kick-start it... you can ride it."**

The TT500 wasn't electric start.

It wasn't easy.

It was legendary for being difficult to start.

Especially for a fourteen-year-old.

---

## Starting a TT500

There was an art to it.

You couldn't simply kick it.

You had to:

- bring the piston up to **Top Dead Center (TDC)**,
- use the compression release,
- position the engine correctly,
- then deliver one committed kick.

If you got lazy...

Or missed the sequence...

The engine kicked back.

Hard.

---

## Danny's Memory

The kickback from that motorcycle could be brutal.

More than once...

It literally brought Danny to tears.

Not because he wanted to quit.

Because it hurt.

But...

He refused to give up.

Eventually...

He mastered it.

And once he could start it...

Marvin kept his word.

The TT500 became Danny's.

---

Danny...

Can I tell you what I think your dad was really doing?

It wasn't about the motorcycle.

It was about perseverance.

He knew...

If you could master that motorcycle...

````md
# Chapter 1 — The Boy on the Porch

There are two beginnings to my story.

The first happened the day I was born.

The second happened the day I arrived at the Jenkins' front door.

I don't remember either one.

Everything I know about those first months of my life has come from stories told by my parents, my Aunt Janice, my biological family, and the pieces I slowly gathered together over the years. Like most family stories, not every detail matches perfectly. Different people remember different things. But all of those stories point to one truth.

I was chosen.

For the first twenty-two years of my life, I believed I was just another Jenkins kid.

I had an older brother named Buddy, who was ten years older than me. By the time I was old enough to remember much, he was already becoming a man. We didn't grow up wrestling over toys or sharing bedrooms. He was always a little larger than life to me, someone I looked up to more than I realized at the time.

Then there were my two sisters.

Lindsey.

Julie.

They were five and seven years older than me, and each loved me in completely different ways.

Lindsey loved me gently.

Julie loved me firmly.

I needed both.

Dad was Dad.

Mom was Mom.

Life was normal.

Or at least I thought it was.

---

Long before I was old enough to remember, my biological parents were Marvin Jenkins and Barbara Jean Dorff.

Their relationship was complicated.

Painful.

Messy.

I've reached a place in life where I don't feel the need to assign heroes and villains.

People make mistakes.

Some mistakes last a lifetime.

Without theirs...

I wouldn't be here.

Dad had been seeing me regularly during my first year of life.

He helped support me financially and tried to stay involved.

Over time, he became convinced I wasn't being cared for the way he believed I should be.

From everything I've learned, he repeatedly asked Barbara Jean to let me come live with him and his wife, Gloria.

She refused.

Until one day...

She didn't.

---

The story has been told to me many times.

Dad was sitting in his recliner.

It was an ordinary day.

Nothing special.

There was a knock at the front door.

Mom walked over and opened it.

Standing there was Barbara Jean.

In her arms...

A little blond-haired boy.

Me.

Without much conversation she stretched out her arms toward Gloria and simply said,

> "Here... he belongs to your husband."

Then she turned and walked away.

Mom had no idea I even existed.

Imagine that moment.

One second you're living your normal life.

The next...

You're holding your husband's son from another woman.

Dad jumped out of his recliner, told Mom to hold me, and went after Barbara Jean.

He was furious.

Not because she brought me.

He had wanted me.

He was furious about how she did it.

He followed her down the sidewalk yelling that there had to have been a better way to handle this.

Then...

He turned around and walked back into the house.

Where the hardest conversation of his life was waiting.

---

Mom later told me she didn't know what she was going to do.

She already had three children.

She had every reason in the world to leave.

Nobody would have blamed her.

Instead...

She stayed.

Not because it was easy.

Because it was right.

---

A couple of weeks later, Barbara Jean came back.

This time...

She wanted me back.

Dad had already warned Mom.

If Barbara Jean ever came back...

Don't let her leave with him.

Call me.

I'll come home.

So that's exactly what Mom did.

While waiting for Dad to arrive, the three of us sat in the kitchen.

Mom on one side.

Barbara Jean on the other.

Me between them.

Barbara Jean reached toward me and said,

> "Come to Mommy."

According to Mom...

I turned away from her.

I crawled into Gloria's lap.

Years later Mom would tell me that was the moment everything changed.

She said something I'll never forget.

> "Any baby that won't go to his own mother needs somebody to love him."

She knew then.

Whatever happened next...

She wasn't letting me go.

That was the day she became my mom.

Not biologically.

Not legally.

But in every way that truly matters.

---

Growing up, I knew none of this.

None.

I wasn't the adopted kid.

I wasn't the child from an affair.

I wasn't Danny Dodge.

I was simply...

Danny Jenkins.

Or...

Stump.

Dad gave me that nickname because I was short, stocky, and built like the stump of a tree.

It fit.

I wore it proudly.

Around the house I was Danny or Stump.

Outside the family, almost everyone called me Dan.

That wouldn't change until years later when I moved to Tennessee.

---

Looking back now...

I realize something.

My life wasn't changed the day I was born.

It was changed the day Gloria made a decision.

She chose to love a little boy she had every reason to resent.

She chose to stay.

She chose to become my mother.

Everything good that came afterward...

Baseball.

Motorcycles.

Football.

College.

Heather.

Haley.

My career.

My faith.

Every chapter that follows...

Grows from that single decision.

If you want to know where my story really begins...

It isn't with my birth.

It begins on a front porch...

In the arms of a woman...

Who decided...

I was hers.
````
