````markdown
# Prologue

There comes a point in life when you realize memories aren't nearly as permanent as you thought they were.

For years I figured I'd always remember.

I'd remember the names.

The stories.

The little sayings that made me smile.

The people who shaped my life.

The moments that seemed far too important to ever forget.

Then one day I caught myself trying to remember the name of someone who had once meant a great deal to me.

It scared me.

Not because I forgot the name.

Because I realized that one day someone might forget mine.

That's why this book exists.

It wasn't written because I think I've lived some extraordinary life.

Matter of fact, I think my life has been pretty ordinary.

I grew up in Southern California.

I rode motorcycles.

I played baseball until it got too dark to see the ball.

I climbed trees.

I got into trouble once in a while.

I had dreams.

Some came true.

Some didn't.

I fell in love.

I married my best friend.

We raised an incredible daughter.

I went to work every day, tried to do the right thing, laughed a lot, cried more than I usually let people see, and spent most of my life trying to become a little better than I was the day before.

There's nothing particularly unusual about any of that.

What makes my life worth writing down isn't me.

It's the people.

My dad.

My mom.

My brother Buddy.

My sisters, Lindsey and Julie.

Heather.

Haley.

My grandparents.

My cousins.

My coaches.

My teammates.

My friends.

The people who walked into my life, sometimes for only a season, and somehow managed to leave fingerprints on the man I eventually became.

Some of them taught me through kindness.

Some taught me through hardship.

Some inspired me.

Some disappointed me.

A few hurt me.

Most loved me.

Every one of them changed me.

I've also learned something about photographs.

They don't tell stories.

They simply remind us that stories exist.

A photograph can show you a little blond-haired boy standing in front of a house.

It can't tell you that the tree beside him became one of his favorite places in the world.

It can't tell you that the little boy had no idea he had another family he knew nothing about.

It can't tell you about the motorcycles, the baseball fields, the coaches, the laughter, or the tears.

Photographs freeze moments.

Stories breathe life back into them.

That's why you'll see a lot of pictures throughout this book.

Not because I want to show you what happened.

Because each one reminds me of something I never want to lose.

Sometimes I look at a picture and immediately remember the story.

Sometimes I have to stare at it for several minutes before something comes back.

More often than not...

One story reminds me of another.

Then another.

Then another.

If you've ever sat around a table with me, you already know that's how I tell stories.

I'll start talking about baseball.

Somehow we'll end up talking about motorcycles.

Then my dad.

Then a wedding.

Then a dirt bike.

Then somehow we'll find our way back to baseball.

I don't always travel in a straight line.

I've learned that some of the best stories are found along the detours.

So if I wander a little...

Just stay with me.

I usually find my way home.

This book isn't about proving anything.

It's not about making anyone look like a hero.

Or a villain.

Life isn't that simple.

Neither are people.

The older I've gotten, the more I've realized that people are wonderfully complicated.

My dad wasn't perfect.

Neither was my mom.

Neither am I.

They made mistakes.

Big ones.

They also loved deeply.

Both of those things can be true at the same time.

You'll read about decisions that changed lives.

Secrets that stayed hidden for decades.

Dreams that came true.

Dreams that didn't.

You'll meet people who probably never realized the impact they had on a little boy growing up in Southern California.

Some of them have been gone for years.

I miss them.

I hope by the time you finish this book...

You'll miss them a little too.

My greatest hope isn't that you remember what I accomplished.

Honestly...

Most of that won't matter much.

Trophies collect dust.

Newspaper articles fade.

Statistics get forgotten.

What matters...

Are the people.

I want Haley to know the grandfather she already knew...

But I also want her to know the little boy I used to be.

I want my grandchildren and great-grandchildren to know Marvin, Gloria, Buddy, Lindsey, Julie, Granny, George, Jack, Jerry, Johnnie, Heather, and all the people who built this family long before they arrived.

I want them to understand that they didn't begin with me.

They're part of a much bigger story.

If this book accomplishes anything...

I hope it preserves those people.

This isn't a finished story.

It probably never will be.

Every time I open another photo album...

Another memory wakes up.

That's okay.

I'd rather leave behind too many stories than not enough.

So...

Pull up a chair.

Let's open the family photo album together.

I'll tell you what I remember.
````

````markdown
Then he follows Barbara Jean down the sidewalk.

From everything I've heard...

He wasn't angry that she brought me.

He had wanted me.

He was angry about how she did it.

He felt she had dumped this impossible situation into Gloria's lap.

Then...

He turned around...

Walked back inside...

And faced one of the hardest conversations of his life.

---

I don't know everything that was said.

I probably never will.

Some conversations belong only to the people who lived them.

What I do know is this.

Mom had a decision to make.

She already had three children.

Buddy.

Lindsey.

Julie.

She had every reason in the world to leave.

Nobody would've blamed her.

Instead...

She stayed.

---

A couple of weeks later...

Barbara Jean came back.

This time she wanted me back.

Dad had already warned Mom.

"If she comes...

Don't let her leave with him.

Call me."

So Mom did.

While waiting for Dad to get home...

The three of us sat in the kitchen.

Mom on one side.

Barbara Jean on the other.

Me between them.

Barbara Jean reached toward me.

Rolled her fingers.

Smiled.

And said,

> "Come to Mommy."

According to Mom...

I turned away.

I crawled into Gloria's lap.

Years later Mom told me that was the moment everything changed.

She said something I've never forgotten.

> "Any baby that won't go to his own mother needs somebody to love him."

That was it.

The decision was made.

Whatever happened after that...

She wasn't letting me go.

---

I didn't know any of this.

Not as a child.

Not as a teenager.

Not even after I graduated high school.

I simply knew I belonged.

Dad was Dad.

Mom was Mom.

Buddy was my brother.

Lindsey and Julie were my sisters.

Life was normal.

Looking back now...

I realize something.

The foundation of my entire life wasn't built the day I was born.

It was built the day Gloria decided...

"I'll be his mother."

Everything else...

Baseball.

Motorcycles.

Football.

Heather.

Haley.

My career.

Whole Life Journey.

Everything...

Grows out of that one decision.

If you've ever wondered where my story really begins...

It isn't in a hospital.

It begins on a front porch.

In the arms of a woman...

Who chose me...
...
Before I ever had the chance to choose her.
````

````markdown
002 - Growing Up a Jenkins.md

---
title: Growing Up a Jenkins
version: 1.0
status: Preservation Draft
---

# Chapter 2
# Growing Up a Jenkins

People ask me sometimes what my childhood was like.

Honestly...

It was good.

Really good.

That's probably not what some people expect after hearing how my life began.

But it's the truth.

I didn't spend my childhood wondering where I came from.

I spent it wondering if there was enough daylight left to play one more baseball game.

---

Our house sat at 22908 Kathryn Avenue in Torrance, California.

If you ever want to understand my childhood...

Start there.

That house wasn't fancy.

It wasn't big.

It was home.

When I think about it today...

I don't first remember the bedrooms.

Or the kitchen.

I remember the front yard.

And one tree.

That tree appears in photograph after photograph throughout my childhood.

I climbed it.

Sat in it.

Played under it.

Thought about life in it.

It became one of the constants in my world.

Funny...

A tree can do that.

---

Dad worked construction.

Hard.

Dark until dark some days.

He believed in work.

He believed boys should earn things.

Nothing was simply handed to me.

Looking back...

I'm grateful.

At the time...

Maybe not so much.

Dad wasn't the kind of father who sat you down for long speeches.

He taught through one-liners.

Challenges.

Nicknames.

Examples.

Sometimes I think I learned more from what he did than what he ever said.

---

Mom balanced all of that.

Dad pushed.

Mom comforted.

Dad challenged.

Mom encouraged.

I didn't appreciate that balance until I became an adult.

Together...

They gave me exactly what I needed.

One taught me strength.

The other taught me grace.

You need both.

---

Then there was Buddy.

My brother.

Ten years older than me.

People sometimes assume we must have grown up together.

Not really.

By the time I was forming memories...

Buddy was already becoming a man.

Our relationship was different than most brothers.

But don't mistake different for unimportant.

He was still my brother.

He still mattered.

And he always will.

---

Lindsey...

She had a gentleness about her.

She let me be me.

She listened.

She loved me without trying to change me.

Years later I'd realize how valuable that was.

Julie loved me too.

She just loved me differently.

Julie believed in accountability.

If I was being stupid...

She told me.

Immediately.

Sometimes loudly.

She wasn't trying to hurt me.

She was trying to make me better.

As a kid...

I appreciated Lindsey's style a little more.

As an adult...

I've become thankful for both.

---

Dad called me Stump.

People laugh when they hear it.

I do too.

The reason wasn't complicated.

I was short.

Stocky.

Broad shouldered.

Strong.

Dad said I looked like the stump of a tree.

So...

Stump.

That became my name around the house.

It never bothered me.

Matter of fact...

I kind of liked it.

It fit.

---

Outside...

The world called me Dan.

Teachers.

Coaches.

Friends.

Scouts.

Everybody.

When I moved south...

Somehow...

Dan disappeared.

Danny came back.

Same person.

Different geography.

Funny how that works.

---

My childhood mostly happened outdoors.

That's one of the blessings of growing up in Southern California.

You can live outside almost year-round.

And I did.

If I wasn't playing baseball...

I was riding a motorcycle.

If I wasn't riding...

I was climbing something.

Building something.

Throwing something.

Playing something.

Mom almost had to force me inside.

The outdoors wasn't where I visited.

It was where I lived.

---

Looking back...

I think childhood gave me something priceless.

Security.

I didn't know my story.

I didn't know the secrets.

I didn't know the pain adults were carrying.

I only knew...

I was loved.

Sometimes...

That's enough.
````

````markdown
003 - The Tree at Kathryn Avenue.md

---
title: The Tree at Kathryn Avenue
version: 1.0
status: Preservation Draft
---

# Chapter 3
# The Tree at Kathryn Avenue

It's funny the things you remember.

People ask me all the time if I remember this event or that event.

Sometimes I do.

Sometimes I don't.

But I can close my eyes today...

More than fifty years later...

And I can still see that tree.

It stood in the front yard of our house at 22908 Kathryn Avenue in Torrance, California.

To anyone driving by...

It was just another tree.

To me...

It was part of childhood itself.

---

I climbed it.

Hung from it.

Sat in it.

Thought in it.

If there was something bothering me...

I'd end up somewhere around that tree.

Sometimes on it.

Sometimes under it.

Sometimes just looking at it while I bounced a baseball in my glove.

Looking back...

I think every kid should have a tree.

Not because trees are magical.

Because every kid needs somewhere that feels like their own little world.

That tree was mine.

---

One of the earliest pictures I have of myself was taken in front of that house.

Every time I look at it now...

I smile.

Not because of how I looked.

Honestly...

I looked like every other little blond-haired California kid.

But because I know something that little boy didn't know.

He had already been through more than he could possibly understand.

Yet there he stood.

Smiling.

Safe.

Loved.

Home.

---

When I was little...

Home wasn't a word I thought about.

Home was simply where Mom and Dad were.

It was where Lindsey and Julie were coming and going.

Where Buddy stopped by.

Where baseball gloves were drying in the garage.

Where motorcycles were waiting for the weekend.

Where Mom called us in for dinner.

Where Dad parked the truck after another long day at work.

It never crossed my mind that home was something special.

It was just...

Home.

Funny how you don't appreciate ordinary things until years later.

---

Southern California in the 1970s was an incredible place to grow up.

People hear California today and immediately think about traffic.

Movie stars.

Crowds.

Politics.

That wasn't my childhood.

My childhood was bicycles.

Neighborhood kids.

Baseball.

Motorcycles.

Walking to school.

Playing until dark.

Parents yelling from the front porch when it was time to come home.

The world felt smaller then.

Safer.

Slower.

Maybe it really was.

Or maybe every generation thinks that about their own childhood.

---

There wasn't much that kept me inside.

Mom almost had to force me into the house.

If I had a choice...

I'd be outside.

There was always something to do.

If I wasn't climbing the tree...

I was throwing a baseball.

If I wasn't throwing a baseball...

I was riding my bike.

If I wasn't riding my bike...

I was pretending I was somewhere else.

Kids don't need expensive toys.

They need imagination.

We had plenty of that.

---

I remember laying in the grass sometimes...

Looking up through the branches.

Watching the wind move the leaves.

Thinking about...

Well...

Honestly, I don't remember what I thought about.

Probably nothing.

Kids are good at that.

Adults should try it more often.

---

Years later...

After I learned my birth story...

After I learned Gloria wasn't my biological mother...

After I learned about Barbara Jean...

I found myself looking back at that house differently.

Not with sadness.

With gratitude.

Because I realized something.

While adults were carrying secrets...

A little boy was simply being loved.

That's an incredible gift.

I didn't spend my childhood wondering where I belonged.

I belonged.

Completely.

Without question.

Without condition.

That understanding didn't come from biology.

It came from Gloria.

It came from Marvin.

It came from the family they built around me.

---

People sometimes ask me if I ever wish I'd known the truth earlier.

That's a complicated question.

Part of me says yes.

Part of me says no.

Would it have answered questions?

Absolutely.

Would it have changed my childhood?

I honestly don't think so.

Because the childhood I remember...

Was filled with love.

Not confusion.

And I'm thankful for that.

---

If someone asked me today where my childhood lives...

I probably wouldn't give them an address.

I'd tell them about a tree.

A baseball.

A little blond-haired kid.

And a house where he never once questioned whether he belonged.

That's where my childhood still lives.

Every time I close my eyes...
...I can still see that tree.
````

````markdown id="ohd6n8"
004 - Gorman, Gold, and Motorcycles.md

---
title: Gorman, Gold, and Motorcycles
version: 1.0
status: Preservation Draft
---

# Chapter 4
# Gorman, Gold, and Motorcycles

If baseball became my safe place...

Motorcycles became my freedom.

I honestly don't remember a time when motorcycles weren't part of my life.

Some kids grew up around football.

Some grew up around hunting.

I grew up around motorcycles.

---

Dad loved adventure.

Looking back now, I realize he wasn't really the kind of guy who enjoyed sitting around the house all weekend.

If there was somewhere to go...

He wanted to go.

If there was something new to learn...

He wanted to learn it.

If there was a machine involved...

Even better.

That's probably where I got it.

---

Some of my favorite weekends started the night before.

Dad would begin loading the truck.

It was usually his Ford F-150 with the camper already mounted on the bed.

Behind it sat a box trailer.

Sometimes it was loaded with dirt bikes.

Sometimes it held the gold dredging equipment.

Sometimes...

It held both.

I can still picture him walking around the truck making sure everything was tied down.

Fuel.

Tools.

Helmets.

Food.

Sleeping bags.

He'd check everything twice.

Meanwhile...

I was about as excited as a little boy could be.

Sleep didn't come easy the night before one of those trips.

I knew adventure was waiting in the morning.

---

We usually headed to Gorman, California.

Today it's a much more regulated riding area.

Back then...

It felt like freedom.

There weren't fences everywhere.

You didn't have designated riding zones every hundred yards.

You just rode.

Miles and miles of hills, dirt, trails, rocks, washes, and open country.

To a little kid...

It might as well have been another planet.

---

The best part wasn't even the motorcycles.

It was the people.

There were usually several families camping together.

Everybody parked their campers in a big circle.

Almost like pioneers circling wagons.

Looking back...

There were probably twenty or thirty kids running around.

Maybe more.

Nobody worried much.

The adults looked after everybody's children.

If one of us wrecked...

The closest dad was already helping.

If a motorcycle quit running...

Whichever dad happened to know engines started fixing it.

That's just how it worked.

Nobody asked,

"Whose kid is this?"

They were all our kids for the weekend.

I wish more of the world still worked that way.

---

My very first motorcycle was a Honda Mini Trail 50.

I was four years old.

Think about that for a minute.

Four.

Today people hear that and think my parents were crazy.

Back then...

It wasn't unusual where we lived.

Dad taught me.

Patiently.

I don't remember the first ride.

I don't remember falling.

I don't even remember learning.

It became as natural as riding a bicycle.

Except...

Much louder.

Much dirtier.

And a whole lot more fun.

---

Not long afterward I moved up to my second motorcycle.

An MR50.

I still have it today.

Matter of fact...

It's sitting in my garage as I write this.

It hasn't been started in years.

But the last time I parked it...

It still ran.

People ask me sometimes why I keep it.

Because it's not just an old motorcycle.

It's a time machine.

Every time I look at it...

I'm a little boy again.

Standing beside Dad.

Helmet in one hand.

Trying to decide where we were going to ride that day.

I wish I still had that little Mini Trail too.

But if I had to choose one to keep...

The MR50 would probably be it.

---

Dad eventually developed another hobby.

Gold dredging.

Now...

If you've never seen a gold dredge...

Picture two pontoons floating in a creek.

A gasoline engine sitting between them.

A giant suction hose.

The dredge would suck rocks, gravel, sand, and everything else off the creek bottom.

Then it would run across a sluice box.

The heavier material...

Including gold...

Would stay behind.

Everything else washed away.

At the end of the day...

We'd collect the black sand.

Then we'd use a gold pan.

Slowly washing the sand away until tiny flakes of gold appeared.

To a little boy...

That was unbelievable.

We were finding treasure.

Real treasure.

---

I had my own shovel.

People laugh now when they see the pictures.

They think the shovel had a short handle.

It did.

Because I was that little.

Dad made sure I could help.

Maybe I wasn't moving much dirt.

But I was part of the crew.

That mattered to me.

Dad always had a way of making me feel included.

---

One of my favorite memories came years later.

I took my gold pan to school.

The teacher wanted everyone to give a presentation.

Normally...

That would've terrified me.

Book reports weren't exactly my thing.

Talking about history I had memorized?

Not good.

Talking about something I had actually lived?

Different story.

I stood in front of my class explaining how the dredge worked.

How black sand collected.

Why gold stayed behind.

I wasn't nervous.

I didn't have to remember anything.

I was simply telling my story.

That was one of the first times I realized speaking becomes easy when you truly know what you're talking about.

I've carried that lesson my entire life.

---

Years later...

Long after Dad was gone...

That gold came full circle.

When Haley got married...

I wanted to give her something that represented Papa.

Not something expensive.

Something meaningful.

I had a bracelet made.

It included a beautiful rose.

Then I took some of Dad's gold...

Real gold that he had recovered himself...

Had it melted down...

And formed into a bead that became the center of that rose.

To most people...

It was just a bracelet.

To us...

It was Papa.

Still protecting his granddaughter on her wedding day.

I don't know that I've ever given a gift that meant more to me.

---

Looking back...

Gorman wasn't really about gold.

It wasn't really about motorcycles.

It wasn't even about camping.

It was about Dad.

Those weekends gave us something that money couldn't buy.

Time together.

Adventure.

Stories.

Memories.

I don't remember how much gold we found.

I don't remember how many miles we rode.

I remember laughing.

I remember dusty boots.

Campfires.

The smell of gasoline.

The sound of motorcycles echoing through the hills.

I remember looking over at Dad and thinking...

Life doesn't get much better than this.

You know...

Looking back...

I think I was right.
````

````markdown id="v9zj2m"
# Chapter 5
# TABB — Where I Found Belonging

People often ask me what made me love baseball so much.

The easy answer is...

I was good at it.

The real answer is...

It was the first place outside my family where I truly felt like I belonged.

---

I was seven years old when I first put on a TABB uniform.

TABB stood for Torrance American Boys Baseball.

To most people around Torrance, it was just Little League.

To me...

It became a second home.

Funny thing is...

I don't think I realized it at the time.

Kids rarely appreciate things while they're happening.

They just live them.

---

My very first team wore Reds uniforms.

I don't remember choosing the Reds.

I think that's simply where they put me.

I played shortstop.

I pitched.

At seven years old, I had no idea what those positions meant.

I just knew I liked throwing the ball.

Years later...

After coaching and watching baseball for many years...

I realized something.

Coaches usually put their best athlete at shortstop.

And if he wasn't playing shortstop...

He was usually pitching.

Nobody ever told me that.

I figured it out decades later.

Apparently...

Somebody saw something in me before I did.

---

The first picture from TABB makes me smile every time I see it.

I'm standing out in the parking lot.

Little uniform.

Stirrups.

Old baseball cleats.

If you've ever seen baseball pictures from the late seventies and early eighties...

You know exactly what I'm talking about.

The uniforms were different.

The socks.

The belts.

Everything.

Even the trees behind me tell a story.

They're eucalyptus trees.

You could smell them before you ever reached the ballpark.

To this day...

That smell instantly takes me back to TABB.

Isn't it funny how smells work?

You can forget a hundred details...

But one smell...

And suddenly you're seven years old again.

---

Baseball quickly became much bigger than just me.

It became part of our family.

Dad coached.

Then coached some more.

Eventually...

He became president of the entire league.

Lindsey coached for a season.

Julie and Lindsey both worked in the concession stand.

If I wasn't playing...

Somebody in my family was doing something.

Looking back...

TABB wasn't just my baseball league.

It was part of our family culture.

---

One thing I loved about TABB was what happened after the games.

The game itself only lasted a couple of hours.

The rest of the day belonged to us.

Pizza.

Arcades.

Sleepovers.

Trading baseball cards.

Running around the complex.

Talking about the game we had just played.

Then...

Talking about the game we were going to play tomorrow.

Baseball never really ended.

It just paused long enough for us to eat.

---

I think baseball became my safe place because it was the first place where I felt respected for something I naturally understood.

School wasn't easy for me.

I wasn't dumb.

Far from it.

I simply learned differently.

Reading a chapter out of a textbook...

Not my thing.

Standing on a baseball field...

Everything made sense.

I could see the whole game unfolding.

Where the next play was going.

What the batter was trying to do.

Where I needed to be.

Nobody had to explain it.

I could just...

See it.

That's a gift.

I didn't know it then.

I do now.

---

As the years went on...

Baseball slowly became part of my identity.

People knew me as the baseball kid.

The coaches expected me to make plays.

Teammates counted on me.

I liked that.

Not because I wanted attention.

Because I wanted responsibility.

I've realized something about myself over the years.

I like carrying responsibility.

Always have.

Put me at shortstop.

Give me the ball.

Let me figure it out.

That pattern has followed me my entire life.

Football.

Work.

Leadership.

Whole Life Journey.

It's all the same wiring.

---

One year something happened that confused me.

There were questions about whether I was eligible to play All-Stars.

It had something to do with my birth certificate.

I didn't understand any of it.

Remember...

I still thought I was simply Danny Jenkins.

I had no idea my legal birth certificate said something completely different.

Dad fought it.

Hard.

At the time...

I thought he was just being Dad.

Years later...

After learning my story...

Everything made sense.

He wasn't fighting over paperwork.

He was fighting for his son.

There's a difference.

One I'll never forget.

---

My second year at TABB was different.

The game had slowed down.

I wasn't thinking as much anymore.

I was reacting.

I started believing...

"I think I'm pretty good at this."

Not in an arrogant way.

More like...

"This feels natural."

There's a big difference.

I wasn't trying to become someone else.

I was discovering who I already was.

---

One of my favorite memories came when I made the All-Star team.

The funny part is...

I was the last one to know.

Dad was already involved in the league.

Mom knew.

My sisters knew.

Everybody knew.

Except me.

They kept it a secret.

For once...

Keeping a secret from me turned out to be a good thing.

When I finally found out...

I remember putting that uniform on.

I can't really explain it.

It wasn't just another jersey.

It meant something.

Somebody believed I belonged with the best players in the league.

I walked a little taller that day.

If you look at the picture...

You can see it on my face.

That's not pride.

That's gratitude.

---

Years later...

People would ask me where my confidence came from.

I honestly think...

It started at TABB.

Not because people constantly praised me.

Because they trusted me.

There's a difference.

Trust builds confidence.

Praise fades.

Responsibility stays with you.

TABB trusted me.

Dad trusted me.

My coaches trusted me.

Eventually...

I learned to trust myself.

Everything that came afterward...

High school.

The draft.

Alabama.

Professional baseball opportunities.

They all started on those dusty little fields in Torrance.

Whenever someone asks me where my baseball career began...

I never say...

"The San Francisco Giants."

Or...

"The University of Alabama."

It began with a little boy...

Standing in a parking lot...

Wearing a Reds uniform...

Completely unaware...

That baseball had just become one of the greatest gifts God would ever give him.
````

````markdown id="aq3mfw"
---
title: Mom Leaves
version: 1.0

---

# Chapter 6
# Mom Leaves

Every childhood has a chapter where things change.

This was mine.

I was fourteen years old.

Old enough to think I understood the world.

Too young to realize I understood almost nothing.

Looking back now, I probably couldn't have picked a worse age for what happened next.

---

My parents fought.

Not every day.

Not every week.

But enough that I knew something wasn't right.

As kids, we don't usually know why adults fight.

We just know they do.

You hear voices.

Doors close a little harder than normal.

Silence lasts longer.

You learn to stay out of the way.

That's about all you know.

---

One night...

I remember hearing them arguing.

I wasn't trying to listen.

It's just hard not to when your parents are raising their voices.

Then I heard Dad say something I'll never forget.

> "If you leave... you're not taking Danny."

There was a pause.

Then Mom quietly answered.

> "I know."

That was it.

Two words.

"I know."

At fourteen years old...

Those two words absolutely crushed me.

---

What do you mean...

"I know?"

You're not even going to argue?

You're not going to fight for me?

Don't you want me?

Did I do something wrong?

Why wouldn't my own mother want to take me?

Those questions lived inside me for years.

Years.

Keep in mind...

I had absolutely no idea Gloria wasn't my biological mother.

None.

As far as I knew...

She was Mom.

Always had been.

Always would be.

So when she simply said...

"I know."

I interpreted that through the mind of a fourteen-year-old boy.

A fourteen-year-old boy who suddenly believed...

Maybe Mom didn't really want him.

---

Looking back now...

I understand something.

She wasn't saying she didn't want me.

She was saying she couldn't.

There's a world of difference between those two statements.

But I wouldn't understand that until I was twenty-two.

Eight years is a long time to carry the wrong story in your heart.

---

The divorce happened.

Dad stayed in the house.

I stayed with Dad.

Mom moved out.

Just like that...

Life changed.

People sometimes ask what that was like.

Honestly...

It's blurry.

Not because it wasn't important.

Because I think my mind protected me.

Trauma has a funny way of doing that.

Certain moments become crystal clear.

Everything else fades into fog.

---

One thing never changed.

Mom stayed Mom.

Even though I was hurt.

Even though I didn't understand.

Even though part of me questioned why she hadn't fought harder...

I still loved her.

She still loved me.

We just carried around a misunderstanding neither one of us could explain.

She couldn't tell me the truth.

Dad hadn't told me the truth.

So we both lived with the consequences of a secret neither of us created.

---

Looking back now...

That may be one of the saddest parts of my story.

Not the divorce.

The silence.

Because silence allows people to write their own stories.

Mine happened to be wrong.

For eight years...

I believed my mother had chosen not to fight for me.

In reality...

She had already fought for me once.

Years before.

When she decided to become my mother.

I simply didn't know it.

---

Those years changed our relationship.

We weren't as close.

Not because she stopped loving me.

Because I was carrying hurt she couldn't explain away.

It's amazing how one misunderstanding can quietly reshape a relationship.

I don't blame either one of us.

She was protecting a promise.

I was trying to make sense of something no fourteen-year-old could have understood.

---

Years later...

When Dad finally told me the truth...

Everything changed.

Not overnight.

But it changed.

I finally understood why Mom had answered...

"I know."

She wasn't giving me away.

She never had me to give.

Legally...

Biologically...

She couldn't fight that battle.

Emotionally...

She had already won it years earlier.

She had become my mother the day she chose to stay.

Nothing could ever change that.

Not biology.

Not divorce.

Not secrets.

Not time.

---

If I could go back...

If I could sit beside that fourteen-year-old boy...

I'd put my arm around him and tell him something.

Your mom loves you.

More than you can imagine.

Don't let two words convince you otherwise.

One day...

You'll understand.

One day...

Those two words won't hurt anymore.

They'll simply become another chapter in a much bigger story.

A story that ends with gratitude instead of bitterness.

I'm thankful for that.

Because carrying bitterness for the rest of my life would have been a terrible burden.

Instead...

God gave me understanding.

And with understanding...

Came forgiveness.

Not because anyone asked me to forgive.

Because once I finally knew the whole story...

There really wasn't anything left to forgive.
````

````markdown id="yv1w6q"
# Chapter 7
# Baseball Was My Safe Place

If I had to pick one place where I felt completely at home growing up...

It would have been a baseball field.

Not my bedroom.

Not school.

Not the neighborhood.

A baseball field.

I don't know exactly why.

Maybe God simply wired me that way.

Maybe it was because everything on a baseball field made sense to me.

Whatever the reason...

That's where I felt the most like myself.

---

School and I had an interesting relationship.

I wasn't dumb.

Matter of fact, I think I was pretty intelligent.

I just didn't learn the way school expected me to learn.

Give me a textbook...

I'd struggle.

Stand me in front of a chalkboard...

You'd probably lose me.

Put me on a baseball field...

Everything slowed down.

Everything became clear.

It wasn't something I had to think about.

I could just...

See it.

---

People sometimes ask what I mean by that.

Here's the best way I know how to explain it.

Most people watched baseball.

I watched patterns.

I watched feet.

I watched shoulders.

I watched where a hitter's hands started.

I watched pitchers.

I watched coaches.

Without realizing it...

I was constantly collecting information.

Then...

When the ball was hit...

I already knew where I needed to be.

It wasn't magic.

It wasn't luck.

It was just how my brain worked.

---

One of the greatest compliments I ever received wasn't something anyone actually said.

It was where coaches put me.

Shortstop.

Pitcher.

Those are positions coaches don't usually hand to average players.

I didn't appreciate that as a kid.

I just thought...

"This is where they told me to play."

Years later...

Looking back...

I realized they trusted me.

That meant something.

---

As I got older...

Baseball became much more than recreation.

It became identity.

The baseball field became the place where I wasn't wondering if I fit in.

I fit in.

The coaches believed in me.

My teammates counted on me.

People expected me to make the play.

Oddly enough...

I liked that pressure.

I've always liked responsibility.

Give me the ball.

Trust me.

Let me figure it out.

That's still who I am today.

Only now the baseball has become payroll systems, HRIS projects, and Whole Life Journey.

The wiring never really changed.

The playing field did.

---

One thing I loved about baseball...

Nobody cared what happened in math class.

Nobody cared if you had a rough day at school.

Nobody cared about yesterday.

The game started over every afternoon.

Every ground ball.

Every pitch.

Every at-bat.

Every inning.

You earned respect all over again.

I liked that.

Life should work that way.

---

I also loved practicing.

Some kids loved games.

I loved both.

I'd hit baseballs until it got dark.

Throw against a wall.

Field ground balls.

Practice my swing.

I wasn't practicing because Dad made me.

He usually didn't have to.

I practiced because I wanted to be better tomorrow than I was today.

That mindset has followed me my entire life.

---

People have asked me before if I ever got burned out.

Honestly...

No.

Not as a kid.

Baseball wasn't work.

It was freedom.

If Mom asked,

"What do you want to do today?"

The answer was almost always baseball.

If nobody else wanted to play...

I'd still find something to do.

Throw against a wall.

Hit wiffle balls.

Anything.

I just loved the game.

---

One thing I've realized over the years...

Baseball gave me confidence before I knew I needed confidence.

As a little boy...

You don't wake up thinking,

"I need self-esteem."

You just know how people make you feel.

Baseball made me feel capable.

Useful.

Trusted.

Important.

Looking back...

Those feelings carried into every other area of my life.

---

It also gave me dreams.

Real dreams.

Not fantasies.

Dreams.

When I was young...

Playing professional baseball wasn't impossible.

It was simply the next step.

I never assumed I'd make it.

But I believed I could.

There's a difference.

Confidence isn't believing you'll always succeed.

Confidence is believing you belong on the field.

I believed I belonged.

---

As I got older...

The game kept opening doors.

Better teams.

Better competition.

Better coaches.

More opportunities.

Every year seemed to bring another challenge.

I loved that.

I never wanted the easy road.

I wanted to know...

How good can I become?

That question drove me for years.

It probably still does.

---

Looking back now...

People sometimes tell me,

"You were gifted."

I agree.

God gave me a tremendous gift.

But here's something else I believe just as strongly.

Talent is only the invitation.

Work is what determines how far that invitation takes you.

I practiced because I loved practicing.

I competed because I loved competing.

The trophies were nice.

The recognition was nice.

None of that kept me coming back.

The game did.

I simply loved the game.

---

Years later...

When baseball eventually ended...

People assumed I lost something.

I don't think I did.

Because baseball had already given me everything it was supposed to give me.

Confidence.

Discipline.

Friendships.

Dreams.

Work ethic.

Perspective.

Some of the greatest people I've ever known.

That's a pretty good return on investment for one little league registration fee.

When I think back on baseball today...

I don't first remember home runs.

Or championships.

Or newspaper articles.

I remember how I felt.

I remember walking onto a field...

Feeling completely at peace.

Like I had arrived exactly where I was supposed to be.

That's why I still say...

Baseball was my safe place.

Not because life couldn't hurt me there.

Because that's where I first discovered who God created me to be.
````

````markdown id="pw3xkt"
# Chapter 8
# The Gift

One of the questions I've been asked over the years is,

"Were you always good at sports?"

The short answer is...

Yes.

The longer answer is a little more complicated.

I believe God gave me a gift.

Not because I was special.

Not because I deserved it.

Simply because that's the way He made me.

The interesting part is...

It took me years to understand exactly what that gift was.

---

When people watched me play, they usually noticed the obvious things.

The strong arm.

The quick reactions.

The ability to hit a baseball.

The quarterback making plays.

The guy diving for balls other people couldn't reach.

Those things were real.

But they weren't the gift.

The gift was seeing the game before it happened.

I don't know how else to explain it.

I could anticipate.

I could react.

I could process what was happening around me almost without thinking.

Whether it was baseball...

Football...

Basketball...

Or years later...

Even pickleball...

The games slowed down for me.

That wasn't something I learned.

It was something God wired into me.

---

That doesn't mean I didn't work.

Actually...

I worked incredibly hard.

Sometimes people see talent and assume everything came easy.

Nothing could be further from the truth.

I practiced because I loved practicing.

I stayed after everyone else went home.

I worked because getting better excited me.

I wasn't chasing trophies.

I was chasing improvement.

There's a difference.

---

One thing that always makes me smile happened during elementary school.

My cousins, Chris and Jon Aycock, came over quite a bit.

We'd head over to Seaside Elementary to play basketball.

Now...

Chris and Jon were both older than me.

Taller than me.

Great athletes.

You'd think they'd beat me pretty easily.

Sometimes they did.

But a lot of times...

I held my own.

Looking back, I understand why.

I wasn't jumping higher.

I wasn't faster.

I just seemed to know where the ball was going before everybody else did.

I'd get rebounds.

Steals.

Loose balls.

Not because I was lucky.

Because I anticipated.

Again...

That's the gift.

---

As I got older...

Something else happened.

Confidence.

Now let me explain that because confidence and arrogance get confused all the time.

Growing up...

People often called me cocky.

I'd usually smile and correct them.

"No...

Confident."

They'd laugh.

"No...

Cocky."

Looking back...

Maybe they weren't completely wrong.

I knew I was good.

Everybody around me knew I was good.

That's not arrogance.

That's simply recognizing reality.

The difference...

At least I hope...

Was how I treated people.

I never believed talent made me better than anyone else.

Matter of fact...

The kids I was usually drawn toward were the ones other people picked on.

The outsiders.

The awkward kids.

The ones who didn't quite fit.

I never liked arrogance.

Confidence?

Absolutely.

Arrogance?

Not so much.

---

If we became close friends...

That was different.

Then all bets were off.

My closest friends and I gave each other grief constantly.

We teased.

Made fun of each other.

Pushed each other's buttons.

That's just how we communicated.

If someone overheard us...

They probably would've thought we hated each other.

Nothing could've been further from the truth.

That's how we showed friendship.

Context matters.

Always.

---

The older I got...

The more talented the people around me became.

High school.

Summer ball.

Semi-pro.

Alabama.

That's where perspective starts changing.

When you're the best player in Little League...

You think you're pretty special.

Then you get to high school.

Everybody was the best player somewhere.

Then you get to college.

Everybody was the best player somewhere.

The higher you climb...

The more talent surrounds you.

It's incredibly humbling.

---

One of the greatest gifts baseball ever gave me wasn't success.

It was perspective.

I got to stand beside people whose ceilings were different than mine.

Take Johnnie Morton.

Johnnie worked incredibly hard.

People see the NFL career and assume he was simply gifted.

He was.

But they don't see the Saturday mornings.

The workouts.

The extra work.

The hours nobody watched.

That's what I remember.

Not Sundays.

Saturdays.

The work.

God gave Johnnie a once-in-a-generation gift.

He also honored it.

Both things are true.

---

I've often described it this way.

God gave me a gift.

He just didn't give me "the" gift.

That's not false humility.

That's perspective.

I stood beside athletes who truly had limitless ceilings.

I didn't.

Mine was exceptionally high.

Higher than most.

Just not all the way.

And you know what?

I'm perfectly okay with that.

For many years...

Playing Major League Baseball was my dream.

It became real enough that the San Francisco Giants drafted me out of high school.

We'll get to that story later.

For a long time...

I wondered,

"What if?"

Today...

I don't.

Because here's what I've learned.

Dreams change.

Purpose doesn't.

If I'd made the Major Leagues...

Would I have met Heather?

Would Haley exist?

Would I have built the career I eventually loved?

Would Whole Life Journey exist?

I don't know.

Neither does anyone else.

All I know is...

I love the life God gave me.

I wouldn't trade Heather.

I wouldn't trade Haley.

I wouldn't trade my friends.

I wouldn't trade the people who built my life.

Not even for a Major League career.

Twenty-year-old Danny probably couldn't have said that.

Fifty-five-year-old Danny absolutely can.

---

Looking back...

The gift God gave me wasn't really sports.

Sports were simply where the gift first became visible.

The real gift...

Was the ability to see.

To anticipate.

To lead.

To compete.

To keep learning.

To keep improving.

That gift eventually left the baseball field.

It followed me into leadership.

Into payroll.

Into HRIS.

Into compensation.

Into building Whole Life Journey.

Different playing field.

Same gift.

God simply changed the game.
````

````markdown id="m8c2yv"
009 - Football, Number Seven, and Friday Night Lights.md

---
title: Football, Number Seven, and Friday Night Lights
version: 1.0

# Chapter 9
# Football, Number Seven, and Friday Night Lights

If baseball was my first love...

Football was my greatest thrill.

There's just something about Friday nights.

I don't know if you can explain it to someone who has never played.

The lights.

The crowd.

The marching band.

The smell of popcorn.

The sound of shoulder pads popping during warmups.

You spend all week preparing for one game.

Then, just like that...

It's over.

Win or lose.

You start preparing for next Friday.

---

I wore number seven.

Eventually...

That number became part of my identity.

People remember me because of it.

Even years later, motorcycles would wear the number.

Race bikes.

Football.

It followed me throughout my life.

I didn't realize then how attached I'd become to it.

It just felt right.

---

I wasn't the biggest quarterback.

I wasn't the fastest quarterback.

But I understood the game.

More importantly...

I loved leading.

That surprised me.

Standing in the huddle never made me nervous.

Matter of fact...

It was one of my favorite places to be.

Those were my guys.

We had been through summer workouts together.

Hundreds of up-downs.

Wind sprints.

Coaches screaming at us.

Practices that seemed to last forever.

You build a bond doing those things.

By Friday night...

There wasn't anybody standing in that huddle I didn't trust.

---

People have asked me over the years what kind of leader I was.

Honestly...

I'm not completely sure.

I wasn't the motivational speech guy.

That wasn't me.

I wasn't the guy giving Hollywood locker room speeches.

I led differently.

I expected a lot.

From myself.

From everybody else.

If you were supposed to line up somewhere...

Line up there.

If you made a mistake...

Let's fix it.

If you made a great play...

Let's celebrate it.

I think people respected that.

I worked hard.

Really hard.

Usually one of the first guys there.

Usually one of the last to leave.

Not because I wanted coaches to notice.

Because I wanted to be better.

---

One of the people beside me almost every Friday night was Johnnie Morton.

Today...

Most people know him as the NFL receiver.

USC.

Detroit Lions.

Kansas City Chiefs.

But when I think of Johnnie...

That's not who I see.

I see the kid who showed up on Saturday mornings.

The kid who worked.

The kid who wanted to get better.

We weren't best friends.

We didn't spend every weekend together.

But we shared something special.

Mutual respect.

We both knew how hard the other worked.

People saw Friday night.

We remembered Saturday morning.

There's a difference.

---

I often say God gave me a gift.

Johnnie...

God gave him *the* gift.

I don't say that to diminish what I accomplished.

Quite the opposite.

Standing beside greatness teaches you perspective.

Johnnie worked every bit as hard as I did.

But he also possessed something rare.

His ceiling seemed limitless.

Mine was exceptionally high.

Just not all the way there.

There's no bitterness in that statement.

Only gratitude that I got to witness it firsthand.

---

One of my favorite memories wasn't actually during a game.

It was Senior Night.

Looking back...

That picture means more to me every year.

Standing there beside me...

Was my dad.

My mom.

They had already been divorced for several years.

I didn't think much about it that night.

I just knew both of them were there.

Looking back...

I realize how difficult that must have been.

They put everything aside for one evening.

Not for themselves.

For me.

That's one of the greatest gifts they ever gave me.

People sometimes ask if it felt awkward.

Honestly...

No.

It felt loved.

That's what I remember.

Love.

Support.

Pride.

Years later...

I realized that may have been the last public event they ever attended together.

If that's true...

I'm thankful it was for their son.

---

Football taught me something baseball couldn't.

Leadership.

Baseball has moments where everyone looks at you.

Football...

The entire offense looks at you every single play.

You don't have the luxury of hiding.

You either lead...

Or somebody else will.

I grew into that role.

It wasn't automatic.

The first few times I stood in the huddle...

I was probably wondering if anybody would listen.

Before long...

Nobody questioned who was in charge.

Not because I demanded it.

Because trust had been earned.

---

The funny thing is...

Looking back over my life...

I still find myself standing in huddles.

They're just different now.

Sometimes it's a payroll team.

Sometimes an HRIS department.

Sometimes it's people building Whole Life Journey.

The field changed.

The huddle didn't.

I'm still trying to help people move in the same direction.

I guess some things never really change.

---

People often ask which sport I loved more.

Baseball or football.

That's like asking which child you love more.

They're different.

Baseball gave me peace.

Football gave me electricity.

Baseball was where I escaped.

Football was where I led.

I wouldn't trade either one.

But if you've never stood under Friday night lights...

With your teammates gathered around you...

Waiting for you to call the first play...

You missed one of the greatest feelings I've ever experienced.

I can still hear it.

The crowd.

The cadence.

The snap.

For just a few seconds...

The whole world became very quiet.

Then...

Everything happened at once.

I loved every second of it.
````

````markdown id="lf4a9n"
---
title: The Draft
version: 1.0

# Chapter 10
# The Draft

Every little boy who falls in love with baseball dreams about one thing.

The Major Leagues.

You don't dream about the minor leagues.

You don't dream about instructional ball.

You don't dream about rookie ball.

You dream about walking into a Major League stadium.

Putting on that uniform.

Hearing your name announced.

That dream lived inside me for a long time.

---

As I got older...

Baseball slowly stopped being just something I loved.

It became something people noticed.

Scouts started showing up.

At first...

I didn't think much about it.

Then one scout kept coming back.

His name was Jack French.

Jack wasn't flashy.

He wasn't loud.

He was an old baseball man.

The kind of guy who had spent his life around the game.

He loved baseball.

He loved finding talent.

One night...

He found me.

---

I had a good game.

Actually...

A really good game.

If I remember correctly, I hit a double and a triple.

I also made several good plays at third base.

After the game...

Jack introduced himself.

That moment changed everything.

---

He invited me to come play with one of the San Francisco Giants' semi-professional teams in the San Fernando Valley.

To me...

That was unbelievable.

Not because I thought I had made it.

Because someone from professional baseball thought I belonged.

Think about that.

I'm still in high school.

Still worrying about homework.

Still trying to figure out girls.

And suddenly...

I'm putting on a Giants uniform.

That'll get a teenage boy's attention.

---

Playing with that team introduced me to another man who would have an enormous impact on my life.

George Genovese.

George wasn't the scout who found me.

Jack was.

George became something different.

A mentor.

A teacher.

A baseball lifer.

He saw things in hitters that most people never noticed.

He threw batting practice to me.

He worked with me.

He challenged me.

He also became famous in my mind for one particular phrase.

Whenever hitters tried to muscle everything...

George would yell,

> "Quit swinging from the ass!"

You'd hear it over and over.

He wasn't telling us not to swing hard.

He was telling us to stop trying to hit home runs.

Hit the ball hard.

Square it up.

Trust your swing.

The power will take care of itself.

I've never forgotten that.

Funny...

That advice applies to a lot more than baseball.

---

As my senior year continued...

Professional baseball slowly became real.

Not fantasy.

Real.

Scouts.

Conversations.

Meetings.

Evaluations.

People asking questions.

People timing me.

Watching me.

Taking notes.

You start realizing...

This isn't Little League anymore.

---

Then came draft day.

1989.

I still remember how surreal it all felt.

The San Francisco Giants selected me in the thirty-fifth round of the Major League Baseball Draft.

Pick number 905 overall.

I've had people over the years say,

"Only the thirty-fifth round?"

They completely miss the point.

Do you know how many high school baseball players dream about hearing their name called?

Almost all of them.

Do you know how many actually do?

Very few.

I wasn't disappointed.

I was grateful.

Somebody believed enough in me to invest a draft pick.

That's something nobody can ever take away.

---

People sometimes misunderstand what happened next.

I didn't almost get drafted.

I was drafted.

Then came the hard part.

The decision.

---

The Giants offered me a contract.

The signing bonus wasn't very much.

Around ten thousand dollars.

To an eighteen-year-old...

Ten thousand dollars sounded like a fortune.

To Dad...

It wasn't nearly enough.

Dad looked at the situation differently.

He wasn't thinking about eighteen-year-old Danny.

He was thinking about forty-year-old Danny.

He knew something I didn't.

Professional baseball is a dream.

It's also a business.

Most kids never make it.

If I signed...

My college eligibility would disappear.

If baseball didn't work out...

College would become much more difficult.

Dad wasn't trying to crush my dream.

He was trying to protect my future.

---

George believed in me.

Enough that he called the General Manager of the Giants.

The General Manager flew down to Southern California.

He watched me take batting practice.

Watched me take infield.

Stayed long enough to watch my first at-bat.

I struck out.

Not exactly the timing I would've chosen.

He left shortly afterward.

Later...

George came back with another offer.

Twenty thousand dollars.

Still not enough.

Dad had always said...

Forty thousand would probably be enough to justify giving up college.

Twenty wasn't forty.

---

Then came one of the biggest decisions of my life.

Professional baseball.

Or college.

At eighteen...

That's not an easy decision.

People have asked me over the years if Dad made the decision for me.

No.

He didn't.

He gave me advice.

Real advice.

Honest advice.

The kind only a father gives.

Then...

He let me choose.

I chose college.

I chose baseball at the University of Alabama.

Looking back...

Some people assume I've regretted that decision.

For a long time...

I wondered.

"What if?"

That's natural.

Today...

I don't.

Because I know something eighteen-year-old Danny couldn't possibly know.

If I'd signed...

Maybe I never move to Tennessee.

Maybe I never meet Heather.

Maybe Haley never exists.

Maybe Whole Life Journey never gets built.

Nobody knows.

Including me.

All I know is this.

God closed one door.

Then quietly opened another.

The older I get...

The more thankful I become for both.

---

People still ask if I wish I'd played professional baseball.

Sometimes.

Mostly because every little boy dreams about it.

But if someone asked me today...

"Would you trade your life for that dream?"

My answer is easy.

No.

Not for anything.

Because while baseball gave me incredible opportunities...

The life waiting beyond baseball gave me something even better.

It gave me my family.

And looking back...

That turned out to be the greatest draft pick of my life.
````

````markdown id="x7b2nd"
# Chapter 11
# El Camino College

People often assume that after I turned down the Giants contract, I packed my bags and headed straight to Alabama.

That's not what happened.

There was another chapter in between.

One that turned out to be incredibly important.

El Camino College.

---

When I decided not to sign with the Giants, baseball wasn't over.

Not even close.

Matter of fact, I believed it was just beginning.

College baseball gave me another opportunity to develop, mature, and hopefully become an even better player.

El Camino College, located in Gardena, California, became the next stop on that journey.

Looking back, I don't think I appreciated how important that year would become.

At the time...

I was simply trying to become good enough to earn the opportunity to play Division I baseball.

---

Walking onto that campus felt different.

High school was over.

Nobody cared what you had done there.

The draft didn't matter anymore.

Everybody on that field had been somebody in high school.

Now...

We all started over.

I liked that.

I've always liked environments where you have to earn respect all over again.

---

The speed of the game changed.

Pitchers threw harder.

Hitters punished mistakes.

Everybody was stronger.

Everybody was older.

There weren't many easy outs anymore.

You learned quickly.

Or you sat on the bench.

Fortunately...

I loved learning.

---

One thing people sometimes misunderstand about athletics is this.

The higher you go...

The less coaching becomes about mechanics.

By the time you're playing college baseball...

Everybody can throw.

Everybody can hit.

Everybody can field.

The difference becomes what happens between your ears.

How you think.

How you prepare.

How you respond after failure.

That's where the game begins separating people.

---

I had always been confident.

College tested that confidence.

Not because I suddenly wasn't good.

Because everybody around me was good too.

That can be humbling.

It should be.

---

Baseball also taught me something else during that season.

Failure follows you no matter how talented you are.

In high school...

You can get away with mistakes.

In college...

Mistakes have consequences.

You learn quickly that baseball has a way of humbling everyone.

The Hall of Famers fail.

The All-Americans fail.

The guys at the end of the bench fail.

Failure isn't the question.

The question is...

What do you do next?

---

I've often said baseball prepared me for leadership.

I think El Camino prepared me for adulthood.

Nobody cared how good I had been.

Nobody cared I had been drafted.

Nobody cared what newspaper articles had been written.

They cared what I did today.

I've tried to live my professional life the same way.

Yesterday's success doesn't buy today's respect.

You earn it again.

Every day.

---

About halfway through that season...

Life changed again.

Dad decided it was time to move home.

Home...

Meaning Tennessee.

That sounded strange to me.

Tennessee wasn't home.

California was.

I'd only been back there one time when I was seven years old.

I barely remembered it.

The smell of Aunt Linda's basement.

Playing with Jeremy.

No sidewalks.

Gardens.

Trees.

That was about it.

Now...

Dad wanted to move back permanently.

He gave me a choice.

Stay in California.

Or go with him.

---

Looking back...

That may have been one of the biggest crossroads in my life.

Stay where everything was familiar.

Or leave everything I'd ever known.

Friends.

Baseball.

California.

The ocean.

Everything.

And head to a place that barely felt familiar.

At eighteen years old...

Those decisions seem enormous.

Because they are.

---

I didn't realize it then...

But God was already arranging the next chapter.

If I'd stayed...

There's a good chance this book would tell a completely different story.

No Heather.

No Haley.

No Tennessee.

No University of Alabama.

No Whole Life Journey.

It's amazing how one decision quietly changes everything that follows.

At the time...

I simply thought I was moving.

I had no idea...

I was walking into the rest of my life.
````

````markdown id="l1h8vr"
# Chapter 12
# Moving to Tennessee

There are moments in life that don't seem very significant when they're happening.

Packing boxes.

Selling a house.

Loading a moving truck.

Driving down a highway.

At the time...

They're just things you have to do.

Looking back...

You realize they were turning points.

Moving to Tennessee was one of those moments.

---

I graduated from South High School in Torrance in 1989.

Not long afterward, my parents' divorce agreement required that the house be sold.

The house on Kathryn Avenue.

The only home I had ever really known.

The house with the tree.

The garage where baseball gloves dried.

The driveway where motorcycles were loaded.

The neighborhood where I learned to ride my bike.

Where I walked to school.

Where I became me.

Watching that chapter close was harder than I realized at the time.

You don't just leave a house.

Sometimes...

You leave an entire version of yourself.

---

Dad had made up his mind.

He wanted to go home.

Not home as I understood it.

Home to him.

Tennessee.

Specifically...

Soddy Daisy.

The place where he had been born.

The place where his brothers and sisters still lived.

The place he had talked about my entire life.

To Dad...

We weren't moving somewhere new.

We were going back.

To me...

We were leaving everything I'd ever known.

---

Dad gave me a choice.

I could stay in California.

Or...

I could go with him.

Looking back...

I'm not sure he would've tried to talk me into either decision.

He simply wanted me to make it.

I've always appreciated that about him.

He gave advice.

Real advice.

Then he trusted me to decide.

---

People ask if I hesitated.

Of course I did.

Everything I knew was in California.

My friends.

My baseball teammates.

My cousins.

The ocean.

The weather.

The only streets I had ever learned to drive on.

Everything.

Tennessee was just...

Stories.

I had only been there once.

I was seven years old.

---

Funny enough...

What I remember most about that trip has nothing to do with famous places.

I remember Aunt Linda's basement.

That probably sounds strange.

It smelled different.

I'd never been in a basement before.

California doesn't have many basements.

This one had that cool, slightly musty smell that old basements have.

Jeremy and I spent hours down there playing.

To this day...

That smell reminds me of him.

Isn't memory strange?

---

I also remember something that made my aunt laugh.

She was digging potatoes out of her garden.

I stood there amazed.

I had no idea potatoes came out of the ground.

I honestly thought they came from the grocery store.

I remember saying something like,

"My mom gets ours in a bag."

Everybody laughed.

To a little California boy...

Gardens weren't part of everyday life.

They were to my Tennessee family.

---

Jeremy and I were about the same age.

He instantly became my favorite cousin in Tennessee.

Not because I loved him more than anyone else.

Simply because we were kids together.

We explored.

Played outside.

Ran through the woods.

Everything seemed enormous.

Those woods behind Aunt Linda's house looked like an endless forest to a seven-year-old.

Looking back...

They probably weren't nearly as big as I imagined.

But childhood has a way of making ordinary places feel magical.

---

So now...

Years later...

Dad wanted to move back there.

Permanently.

I had a decision to make.

Stay where life was comfortable.

Or follow Dad into the unknown.

I chose Dad.

Looking back...

I'm thankful I did.

Not because Tennessee was better than California.

It wasn't.

They were simply different.

California gave me my childhood.

Tennessee gave me my adulthood.

Without Tennessee...

There would be no Heather.

No Haley.

No career that eventually led me into HR and technology.

No Whole Life Journey.

No rediscovery of my biological family.

Almost everything that defines my adult life traces back to one moving truck headed east.

At the time...

It just felt like a move.

Today...

I recognize it as one of God's quiet turning points.

One of those moments where He changes the direction of your life without telling you exactly why.

You simply start driving.

Years later...

You finally understand where the road was leading.

I think that's how God often works.

He usually doesn't show us the destination.

He simply asks us to trust Him enough to take the next step.

For me...

That next step happened to be about two thousand miles long.
````

````markdown id="g2m4xs"
# Chapter 13
# Arriving at Alabama

January.

1992.

I was finally headed to the University of Alabama.

Even writing those words today still makes me smile.

For years...

Alabama wasn't just another school.

It was *the* school.

If you had asked me as a little kid where I wanted to play college baseball, I probably couldn't have answered.

By the time I graduated high school...

I could.

I wanted Alabama.

And somehow...

God opened that door.

---

Driving into Tuscaloosa was exciting.

Terrifying.

Overwhelming.

I had never really lived away from home before.

Sure...

I'd spent nights with friends.

Road trips.

Baseball tournaments.

But this was different.

This wasn't a visit.

This was life.

Everything from this point forward depended on me.

That realization hits you pretty quickly.

---

I found my apartment at University Downs.

At the time it was one of the nicer apartment complexes around.

Baseball players lived there.

College students.

It felt like the beginning of adulthood.

The apartment itself wasn't anything extraordinary.

But to me...

It represented freedom.

Responsibility.

And honestly...

A little fear.

I didn't know anybody I was living with.

That'll get your attention.

---

When I first walked in...

Jerry Stubbs was already there.

Jerry was from Pennsylvania.

Just like me...

He was green.

He'd never really been away from home either.

Looking back...

That probably helped both of us more than we realized.

Neither one of us knew what we were doing.

So...

We figured it out together.

Over time...

Jerry became one of my closest friends in college.

Matter of fact...

If someone asked me today who my closest college friend was...

I'd answer Jerry without hesitation.

---

The funny thing is...

Our friendship didn't begin with some deep conversation.

It began with confusion.

Neither one of us had any idea how to be adults.

Looking back now...

It's hilarious.

At the time...

It felt perfectly normal.

---

One of our first nights together still makes me laugh.

We had baseballs sitting on top of our dressers.

Sometime during the middle of the night...

We heard a train whistle.

Way off in the distance.

Neither one of us thought much about it.

Then...

The apartment started shaking.

Not violently.

Just enough.

The baseballs started rolling across the dresser.

One.

By.

One.

Thunk.

Thunk.

Thunk.

Jerry and I just laid there laughing.

Neither one of us had ever lived that close to railroad tracks before.

Welcome to college.

---

Not long after that...

We decided to lock the sliding glass door.

Simple enough.

Except...

We couldn't figure out how.

We honestly thought the lock was broken.

So...

We called maintenance.

The guy walks in.

Looks at us.

Flips one little latch.

Looks back at us.

"All fixed."

Then walks out.

Jerry and I just looked at each other.

We'd officially become college students.

---

Those first weeks taught me something.

Growing up...

Adults always seem like they know everything.

Then you become one.

And realize...

Nobody knows as much as you thought they did.

We're all just figuring things out.

Jerry and I were certainly figuring things out.

Sometimes successfully.

Sometimes...

Not so much.

---

The baseball program itself was everything I hoped it would be.

The competition was unbelievable.

Actually...

Let me take that back.

Matthew McConaughey later convinced me "unbelievable" is a stupid word.

The competition was very believable.

Because every player there had earned the opportunity.

Everybody had been the star somewhere.

Everybody had been the best player on somebody's team.

Now...

Nobody cared.

You started over.

Again.

I loved that.

I've always loved environments where respect has to be earned instead of inherited.

---

Practice was different.

Everything moved faster.

The expectations were higher.

Mistakes mattered.

Nobody yelled because they enjoyed yelling.

They yelled because excellence mattered.

That fit me.

I wanted excellence too.

---

One thing I realized pretty quickly...

I wasn't intimidated.

Respected?

Absolutely.

Intimidated?

No.

I'd worked too hard to get there.

I belonged.

Not because someone gave me a uniform.

Because I'd earned one.

That's an important distinction.

---

If you had walked into my apartment during those first few weeks...

You probably would've thought two little boys were pretending to be adults.

You wouldn't have been completely wrong.

But something beautiful happens during those years.

Little by little...

Without realizing it...

You grow up.

Not all at once.

One mistake at a time.

One friendship at a time.

One responsibility at a time.

Looking back...

University Downs wasn't just where I lived.

It was where adulthood quietly began.
````

````markdown id="d4k8rm"
014 - University Downs.md

---
title: University Downs

# Chapter 14
# University Downs

I don't know that anyone is ever completely prepared to live on their own.

I certainly wasn't.

If someone had looked at Jerry Stubbs and me that first semester, they probably would've wondered how either one of us planned to survive adulthood.

Somehow...

We did.

Mostly.

---

Jerry and I were complete opposites in some ways.

He grew up in Pennsylvania.

I grew up in Southern California.

He had his experiences.

I had mine.

But we had something in common.

Neither one of us had ever really been out on our own.

Neither one of us knew how to run an apartment.

Neither one of us knew how much we didn't know.

Looking back...

That was probably the best thing that could've happened.

We learned together.

Usually...

The hard way.

---

One of the first lessons involved a dishwasher.

Now...

You have to understand.

Neither one of us had ever really paid attention to how dishwashers worked.

You put dishes in.

You put soap in.

You push a button.

Simple.

Right?

Well...

We knew there was supposed to be special dishwasher detergent.

We just didn't have any.

Standing there looking at the bottle of regular dish soap...

One of us—I honestly don't remember which one—said,

"I think you're only supposed to use a couple drops."

That sounded reasonable.

Then the other genius in the apartment...

Probably me...

Said,

"Why don't we just fill it up?"

That sounded reasonable too.

At least at the time.

So...

We did.

We completely filled the detergent compartment with regular dish soap.

Turned the dishwasher on.

Then went back into the bedroom.

Life was good.

---

A little while later...

Jerry walked into the kitchen.

A few seconds passed.

Then I heard him yell,

"DJ!!"

Not a panic yell.

More like...

"You've got to come see this."

I walked into the kitchen.

There were bubbles.

Everywhere.

Not a few bubbles.

Not enough bubbles to make you think,

"Oops."

I'm talking bubbles a foot high...

Rolling across the kitchen floor...

Making their way into the dining room.

The dishwasher looked like it had declared war on us.

For a second...

We just stood there staring.

Then we started laughing so hard we could barely breathe.

Eventually we fought our way through the bubbles, turned the dishwasher off, and spent the next couple of hours cleaning the apartment.

To this day...

Whenever I see somebody accidentally use the wrong soap...

I smile.

Been there.

Done that.

---

Cleaning the apartment wasn't exactly one of our strengths.

Actually...

That's being generous.

Jerry and I had a system.

A terrible system.

But it was a system.

Neither one of us particularly liked cleaning.

So...

Neither one of us cleaned.

Until...

The apartment became disgusting.

Then...

One of us would finally say,

"Okay... that's enough."

The amazing part was what happened next.

The other one never complained.

If Jerry started cleaning...

I'd jump in immediately.

If I started...

He was right beside me.

Within a couple of hours...

The entire apartment looked brand new.

Then...

We'd start the whole cycle over again.

It wasn't laziness.

It was two college guys with priorities that didn't include mopping floors.

---

Then there were the pizza boxes.

College students eat pizza.

A lot of pizza.

We were no exception.

Every time we ordered one...

Instead of taking the empty box to the dumpster...

We set it on the kitchen counter.

Then another.

Then another.

Then another.

Eventually...

The counter disappeared.

One day...

One of us—I have no idea which one—decided the solution was to stack them outside the front door.

Great idea.

Until it wasn't.

Week after week...

The stack kept growing.

Soon it was taller than either one of us.

Sometimes we'd have to throw a box up on top and then use a broom handle to straighten the pile.

Looking back...

I'm amazed the apartment manager never said anything.

Maybe they were too busy laughing.

Eventually...

The pizza crusts we had left inside the boxes started smelling.

That's usually a sign you've waited too long.

---

Dad came to visit one weekend.

He walked up the stairs.

Stopped.

Looked at the mountain of pizza boxes.

Then looked at us.

"What in the hell are y'all doing?"

Good question.

Neither one of us had a good answer.

That afternoon...

The pizza box mountain disappeared.

Funny how parental visits improve housekeeping.

---

One of my favorite college stories almost got me killed.

Or at least...

It should have.

The Blizzard of 1993 hit Tuscaloosa.

If you've never lived in Alabama...

Snow like that is a big deal.

Everybody went outside.

We were having a huge snowball fight.

Dad happened to be visiting.

He was standing on one of the upper balconies taking pictures with his good camera.

Jerry looked at me and said,

"I bet you can't hit him."

Now...

You need to understand.

I'm a baseball player.

That wasn't a dare.

That was a challenge.

I packed a snowball as tight as I possibly could.

Honestly...

It was closer to an ice ball.

I reared back and let it fly.

At first...

I was excited.

It had a chance.

Then...

As it got closer...

I started getting nervous.

Finally I yelled,

"LOOK OUT!"

Too late.

The snowball hit the camera lens perfectly.

It exploded all over Dad's face.

Silence.

For about one second.

Then...

Rhonda started laughing.

Hard.

Jerry laughed so hard he collapsed on the ground.

I'm convinced that laughter saved my life.

Because Dad wasn't laughing.

Not at first.

Looking back...

I'm lucky to still be here.

---

That's what University Downs was.

Not just an apartment.

It was where two young men slowly figured out how to become adults.

Sometimes we learned through responsibility.

Sometimes...

We learned through pizza boxes.

Or bubbles.

Or snowballs.

Either way...

We learned.

And looking back...

Those lessons were worth every minute.
````
