# Chapter 15
# Jerry Stubbs

When people ask me who my closest friend was in college...

The answer comes quickly.

Jerry Stubbs.

Matter of fact...

If you looked through my wedding pictures, you might assume someone else held that title.

You'd be wrong.

Jerry wasn't in my wedding.

Not because I didn't want him there.

Because he couldn't be.

He had signed with the Montreal Expos organization and was playing professional baseball in West Palm Beach, Florida.

The season didn't stop because I was getting married.

I understood that.

Matter of fact...

I was proud of him.

But we'll come back to that later.

First...

You need to meet Jerry.

---

Jerry was my roommate.

He was also one of the funniest people I've ever lived with.

Not because he tried to be.

Because life seemed to happen around him.

And somehow...

I usually ended up right in the middle of it.

---

One thing people should probably know about Jerry and me...

Neither one of us knew what we were doing.

We looked like adults.

We had an apartment.

We were playing baseball for Alabama.

But if you looked a little closer...

We were still just two kids trying to figure life out.

Some lessons came easier than others.

---

One afternoon we got bored.

That should probably worry you already.

Bored college baseball players don't usually make great decisions.

Somebody had a dart board.

Somebody else had an idea.

Actually...

It might have been my idea.

That's usually how these stories go.

We started throwing darts into the ceiling.

Not because we wanted to ruin the ceiling.

We wanted to see if we could jump up and grab the dart before it fell.

Started easy.

Worked great.

So naturally...

We made it harder.

Eventually I stuck one about eleven feet up the wall near the vaulted ceiling.

Jerry backed up.

Got a running start.

Jumped.

Missed.

When he landed...

He lost his balance.

Started stumbling backward.

To catch himself...

He threw his foot behind him.

Right through the wall.

Not into the wall.

Through the wall.

Jerry wore about a size twelve shoe.

That's a pretty good-sized hole.

We both just stood there.

Looking at the hole.

Looking at each other.

Then started laughing.

Fortunately...

Dad had spent his life building houses.

I'd watched him enough over the years that I actually knew how to repair drywall.

So...

We patched it.

Sanded it.

Painted it.

To this day...

I don't know if the apartment ever figured out what happened.

I'd like to think they didn't.

---

Then there was the snowball.

Actually...

The ice ball.

That story probably deserves repeating because Jerry's part in it always makes me smile.

The Blizzard of '93 hit Tuscaloosa.

Everybody was outside.

Dad happened to be visiting.

He was standing on the balcony taking pictures.

Jerry looked over at me and said,

"I bet you can't hit him."

He should've known better.

Never challenge a baseball player to hit a target.

Especially one dumb enough to accept the challenge.

I packed the snowball into something much closer to ice.

Threw it.

Hit Dad's camera lens perfectly.

Jerry laughed so hard...

He literally fell to the ground.

He couldn't stand up.

I, on the other hand...

Was trying to decide whether running or apologizing would be the better survival strategy.

Thankfully...

Rhonda laughed before Dad got too mad.

I'm convinced that laughter saved my life.

---

Jerry also had an unbelievable ability to get me into conversations that started with,

"You think we can..."

Those words almost never ended well.

But they always ended with a story.

And somehow...

That's okay.

College should probably include a few stories you'll laugh about fifty years later.

Jerry gave me plenty of those.

---

Looking back...

People often think college friendships are built because you live together.

I don't think that's true.

I think they're built because you grow up together.

Jerry and I weren't just sharing an apartment.

We were learning life together.

Bills.

Responsibilities.

Baseball.

Dating.

Cooking.

Cleaning.

Failure.

Success.

Every day brought something neither one of us had experienced before.

It's hard not to become close when you walk through that season together.

---

One thing I admired about Jerry was his baseball ability.

He could play.

Really play.

Eventually...

Professional baseball came calling.

He signed with the Montreal Expos organization.

I was proud of him.

There wasn't a jealous bone in my body.

Matter of fact...

Watching someone you care about achieve a dream is a pretty incredible thing.

People sometimes assume athletes compete against one another all the time.

Not really.

We compete with one another.

There's a difference.

I wanted Jerry to succeed.

He wanted me to succeed.

That's what real teammates do.

---

Years later...

When Heather and I got married...

Jerry wasn't standing beside me.

Not because our friendship had changed.

Because he was chasing the very dream we'd both worked toward for years.

Professional baseball.

If anyone deserved to be there...

It was Jerry.

And if anyone had a good excuse for missing the wedding...

Professional baseball is probably it.

I missed him that day.

But I never questioned where he was.

He was exactly where he was supposed to be.

---

Looking back...

When I think about Alabama...

Jerry is one of the very first faces that comes to mind.

Not because of the baseball.

Not because of the apartment.

Not because of the pizza boxes.

Because friendships formed during those years become part of who you are.

Jerry helped me grow up.

I hope I helped him too.

Some friendships slowly fade over time.

Others become part of your story forever.

Jerry Stubbs will always be part of mine.
````

# Chapter 16
# Meeting Heather

Every now and then people ask me,

"How did you know?"

How did you know Heather was the one?

I wish I could give you some deep, romantic answer.

I can't.

I just knew she was different.

I recognized it almost immediately.

Not because she was the prettiest girl I'd ever met.

Although I certainly thought she was beautiful.

Not because she was popular.

Not because we had some magical Hollywood moment.

I simply remember thinking...

"This one is different."

And she was.

---

I met Heather through one of my friends.

Vance Traffanstedt.

Now...

You need to understand something about Vance.

He was a good friend.

Still is.

But he also knew my reputation.

College Danny wasn't exactly known for long-term relationships.

I dated.

A lot.

Not because I was trying to hurt anyone.

I just hadn't met the right person yet.

Relationships came and went.

That was pretty normal in college.

At least it seemed normal then.

Vance knew that.

He also knew Heather.

He liked Heather.

He respected Heather.

And...

Behind my back...

He warned her about me.

---

Years later Heather told me what Vance had said.

Something along the lines of,

"Don't go out with Danny."

"He'll probably hurt you."

Looking back...

I can't even be mad at him.

He was trying to protect his friend.

If our positions had been reversed...

I probably would've done exactly the same thing.

---

The funny part is...

Heather still agreed to go out with me.

Not because she ignored Vance.

Because she decided to find out for herself.

I'm really thankful she did.

---

The first few dates were different.

Not because of Heather.

Because of me.

Without realizing it...

I completely changed the way I approached relationships.

If this had been another college date...

I probably would've tried to impress her.

Push things.

Move too fast.

Instead...

Something told me not to.

I honestly believe that something was God.

I didn't want to scare her away.

I didn't want to blow it.

I didn't even fully understand why.

I just knew she mattered.

---

One evening I went over to her apartment to study.

At least...

That was the official reason.

We actually did study.

Imagine that.

Eventually it was time for me to leave.

We walked to the front door.

I remember standing there thinking,

"I'd really like to hug her."

Not kiss her.

Not make some big romantic move.

Just hug her.

So I asked.

"Would it be okay if I gave you a hug?"

That probably doesn't sound like much.

To Heather...

It meant everything.

Because it wasn't what she expected.

It wasn't what I would've done with anyone else either.

Something about her made me slow down.

Looking back...

That hug probably told her more about my intentions than anything I could've said.

---

As our relationship grew...

I realized something.

I didn't have to pretend around Heather.

That's rare.

Most of us spend a lot of time trying to impress people.

With Heather...

I could simply be Danny.

She laughed at my jokes.

She rolled her eyes when I deserved it.

She challenged me.

She listened.

She believed in me.

More importantly...

She never tried to turn me into somebody else.

She loved the person standing in front of her.

I didn't realize how unusual that was until much later.

---

One of the things I admired most about Heather was her faith.

She had a steadiness about her.

Not loud.

Not showy.

Just...

Steady.

The older I get...

The more I appreciate steady people.

Life has enough drama on its own.

Heather never needed to create any.

She brought peace wherever she went.

I don't think I recognized that at twenty-two years old.

I certainly recognize it now.

---

Somewhere along the way...

Dating quietly became something much bigger.

I stopped wondering whether we were compatible.

I started wondering what life would look like together.

There's a difference.

One asks,

"Can this work?"

The other asks,

"What could we build together?"

Without realizing it...

I'd already started thinking about forever.

---

People have asked me over the years if I believe in love at first sight.

Honestly...

No.

I believe in something better.

I believe you can recognize character before you fully understand it.

That's what happened with Heather.

I didn't fall in love with her in one afternoon.

I recognized something in her that I couldn't quite explain.

Then...

Over time...

Everything I discovered confirmed that first impression.

She really was different.

---

I've often joked that marrying Heather was the best decision I ever made.

Actually...

It's not really a joke.

It's the truth.

Because if you trace almost every wonderful thing in my adult life...

Most of those roads eventually lead back to one young woman...

Who ignored her friend's advice...

And decided to go out with me anyway.

I'm thankful she did.

Every single day.
````

# Chapter 17
# Falling in Love

I don't know the exact day I fell in love with Heather.

I wish I could tell you there was one magical moment.

There wasn't.

It happened quietly.

One conversation at a time.

One date at a time.

One laugh at a time.

Before I realized it...

I couldn't imagine my life without her.

---

One of the things that made Heather different was how comfortable I felt around her.

That's hard to explain.

I had dated enough girls in college to know what dating usually felt like.

There was always some pressure.

Trying to impress.

Trying to say the right thing.

Trying to be funny.

Trying to be interesting.

With Heather...

That pressure disappeared.

I could just be me.

That may not sound like much.

It meant everything.

---

I also noticed something else.

I wanted her to like me...

For the right reasons.

Not because I played baseball.

Not because I was an athlete.

Not because people knew who I was.

I wanted her to know Danny.

The real one.

The one who laughed too hard.

The one who sometimes got emotional.

The one who loved motorcycles almost as much as baseball.

The one who loved God but still had a lot to learn.

The one who wasn't nearly as confident off the field as people probably assumed.

I wanted *that* guy to be enough.

---

One evening we were talking, and I caught myself thinking,

"I don't want to mess this up."

That thought had never really crossed my mind with anyone else.

Normally, if a relationship didn't work out...

Life went on.

With Heather...

The idea of losing her bothered me.

That's when I knew something had changed.

---

People sometimes ask what made her so special.

Honestly...

It wasn't one thing.

It was a hundred little things.

She listened.

Really listened.

She laughed at my stories.

She cared about people.

She loved her family.

She didn't need to be the center of attention.

She had a goofy side that would sneak out when you least expected it.

She loved God in a quiet, authentic way.

She didn't perform her faith.

She lived it.

That impressed me.

Still does.

---

One of the biggest surprises for me was how peaceful our relationship felt.

I've heard people describe relationships as emotional roller coasters.

Ours wasn't.

It was steady.

Healthy.

Comfortable.

Looking back...

I think that's because neither one of us was trying to win.

We were trying to understand each other.

That's a very different approach.

---

We talked.

A lot.

About everything.

Family.

Dreams.

Faith.

Our futures.

Sometimes we'd sit for hours.

Neither one of us felt the need to constantly entertain the other.

Just being together was enough.

I've come to realize that's pretty rare.

---

One thing I admired about Heather was the relationship she had with her parents.

Larry and Linda Puller were good people.

The first time I spent much time around them, I noticed something.

Their family enjoyed being together.

That may sound obvious.

It isn't.

Some families tolerate each other.

The Pullers genuinely enjoyed each other.

That attracted me.

I wanted that.

---

There's a funny story that still makes me smile.

One evening I was over at Heather's house.

We were standing in the kitchen.

I leaned in to kiss her.

She backed away.

"No."

"My mom's in the next room."

I remember laughing.

"Seriously?"

"She's in the next room."

"So?"

Heather still wasn't convinced.

Finally she let me kiss her.

About halfway through the kiss...

Linda walked into the kitchen.

Without missing a beat she started giggling.

"Oh..."

"Excuse me."

Then she turned around...

Still laughing...

And walked back out.

I don't know if Heather was embarrassed.

I know I was trying not to laugh.

That's one of my favorite Linda stories.

It tells you everything you need to know about her personality.

She wasn't angry.

She wasn't upset.

She simply thought it was funny.

That was Linda.

---

As our relationship continued...

Something else quietly happened.

I stopped thinking in terms of "my future."

Without realizing it...

It became "our future."

I wasn't making plans for me anymore.

I was making plans for us.

That's a pretty important shift.

---

Looking back...

I think one of the reasons Heather and I have had such a strong marriage is because our friendship came first.

Long before she became my wife...

She became my favorite person to spend time with.

That's still true today.

We've been married for decades now.

People ask us if we've ever had a fight.

Not really.

Disagreements?

Of course.

Serious conversations?

Absolutely.

Yelling?

No.

Cussing at each other?

Never.

Not because we're perfect.

Because somewhere early in our relationship we decided respect mattered more than winning.

Sometimes one of us walked away to cool off.

Not out of anger.

Out of respect.

That's one of the greatest gifts we've ever given each other.

---

There came a point where I realized something.

I didn't just love Heather.

I trusted her.

Given my story...

That's a much bigger statement than it might sound.

Trust has always been a huge issue for me.

My life had been built on secrets I didn't know existed.

Discovering those secrets later changed me.

Heather wasn't part of any of that.

She was the first person in my life I found myself running toward...

Instead of away from.

That realization changed everything.

I didn't know it yet...

But I'd just met my teammate for life.
````

# Chapter 18
# Asking Heather to Marry Me

Some moments in your life stay crystal clear forever.

Other moments...

You remember more by feeling than by detail.

Asking Heather to marry me falls somewhere in between.

I remember enough.

I mostly remember how I felt.

---

At the time I was working for The Pinnacle Group.

I had landed my first professional job after college.

Consulting.

Lots of travel.

Long hours.

It was exciting.

It was also exhausting.

The company was getting ready for one of its annual trips, and that year we were headed on a cruise to the Bahamas.

I had already bought the ring.

I already knew she was the one.

I already knew I was going to ask her.

The only question left was...

When?

---

My plan was pretty simple.

Wait until we were out at sea.

Find the perfect moment.

Ask her.

It sounded romantic.

At least it did in my head.

God apparently had different plans.

---

People around the company somehow figured out what I was about to do.

I still don't know exactly how.

Maybe somebody saw the ring.

Maybe I wasn't as subtle as I thought.

Whatever happened...

People started congratulating us...

Before I had even asked.

Think about that.

You're trying to plan one of the biggest moments of your life...

And coworkers keep walking up saying,

"Congratulations!"

Heather looked at me.

I looked at them.

The surprise was disappearing by the minute.

At that point I realized...

I wasn't going to make it to the cruise.

---

So...

I improvised.

We were staying at a hotel before leaving for the trip.

Outside the hotel there was a garden.

Nothing elaborate.

Just quiet.

Peaceful.

I asked Heather if she'd take a walk with me.

She didn't know anything was wrong.

Or right.

She just thought we were taking a walk.

---

I remember my heart pounding.

Now...

I've played baseball in front of large crowds.

I'd quarterbacked football games.

Pressure didn't usually bother me.

This was different.

Completely different.

There was no crowd.

No scoreboard.

No teammates.

Just one woman.

One question.

And a future hanging on her answer.

---

I honestly don't remember every word I said.

I wish I did.

I'd love to tell you I gave some incredible speech.

Knowing me...

It was probably pretty simple.

I got down on one knee.

Opened the ring.

Asked her to marry me.

Then...

Waited.

Those few seconds felt like forever.

---

She smiled.

Then she said,

"Yes."

Just like that.

One word.

One beautiful word.

Everything changed.

---

I've often joked that was one of the happiest days of my life.

Actually...

It's not much of a joke.

It really was.

Not because she made me happy.

Because she gave me the opportunity to spend the rest of my life trying to make *us* happy.

There's a difference.

Marriage isn't about finding someone who completes you.

It's about finding someone you want to build a life with.

I had found her.

---

People have asked me over the years if I was nervous.

Absolutely.

Terrified might be a better word.

Not because I thought she'd say no.

Because I understood what I was asking.

Marriage isn't just a wedding.

It's not just a ring.

It's a promise.

One I intended to keep.

---

Looking back now...

It's funny.

I can remember baseball games from high school.

I can remember football plays.

I can remember motorcycle rides.

But I can't remember every word I said when I proposed.

That used to bother me.

It doesn't anymore.

Because I remember the important part.

She said yes.

Everything else...

Worked itself out.

---

If someone asked me today what the best decision of my life has been...

The answer is easy.

Marrying Heather.

Not because life suddenly became easy.

It didn't.

We'd face illness.

Financial stress.

Career changes.

The loss of parents.

Disappointments.

Dreams that changed.

Life.

But we faced it together.

And that's made all the difference.

---

Every wonderful thing that followed...

June 7, 1997.

Haley.

Our home.

Our family.

Every anniversary.

Every Christmas.

Every ordinary Tuesday night sitting on the couch together.

Every one of those moments traces back to one walk through a hotel garden...

Where a young man...

Holding a little ring...

Asked the best question he would ever ask.

And was blessed enough...

To hear the answer he was praying for.
````

# Chapter 19
# The Best Worst Day of My Life

I've told people for years that my wedding day was the best worst day of my life.

The funny thing is...

Both parts of that statement are absolutely true.

It was the best day because I married Heather.

It was the worst day because I don't think I've ever been that nervous in my entire life.

Not before.

Not since.

---

That surprises people.

After all...

I'd played baseball in front of large crowds.

I'd quarterbacked football games under Friday night lights.

I'd hit home runs.

I'd struck out with people watching.

I'd been drafted by the San Francisco Giants.

Pressure wasn't exactly new to me.

None of it compared to standing in that little chapel waiting for Heather.

Nothing.

---

We chose to get married at Jim Oliver's Smokehouse in Monteagle, Tennessee.

Some people probably wondered why.

The answer was pretty simple.

It was about halfway between our families.

Neither one of us wanted an extravagant wedding.

We didn't have extravagant money.

Even if we had...

I don't think either one of us would've wanted that.

The place fit us.

There was a little chapel.

A restaurant.

A hotel.

Everything in one place.

Best of all...

It sat out in the country.

When you walked outside the chapel...

You could look out across the fields and see cows grazing.

That felt right.

Heather grew up in the country.

Dad's family came from the country.

Even though I was raised in California...

Country never felt foreign to me.

It felt familiar.

---

People have asked if I remember much about the ceremony.

Honestly...

Not really.

That's one of the strangest things about that day.

I remember pieces.

Snapshots.

Not a continuous movie.

I remember standing there.

Sweating.

A lot.

We had the air conditioning turned down into the low sixties.

The bridesmaids were freezing.

I was absolutely drenched.

Sweat running down my face.

You can actually see it in some of the photographs.

Looking back...

It wasn't the temperature.

It was me.

Pure nerves.

---

Then...

There were the vows.

I'll never live this one down.

I was supposed to say,

> "God's holy ordinance."

Instead...

I confidently announced,

> "God's holy orbits."

Orbits.

As in planets.

I didn't even realize what I'd said until later.

People still laugh about it.

Honestly...

I do too.

At least I got married.

Imagine if I'd accidentally married Jupiter.

---

The minister gave a sermon.

Only...

It wasn't exactly what anyone expected.

Somehow he decided to tell the story of a prostitute who had been saved by Jesus.

To this day...

Neither Heather nor I know why that became the chosen illustration for our wedding ceremony.

We still laugh about it.

It came completely out of nowhere.

If you had asked either one of us to predict what the sermon would be about...

That would've been somewhere around number two thousand on the list.

---

One of my favorite wedding photographs has always puzzled us.

Heather is looking at me...

And she has that look.

You know the look.

The,

"You better stop."

look.

People have asked us for years,

"Were y'all arguing?"

Absolutely not.

Matter of fact...

We've talked about that photograph more than once trying to remember what happened.

Neither one of us knows.

My best guess?

I probably made a joke.

Knowing me...

Probably something about getting naked.

Or streaking.

Or what we were going to do now that the ceremony was over.

Completely inappropriate.

Especially with grandparents standing nearby.

That sounds exactly like something twenty-five-year-old Danny would've done.

Heather's expression says,

"Not now."

Looking back...

She's probably right.

---

One thing I do remember clearly...

Heather.

She was beautiful.

Absolutely beautiful.

People often ask what I remember most about that day.

That's it.

Her.

The dress.

The smile.

Standing there waiting to become my wife.

I don't remember decorations nearly as well.

Or flowers.

Or food.

I remember looking at her and thinking,

"I can't believe she's marrying me."

Thirty years later...

I still think that once in a while.

---

After the ceremony...

We climbed into a limousine.

Now...

Don't picture some fancy Hollywood limousine.

This thing had seen better days.

Even then we laughed about how old it looked.

Didn't matter.

We were married.

It could've been a pickup truck.

I don't think either one of us would've cared.

---

We headed to Opryland Hotel.

Another funny memory.

Everywhere we turned...

Champagne.

There was champagne at the reception.

Champagne in the limousine.

Champagne waiting in the hotel room.

Champagne at dinner.

I don't think I've had a glass of champagne since.

Not because I don't like it.

I think I just reached my lifetime limit in one weekend.

---

Here's another thing people don't usually expect.

When we finally got to the hotel...

We were exhausted.

Not romantic.

Not starry-eyed.

Just...

Tired.

We basically fell into bed and went to sleep.

I don't even remember talking very much.

The day had simply worn us out.

---

You know when it finally hit me?

Not during the ceremony.

Not at the reception.

Not in the limousine.

The next morning.

I woke up.

Looked over.

Saw Heather.

And thought,

"I'm married."

That's when it became real.

Not during all the excitement.

During the quiet.

---

Looking back...

I realize something.

Heather and I weren't excited about the wedding.

We were excited about the marriage.

There's a huge difference.

One lasts a day.

The other lasts a lifetime.

If I had to choose again...

I'd still choose the little chapel.

I'd still choose the simple ceremony.

I'd still choose every nervous moment.

Because at the end of it...

I got Heather.

And that has turned out to be the greatest blessing of my adult life.

So yes...

It really was...

The best worst day of my life.
````

# Chapter 20
# The Honeymoon Begins

People often think the honeymoon begins when you get on an airplane.

Ours started much earlier than that.

Matter of fact...

I think it started the morning after the wedding.

---

I woke up.

Rolled over.

Looked at Heather.

And smiled.

Not because something exciting was about to happen.

Because something already had.

We were married.

For the first time in my life...

I wasn't thinking about dating.

Or girlfriends.

Or wondering what the future might hold.

I was looking at my wife.

That's still one of my favorite words.

Wife.

It carried weight then.

It still does.

---

People sometimes ask if marriage felt different immediately.

Absolutely.

Not because Heather changed.

She was still the same wonderful woman I'd fallen in love with.

I changed.

The responsibility felt different.

The commitment felt different.

The words,

"My wife..."

felt different.

Everything became...

"Ours."

Our apartment.

Our plans.

Our future.

Our problems.

Our dreams.

That's one of the beautiful things about marriage.

Life stops being just about you.

---

Looking back...

Heather and I started marriage with something that I think helped us tremendously.

Neither one of us expected perfection.

We expected partnership.

There's a huge difference.

We weren't looking for someone to complete us.

We were looking for someone to walk beside us.

We found exactly that.

---

People have asked us over the years what the secret is.

Honestly...

There isn't one.

It's a thousand little decisions.

Respect.

Patience.

Forgiveness.

Choosing your words carefully.

Walking away when you're frustrated instead of saying something you'll regret.

Listening.

Really listening.

Those little things become decades.

---

One thing I'm especially thankful for...

We've never had a knock-down, drag-out fight.

Now...

That doesn't mean we've never disagreed.

Of course we have.

Sometimes strongly.

But we've never yelled at each other.

We've never cussed at each other.

Sometimes one of us would say,

"I need a little time."

Then we'd come back.

Talk.

Work through it.

That wasn't weakness.

That was respect.

I've had heated arguments with plenty of people in my life.

For some reason...

When it came to Heather...

I just couldn't.

I loved her too much.

Hurting her with my words simply wasn't an option.

---

I've thought about that quite a bit over the years.

Why?

Why was our relationship different?

I think part of the answer goes back to trust.

Trust has always been a huge issue for me.

I didn't know that when I was young.

I know it now.

Growing up, I eventually discovered my life had been built around secrets I didn't know existed.

Not malicious secrets.

Protective ones.

But secrets all the same.

That changes a person.

You start wondering.

Questioning.

Holding pieces of yourself back.

Then Heather came along.

For the first time...

I found someone I wanted to run toward...

Instead of away from.

That changed everything.

---

Marriage also taught me something else.

Love isn't mostly about big moments.

It's about ordinary Tuesdays.

It's paying bills together.

Going to the grocery store.

Cleaning the house.

Laughing over something completely stupid.

Watching television.

Taking walks.

Living life.

People spend so much time chasing extraordinary moments that they sometimes miss extraordinary ordinary days.

Most of our marriage has been wonderfully ordinary.

That's one of the things I treasure most.

---

As the years passed...

People occasionally asked us if marriage was hard.

Sometimes.

Life is hard.

Marriage isn't supposed to remove hardship.

It's supposed to give you somebody to face it with.

That's exactly what Heather became.

My teammate.

My encourager.

My best friend.

My safe place.

---

It's funny.

I've spent a lifetime on teams.

Little League.

Football.

Basketball.

College baseball.

Work.

Leadership.

If somebody asked me today...

"What was the best team you were ever part of?"

The answer comes instantly.

Heather and me.

Not because we've never struggled.

Because we've never stopped pulling in the same direction.

That's what teammates do.

---

Years later...

People sometimes compliment our marriage.

They'll say,

"You two seem so happy."

We are.

Not because life has been easy.

Because we've chosen each other over and over again.

Every season.

Every challenge.

Every disappointment.

Every victory.

Marriage isn't built on one decision made at an altar.

It's built on thousands of little decisions made afterward.

I'm thankful Heather kept choosing me.

I know I certainly won the lottery when I got to choose her.

---

If someone asked me to summarize my marriage in one sentence...

I think I'd simply say this.

As many teams as I've played on...

As many championships as I've been part of...

As many incredible athletes as I've stood beside...

The greatest teammate I've ever had...

Has always been Heather.

And somehow...

After all these years...

She still is.
````

# Chapter 21
# Haley

October 5, 2002.

There are only a handful of days in my life where I can tell you exactly where I was, exactly how I felt, and exactly what was going through my mind.

This is one of them.

The day Haley was born.

People have asked me over the years what it feels like to become a father.

The best word I've ever found is...

Overwhelming.

Not because it was emotional.

Although it certainly was.

Because in one instant...

Your entire understanding of life changes.

Everything.

Priorities.

Dreams.

Worries.

Responsibility.

Love.

Everything.

---

Heather's pregnancy had gone well.

We were excited.

Nervous.

Reading books.

Talking to other parents.

Pretending we knew what we were doing.

The truth?

We had no clue.

Just like every first-time parent.

You prepare.

You buy the crib.

Paint the room.

Read the books.

Then reality shows up.

---

The delivery didn't go the way we expected.

Heather wasn't progressing the way the doctors hoped.

Eventually Dr. Wakefield made the decision.

We couldn't wait any longer.

A Caesarean section was necessary.

I remember sitting there thinking,

"Okay...

This isn't what we planned...

But everything will be fine."

That's what I kept telling myself.

Everything will be fine.

---

Then...

Everything changed.

Haley was born.

She wasn't breathing.

I can still see it.

The doctor working frantically.

Trying to stimulate her.

Rubbing her.

Patting her.

Trying to get her lungs to open.

Nothing.

No cry.

No sound.

Nothing.

Time stopped.

People talk about seconds.

Those weren't seconds.

Those were lifetimes.

---

The doctor finally scooped her up and ran out of the room.

One of the nurses looked at me and said,

"Go with your daughter."

Think about that.

My wife was still lying on the operating table.

She didn't even know what was happening.

She didn't know whether our daughter was alive.

And I was running down the hallway after a doctor carrying my baby.

Those moments are burned into my memory forever.

---

Eventually...

She cried.

I've never been so relieved to hear a sound in my entire life.

That little cry...

Changed everything.

I've joked over the years that hearing your child cry is one of the happiest sounds you'll ever hear.

Then...

After they grow up...

It becomes one of the hardest sounds you'll ever hear.

Both are true.

---

Haley spent time in the NICU.

They watched her closely.

She also developed jaundice.

So our first days as parents weren't exactly what we'd imagined.

Instead of taking our baby home immediately...

We found ourselves sitting beside an incubator.

Watching monitors.

Learning words we never wanted to learn.

Praying.

Waiting.

Hoping.

---

I remember looking through the glass.

She was so tiny.

So helpless.

So completely dependent on us.

At that moment something happened inside me.

I'd always been willing to work hard.

Now...

Failure wasn't an option.

Because failure no longer affected only me.

It affected her.

That's a different kind of motivation.

---

People ask if becoming a father changed me.

Absolutely.

Immediately.

Not because someone told me to change.

Because the moment I looked into Haley's eyes...

Life stopped being about Danny.

Everything became,

"How does this affect her?"

Every decision.

Every job.

Every move.

Every opportunity.

Every risk.

I wasn't just making decisions for myself anymore.

I was making decisions for my family.

---

As Haley grew...

One of my greatest joys became sharing my passions with her.

Motorcycles.

Sports.

Adventure.

Not because I wanted her to become me.

I never wanted that.

I simply wanted to invite her into the things that had brought me joy.

There's a difference.

When I bought her little Yamaha PW50...

She loved it.

But she wanted something else too.

She wanted it to look like Daddy's KTM.

So...

We replaced all the blue plastic with orange.

Now it looked like a KTM.

She was thrilled.

We spent countless hours riding around our property at 707 Briar Road.

Some of my favorite memories aren't of racing.

They're of looking over and seeing a tiny little orange motorcycle following me through the woods.

Eventually...

She started leading.

I started following.

That's exactly how it should be.

---

Years later...

When Haley got married...

I wanted to give her something she could carry forever.

Not just jewelry.

Meaning.

I remembered the gold Dad and I had recovered together years earlier in Gorman.

I had some of that gold melted into a bead and placed inside a beautiful bracelet with a rose.

It wasn't just a gift from me.

It was a gift from Papa too.

Even though he wasn't standing there that day...

Part of him was.

That's what legacy looks like.

---

If someone asked me today what accomplishment I'm most proud of...

It wouldn't be baseball.

It wouldn't be football.

It wouldn't be my career.

It wouldn't even be Whole Life Journey.

It would be hearing Haley call me Dad.

Nothing else comes close.

People sometimes tell me,

"You've done a lot in your life."

Maybe.

But none of it compares to the privilege of being her father.

Not even close.

---

One day...

If Haley reads this chapter...

I hope she knows something.

She changed me.

More than she'll probably ever realize.

She made me a better man.

A better husband.

A better son.

A better leader.

A better follower of Christ.

Children have a way of doing that.

They don't just become part of your life.

They quietly become one of God's greatest tools for shaping it.

Thank you, Haley.

Being your dad has been the greatest honor of my life.
````

# Chapter 22
# Dad's Stroke

There are days in your life you can never completely leave behind.

June 21, 2001...

Is one of mine.

No matter how many years pass...

I can still feel that night.

---

It was late.

Around eleven o'clock.

The phone rang.

Nobody likes late-night phone calls.

Almost never does anything good begin with a phone ringing that late.

I answered it.

It was Dad's neighbor.

His voice didn't sound right.

He told me they had found Dad lying on the bathroom floor.

They didn't know if he was going to make it.

I don't remember much after that.

Not because it wasn't important.

Because everything happened so fast.

---

Dad had a routine.

Every evening he'd get on one of my four-wheelers that I'd loaned him.

He'd ride around the neighborhood visiting people.

He wasn't a fan of large crowds.

Never really had been.

But he loved people.

He loved conversations.

He loved checking in on neighbors.

He'd stop by Andy and Lisa's house almost every night.

That particular evening...

He never showed up.

---

Andy and Lisa thought it was strange.

They sent their son Kevin over to check on him.

Dad's truck was there.

The lights were on.

Nobody answered the door.

Kevin called his parents.

They told him to see if the door was unlocked.

It was.

He walked inside.

Dad was lying on the bathroom floor.

He'd been there...

For more than eleven hours.

---

By the time the ambulance arrived...

Things were critical.

They actually had to resuscitate Dad twice.

Twice.

Eventually they airlifted him to Erlanger Hospital in Chattanooga.

Meanwhile...

I was packing.

Fast.

Heather was five months pregnant with Haley.

Neither one of us knew what the next few hours were going to bring.

---

I wasn't in a good place.

That's probably an understatement.

I drove faster than I ever should have.

There were times I know I was well over one hundred miles an hour.

My eyes were blurry.

Partly from tears.

Partly because I couldn't believe what was happening.

Heather sat beside me.

Scared.

Not for herself.

For all of us.

Dad.

Me.

Our unborn daughter.

She never once complained.

She just sat beside me.

That's who Heather is.

---

When we finally arrived at the hospital...

I think Aunt Pat and Carol met me.

Nobody had really seen Dad yet.

Nobody knew much.

I walked to the nurses' station.

Asked where he was.

They took me back.

I'll never forget what I saw.

Dad was lying there.

Completely still.

The only part of him that moved...

Were his eyes.

He looked at me.

I grabbed his hand.

Squeezed it.

Then realized...

He couldn't feel me.

He couldn't move.

He couldn't speak.

He couldn't even nod.

The strongest man I'd ever known...

The man who had always fixed everything...

Could do nothing but look at me.

That image has never left me.

---

People sometimes ask me what I was thinking.

Honestly...

I wasn't.

I was surviving.

You don't think much during moments like that.

You react.

You pray.

You hope.

You hold on.

That's about it.

---

The doctors explained what had happened.

Dad had suffered a massive stroke.

The arteries in his neck had become severely blocked.

Because he'd been lying there so long before anyone found him...

The damage was extensive.

Nobody could tell us what life would look like.

If there would even be much of one.

---

I remember making a decision.

Not a dramatic one.

Not one I announced.

Just a decision.

Dad wasn't going through this alone.

Whatever happened next...

I was staying.

I called my employer.

Explained the situation.

Then quit.

Just like that.

People have asked me if I regret that decision.

Not for one second.

Jobs come and go.

You only get one dad.

---

Dad spent two weeks in the hospital.

Then another five weeks at Siskin Rehabilitation Hospital.

During those weeks...

I stayed with him.

Every day.

Every night.

Learning.

Helping.

Waiting.

Praying.

Sometimes celebrating the smallest victories.

A finger moving.

A little more speech.

A tiny bit more strength.

You learn quickly not to take small victories for granted.

---

One thing amazed me.

Dad never quit.

I never heard,

"Why me?"

Never.

He worked.

Every single day.

Physical therapy.

Speech therapy.

Occupational therapy.

Again.

And again.

And again.

The same stubborn determination that had built houses...

Was now rebuilding his own body.

---

Eventually...

He started improving.

Not completely.

Life would never be the same.

But better.

Much better than anyone first expected.

The paralysis slowly eased.

Speech slowly returned.

Hope slowly returned.

---

That stroke changed both of us.

Dad lost independence.

I gained perspective.

Until then...

Parents always seemed permanent.

That illusion disappeared overnight.

Suddenly...

The man who had always protected me...

Needed me.

That's a strange feeling.

One I wasn't prepared for.

---

Looking back...

I don't remember those weeks as being miserable.

Hard?

Absolutely.

Heartbreaking?

Without question.

But they were also a gift.

Very few people get the opportunity to give back to the parent who gave so much to them.

God gave me that opportunity.

It wasn't the way I would've chosen.

But I'm thankful I had it.

---

That night changed the direction of my life.

Not just because of the stroke.

Because of what happened afterward.

Eventually...

Dad would come live with us.

Heather.

Haley.

Me.

For years.

Some people saw it as a sacrifice.

I never really did.

To me...

It was simply my turn.

Dad had spent his life taking care of me.

Now...

It was my turn to take care of him.

I'd do it all over again.

Without hesitation.

Without regret.

Every single time.
````

title: Nine Years with Dad

# Chapter 23
# Nine Years with Dad

People have asked me over the years if taking care of Dad after his stroke was difficult.

Yes.

It was.

But probably not for the reasons most people think.

The physical part wasn't the hardest.

Watching the strongest man I'd ever known struggle...

That was hard.

---

After Dad left rehabilitation, we had decisions to make.

He couldn't safely live by himself.

Not anymore.

There were too many things that could go wrong.

He needed help.

Real help.

Not somebody checking on him every few days.

He needed family.

So...

He became part of ours.

---

Looking back...

It's amazing how God prepares you for things you don't even know are coming.

Heather was pregnant.

We were building our own family.

Starting our own lives.

Most young couples are focused on careers, buying houses, and preparing for children.

We were doing all of that...

While figuring out how to care for my father.

I couldn't have done it without Heather.

Not even close.

---

People have complimented me over the years for taking care of Dad.

Honestly...

I don't know that I deserve much credit.

I was simply doing what sons should do.

Dad had spent his entire life taking care of me.

Working.

Providing.

Teaching.

Protecting.

One day...

The roles changed.

That happens in life.

Sometimes slowly.

Sometimes overnight.

Our change happened overnight.

---

One thing I don't ever want people to overlook is Heather's role in all of this.

She didn't marry my dad.

She married me.

Yet she never complained.

Matter of fact...

She loved Dad.

Respected him.

Helped care for him.

Treated him with dignity.

There were days when I honestly don't know how she managed everything.

Pregnancy.

A newborn.

Me.

Dad.

Life.

She just kept showing up.

That's Heather.

She has always quietly carried more than most people realize.

---

Eventually we moved to 707 Briar Road in Soddy Daisy.

Sixteen acres.

Dad's property.

That place became home for almost a decade.

When people hear that...

They usually picture sacrifice.

I picture life.

Some of the greatest memories our family ever made happened there.

---

Dad watched Haley grow up.

That's a gift not every grandfather gets.

She wasn't just his granddaughter.

She became his little buddy.

She'd sit with him.

Talk to him.

Love on him.

He adored her.

Watching those two together healed something inside me.

Dad had been given another chance to enjoy family.

Haley gave him that.

---

The property itself became part of our story.

It wasn't just land.

It became a place where life happened.

I built a motocross practice track back in the woods.

Not because I had to.

Because I wanted to become better.

I even built a jump.

Of course I built a jump.

Why wouldn't I?

If you're going to have a practice track...

You need a jump.

---

Those woods heard a lot of motorcycles.

First my Honda XR650R.

Then my KTM.

Hours.

Days.

Years.

I'd ride until I was exhausted.

Then come inside.

Dad would ask how it went.

Sometimes we'd laugh about crashes.

Sometimes we'd talk about races.

He enjoyed watching me enjoy life.

I think parents never really stop doing that.

---

Then Haley got interested.

That may be one of my favorite memories from those years.

I bought her a little Yamaha PW50.

Originally...

It was blue.

That wasn't going to work.

Daddy rode orange KTMs.

She wanted to look like Daddy.

So...

Off came the blue plastic.

On went orange plastic.

Now...

Her little Yamaha looked like a KTM.

She thought it was the greatest thing in the world.

Honestly...

So did I.

---

Some of my favorite pictures from that time aren't race pictures.

They're pictures of Haley and me sitting on our motorcycles talking.

Sometimes she'd be looking up at me while I explained something.

Sometimes she'd take off down the trail with me following her.

People probably thought I was teaching her to ride motorcycles.

Maybe.

I think I was really teaching her something much more important.

Life is better when you share it with people you love.

---

During those years I also started racing hare scrambles.

Most people start racing motorcycles when they're teenagers.

Not me.

I was around thirty-five years old.

Looking back...

That's a little crazy.

Actually...

Probably a lot crazy.

But I loved it.

The competition.

The woods.

The challenge.

Everything about it.

Until...

The second ACL.

That ended my racing days.

I often joke,

"That's what happens when you start racing motorcycles at thirty-five."

There's probably more truth in that statement than I'd like to admit.

---

Living with Dad also gave us something I never expected.

Time.

Real time.

Not holiday visits.

Not phone calls.

Daily life.

We talked.

A lot.

Sometimes about baseball.

Sometimes motorcycles.

Sometimes nothing important at all.

Looking back...

Those ordinary conversations became extraordinary memories.

I didn't know we were making final memories.

None of us ever do.

---

People sometimes ask whether I'd do it all again.

Move in.

Change our lives.

Care for Dad.

The answer comes quickly.

Absolutely.

Without hesitation.

Those nine years weren't something I gave up.

They were something I was given.

God gave me nine more years with my father.

Not everyone gets that.

I did.

For that...

I'll always be grateful.

Looking back now...

707 Briar Road wasn't just Dad's house.

It became one of the most important places in my entire life.

It was where generations overlapped.

Where a grandfather watched his granddaughter grow up.

Where a son became a caregiver.

Where a husband watched his wife quietly serve without complaint.

Where motorcycles echoed through the woods.

Where family happened.

That's what I remember most.

Not the hardship.

The family.
````

# Chapter 24
# The Secret

Some conversations change your life forever.

Not because they last a long time.

Because they completely change how you understand your past.

This was one of those conversations.

---

I was around twenty-two years old.

I had come home from college.

I don't remember exactly why I was back.

Probably a weekend.

Maybe a holiday.

What I do remember...

Is that I'd gone out with my Uncle Charles.

We had a couple of beers.

Nothing crazy.

Just two adults spending time together.

When I got home...

Dad wasn't happy.

---

He started talking about drinking.

That struck me as odd.

Looking back...

Dad had struggled with alcohol after the divorce.

He had gotten through those years.

By this point in his life it wasn't controlling him anymore.

Still...

Hearing him lecture me about alcohol felt strange.

I remember thinking,

"Seriously?"

I'm twenty-two years old.

I had a couple beers with your brother.

What's the big deal?

---

Then he said something.

Something he'd been hinting at for years.

Growing up...

Dad occasionally told me,

"One day I'll tell you."

I hated those words.

One day.

When?

When I was thirty?

Forty?

Fifty?

How old do you have to be before "one day" finally arrives?

That night...

I'd had enough.

I don't remember my exact words.

I do remember the attitude.

I basically told him,

"If it's about my life...

I'm old enough to know.

If you're not going to tell me...

Then don't ever bring it up again."

Probably not my finest moment.

But it was honest.

---

Dad looked at me.

Then quietly said,

"You know...

Gloria isn't your biological mother."

Everything stopped.

I honestly don't remember much of what happened for the next several seconds.

Maybe minutes.

It's amazing what your brain does when something that significant lands.

People think your mind races.

Mine didn't.

It froze.

---

Wait.

What?

What do you mean...

She's not my biological mother?

How?

Who is?

Does Mom know?

Do Buddy...

Lindsey...

Julie...

Know?

How long has everybody known?

Why didn't anybody tell me?

Question after question started flooding in.

I don't even remember asking them in order.

I just remember trying to catch up with twenty-two years of information in a matter of minutes.

---

Dad kept talking.

One sentence in particular stayed with me.

He told me my biological mother had struggled with alcohol and drugs.

He said doctors believed I had been born addicted.

He also said they'd warned him that because of that...

I might someday struggle with addiction too.

Suddenly...

The conversation about beer made sense.

It wasn't really about beer.

It was about fear.

Dad had spent twenty-two years quietly watching...

Wondering if one day I'd become addicted too.

That's why he'd reacted.

Not because I'd had a couple beers.

Because he was scared.

Looking back...

I understand that now.

I didn't then.

---

Then another realization hit me.

Mom.

Why had she never told me?

Did she know?

Of course she knew.

She had to know.

Then...

Why?

Why would someone keep something like that from a child?

The answer wouldn't come until much later.

At that moment...

All I felt was confusion.

Not anger.

Confusion.

My whole life suddenly looked different.

Every memory.

Every photograph.

Every family gathering.

Everything.

It was like someone had handed me a thousand-piece puzzle...

Then dumped another thousand pieces on top of it.

---

One memory immediately came rushing back.

The divorce.

I was fourteen years old again.

Standing there hearing Dad say,

"If you leave...

You're not taking Danny."

Then hearing Mom quietly answer,

"I know."

For eight years...

I'd believed she didn't fight for me.

Now...

Everything changed.

She couldn't.

Not legally.

Not biologically.

She wasn't saying she didn't want me.

She was acknowledging something she couldn't change.

I remember sitting there...

Realizing I'd carried the wrong story in my heart for almost a decade.

That hurt.

Not because Mom had done something wrong.

Because I'd unknowingly judged her for something she never did.

---

People have asked me if I got angry.

Honestly...

Not really.

Shocked?

Absolutely.

Confused?

Without question.

Angry?

Not the way people expect.

Mostly...

I wanted answers.

Who was my biological mother?

Did I have brothers?

Sisters?

Grandparents?

Did they know about me?

Were they alive?

Had anybody ever looked for me?

Questions.

Questions.

Questions.

It felt like my entire identity had been picked up and shaken.

---

The strange part is...

Nothing really changed.

The next morning...

Mom was still Mom.

Dad was still Dad.

Buddy was still Buddy.

Lindsey was still Lindsey.

Julie was still Julie.

The people I loved hadn't changed.

Only my understanding of them had.

That taught me something.

Truth changes perspective.

It doesn't always change love.

Matter of fact...

In my case...

The truth made me love Mom even more.

Because now I understood the choice she'd made.

She hadn't simply raised me.

She had chosen me.

There's a difference.

A big one.

---

Looking back...

That conversation divided my life into two parts.

Everything before I knew.

Everything after.

The amazing thing is...

Both parts still belong to me.

Neither one cancels the other.

I didn't stop being a Jenkins.

I simply discovered another branch of my family tree.

One I never knew existed.

And that discovery...

Would eventually lead me to another family...

Waiting quietly...

On the other side of an Ancestry website.
````

# Chapter 25
# Finding My Family

For years...

I knew there was another part of my story.

I just didn't know where to find it.

Dad had finally told me that Gloria wasn't my biological mother.

He had told me my biological mother's name.

Barbara Jean.

That was about it.

No photographs.

No addresses.

No stories.

Just...

A name.

It was enough to make me curious.

Not enough to satisfy that curiosity.

---

I've been asked over the years why I wanted to know.

The answer surprises some people.

I wasn't looking for another mom.

I already had one.

Gloria had earned that title a thousand times over.

Nothing was ever going to change that.

I wasn't looking for someone to replace her.

I was looking for understanding.

Who did I look like?

Where did I get my personality?

Did I have brothers?

Sisters?

Grandparents?

Medical history?

Simple questions.

Questions most people never have to ask.

---

Then something happened that changed everything.

Ancestry.com.

Today people take websites like Ancestry for granted.

Back then...

It was still pretty new.

I decided to create an account.

Not because I expected much.

Honestly...

I didn't know what to expect.

I started entering what little information I knew.

Then I came to the section asking about my parents.

That was harder than I expected.

Who do I put?

Gloria?

Barbara Jean?

My heart wanted to type Gloria.

The website wanted biological information.

So...

With a strange feeling in my stomach...

I typed Barbara Jean.

That may not sound like a big deal.

To me...

It was.

It felt almost disloyal.

Even though it wasn't.

---

After entering the information...

A little green leaf appeared.

If you've ever used Ancestry...

You know exactly what that means.

A hint.

The website thought it knew something.

I clicked it.

Barbara Jean appeared on someone else's family tree.

I stared at the screen for a long time.

Then...

I sent a message.

Something simple.

Introducing myself.

Explaining who I believed I was.

Then I waited.

Not really expecting anything.

---

A few days later...

I opened my email.

There was a response.

From a woman named Karen.

She claimed to be my sister.

She left a phone number.

Asked me to call.

I remember sitting there looking at the email.

Thinking...

"This can't be real."

It had to be some kind of mistake.

Didn't it?

Heather and I talked about it.

We decided...

What do I have to lose?

I picked up the phone.

---

A woman answered.

She couldn't even speak.

She was crying so hard.

Finally...

Between sobs...

She managed to say,

"Hi, Danny."

That conversation lasted around three hours.

Looking back...

I don't remember much of what we actually talked about.

I remember the emotion.

She laughed.

She cried.

Then laughed again.

I...

Didn't.

Not because I didn't care.

Because I was still trying to decide if any of this was real.

Imagine being told you have sisters you've never met.

How exactly are you supposed to react?

I honestly didn't know.

---

Near the end of the conversation she said,

"You need to call Uncle Danny."

Apparently...

He knew my father.

He knew me as a baby.

If anyone could verify the story...

It would be him.

So I called.

---

Talking to Uncle Danny felt different.

There was something calming about him.

Straightforward.

Matter-of-fact.

Kind.

We talked for quite a while.

Then he asked me something I'll never forget.

He said,

"You've seen pictures of your mom, right?"

I answered,

"No."

There was silence.

Then he said,

"Really?"

He couldn't believe it.

Within minutes...

He was emailing photographs.

Barbara Jean.

Her brothers.

Her sisters.

My biological family.

For the first time in my life...

I was looking at faces that looked like mine.

That was surreal.

---

Even then...

Part of me still wondered.

"What if this is wrong?"

So...

I printed the photographs.

Drove over to Dad.

Laid them in front of him.

He looked at them.

One by one.

Then...

He started crying.

He recognized almost everyone immediately.

When he reached one particular sister...

He shook his head.

No.

Later I learned why.

She hadn't been part of that crowd.

She lived differently.

Uncle Danny had already explained that.

That moment settled it.

Everything was real.

Every doubt disappeared.

---

Not long afterward...

Plans were made.

I flew back to California.

Heather and Haley stayed with Mom.

I caught another flight to Sacramento.

Waiting at the airport...

Was my sister Rachelle.

I don't know what I expected.

Awkwardness maybe.

Instead...

She wrapped me in a hug.

Just like we'd known each other forever.

Sometimes...

God has a way of making difficult things unexpectedly peaceful.

That hug was one of those moments.

---

As I look back now...

Finding my biological family didn't replace anyone.

It expanded my story.

That's an important distinction.

I didn't lose Mom.

I gained history.

I didn't stop being a Jenkins.

I simply discovered another branch of the tree.

And as incredible as that first phone call had been...

The most emotional meeting was still waiting for me.

Her name was Sharron.

And meeting her would change both of us forever.
````

# Chapter 26
# Sharron

Of all the people I met after discovering my biological family...

Sharron probably affected me the most.

Not because we spent the most time together.

Not because we became especially close afterward.

Because I realized...

She had loved me first.

---

Before I ever lived with Dad...

Before Gloria became my mom...

Before I even had memories...

Sharron was taking care of me.

She was only about seventeen years old.

Think about that for a minute.

Seventeen.

Most seventeen-year-olds are worried about school.

Friends.

Dating.

Cars.

Sharron was helping raise a baby.

Me.

---

The more I learned...

The more I realized she had sacrificed far more than I ever knew.

She loved me.

Then...

One day...

I disappeared.

From her perspective...

I was simply gone.

Imagine loving a little brother...

Helping raise him...

Then never seeing him again.

Not for a year.

Not for five years.

For decades.

That's a different kind of loss.

---

When I finally met my biological family...

Everyone welcomed me.

Karen.

Rachelle.

Vickie.

Their families.

Everybody seemed excited.

Everybody...

Except Sharron.

She was polite.

Friendly enough.

But...

Reserved.

Watching.

Almost skeptical.

I couldn't quite figure it out.

---

Before making that trip...

I'd put together little photo albums for everyone.

I thought it would help.

Each album started with pictures of me as a little boy.

Then moved through childhood.

Sports.

College.

Heather.

Haley.

Basically...

My life.

I handed one to each sister.

They all started flipping through it.

Then...

Something happened.

Sharron quietly got up...

Walked into the kitchen...

And disappeared.

---

One of my sisters looked at me and said,

"You need to go talk to her."

So I did.

I walked into the kitchen.

She was standing there...

Looking at the photo album.

Crying.

I started talking.

Small talk mostly.

Not really sure what to say.

Suddenly...

She turned around...

Wrapped her arms around me...

Kissed me...

And just cried.

Really cried.

---

She finally explained.

Until she saw those photographs...

She wasn't completely convinced.

Not because she didn't want me to be her brother.

Because after all those years...

It almost seemed too impossible to believe.

Then she saw pictures of me with Dad.

Pictures only her little brother could have.

That's when it became real.

Her baby brother...

Had actually come home.

---

That night...

Plans changed.

Originally I was supposed to go back and stay with Rachelle.

Sharron had other ideas.

"No."

"He's staying with me."

Nobody argued.

They understood.

We stayed up almost the entire night talking.

Pictures covered the table.

Story after story.

Question after question.

For the first time in my life...

Someone was telling me about my earliest months.

Things no one else could tell me.

Things only she remembered.

I soaked it all in.

---

Then she told me something I'll never forget.

She said that after I went to live with Dad...

She continued coming around for a while.

Eventually...

I started asking where she was.

She realized that if she kept coming...

I'd continue asking.

So...

She disappeared.

Not because she stopped loving me.

Because she wanted me to completely bond with my new family.

Think about that.

A teenage girl...

Making one of the hardest decisions of her life...

For the good of her little brother.

I've thought about that many times.

I don't know if I could've done what she did.

---

She also told me something else.

This conversation...

This night...

Could only happen once.

She had spent years putting that part of her life into a box.

A box she rarely opened.

Seeing me had opened it.

She was willing to answer every question I had.

Share every story she remembered.

Cry every tear that needed crying.

But afterward...

The box had to be closed again.

Not because she didn't love me.

Because the pain was too great.

I understood.

At least...

As much as I could.

---

Looking back...

That night was a gift.

Not because every question got answered.

Some never will.

It was a gift because I got to know my sister.

Not just her name.

Her heart.

I saw her strength.

Her pain.

Her love.

Her sacrifice.

Those things matter much more than facts.

---

People sometimes ask me how many sisters I have.

That's actually harder to answer than you'd think.

Biologically...

Several.

Growing up...

Two.

Emotionally...

All of them.

Life doesn't always fit into neat little categories.

Neither do families.

Mine certainly doesn't.

---

I don't get to talk with Sharron very often.

Life has a way of taking people different directions.

But every time I think about her...

I remember one thing.

Long before I knew her name...

Long before I knew my own story...

She loved me.

Sometimes...

Love looks like holding on.

Sometimes...

Love looks like letting go.

Sharron did both.

I'll always be grateful for that.
````

# Chapter 27
# Baseball Dreams

Looking back now, I think baseball and I found each other at exactly the right time.

Some kids find music.

Some find art.

Some find cars.

I found baseball.

Or maybe baseball found me.

Either way...

It became the place where I discovered not only what I could do...

But who I was.

---

People have asked me if I loved football more than baseball.

No.

Football thrilled me.

Baseball became part of my identity.

There's a difference.

Football happened on Friday nights.

Baseball happened almost every day.

Baseball was where I escaped.

Baseball was where I thought.

Baseball was where I dreamed.

---

I loved everything about the game.

The smell of freshly cut grass.

The sound of batting practice.

The dirt around home plate.

The feel of pine tar on a bat.

The sound a baseball makes when you hit it perfectly.

There's a sound baseball players understand immediately.

You don't have to watch the ball.

You hear it.

When you square one up...

It sounds different.

Cleaner.

Harder.

Almost effortless.

There's no better feeling in sports.

---

I also loved practice.

Some people think athletes only enjoy games.

Not me.

I honestly loved practice almost as much.

That's where you got better.

That's where you figured things out.

That's where tomorrow's success was built.

Games were simply an opportunity to see whether practice had worked.

---

Dad rarely had to tell me to practice.

Matter of fact...

He usually had to tell me to come inside.

I'd hit baseballs until it got too dark to see.

Throw against the garage.

Field imaginary ground balls.

Sometimes there wasn't anybody else around.

Didn't matter.

I wasn't practicing because somebody expected me to.

I practiced because I loved becoming better.

Looking back...

That mindset has followed me my entire life.

Whether it was baseball...

Payroll...

Leadership...

Or Whole Life Journey...

I enjoy building something.

Improving something.

Learning something.

That started on a baseball field.

---

One thing baseball gave me was confidence.

Not arrogance.

Confidence.

There's a difference.

Confidence says,

"I've prepared."

Arrogance says,

"I'm better than you."

Those aren't the same thing.

Now...

Did I occasionally cross that line as a teenager?

Probably.

Teenagers have a way of doing that.

But my confidence never came from believing I was more important than someone else.

It came from believing I'd done the work.

When you've hit thousands of baseballs...

Taken thousands of ground balls...

Thrown thousands of throws...

Confidence naturally follows.

Not because somebody handed it to you.

Because you earned it.

---

As the years passed...

The dreams grew too.

Little League dreams became high school dreams.

High school dreams became college dreams.

College dreams became professional dreams.

None of it felt unrealistic.

It simply felt like the next step.

That's one thing people sometimes misunderstand.

I never walked around thinking,

"I'm definitely going to play Major League Baseball."

I thought,

"I'm going to become as good as I possibly can...

...and see where God takes it."

That's a healthier dream.

One focused on growth instead of outcomes.

I wish I'd understood that even better back then.

---

Baseball also taught me humility.

Every hitter fails.

The greatest hitters in history failed almost seven out of every ten at-bats.

Think about that.

You can fail seventy percent of the time...

And still become a Hall of Famer.

That's a remarkable lesson for life.

Failure isn't final.

Failure is expected.

The question isn't whether you'll fail.

The question is what you'll do after you fail.

Baseball taught me to let yesterday stay yesterday.

Strike out?

Fine.

There's another at-bat coming.

Boot a ground ball?

Fine.

The next one is already on its way.

I've tried to carry that into every area of my life.

It's made me a better leader.

---

There came a point where I realized baseball wasn't simply something I loved.

It was opening doors.

Scouts.

Invitations.

Conversations.

Summer teams.

Higher levels of competition.

Every season seemed to bring another opportunity.

That was exciting.

It was also humbling.

Because the higher I climbed...

The more I realized just how many incredible athletes were out there.

Everywhere I went...

Somebody else had been the star of their hometown.

Now we were all standing on the same field together.

That perspective stays with you.

---

One thing I've thought about often over the years...

Why baseball?

Why not football?

Why not basketball?

I honestly don't know.

Maybe because baseball mirrors life better than any other sport.

It's patient.

It's strategic.

It's individual.

It's team-oriented.

You can do everything right...

...and still make an out.

You can do everything wrong...

...and bloop a hit over second base.

Sometimes life works that way too.

The trick is showing up again tomorrow.

Ready to play.

---

When I look back now...

I don't remember every home run.

I don't remember every championship.

I don't remember every batting average.

I remember the feeling.

Walking through the gate.

Hearing batting practice.

Putting on the uniform.

Looking across the infield before the first pitch.

Feeling completely...

At home.

That's what baseball gave me.

Not just a dream.

A place where I discovered who God created me to become.

Everything else...

Started there.
````

title: George and Jack
version: 1.0

# Chapter 28
# George and Jack

Every athlete has people who quietly change the direction of their career.

Mine were named Jack French and George Genovese.

If you only looked at a baseball résumé, you'd probably miss how important those two men became.

I never will.

---

Jack French was the man who found me.

That distinction matters.

Over the years I've accidentally mixed their roles together in conversation, so let me get it right here.

Jack was the scout.

George became the mentor.

Two very different roles.

Both equally important.

---

I still remember the night Jack first introduced himself.

I'd had a good game.

Actually...

A really good game.

If memory serves me correctly, I hit a double and a triple.

I also made several plays at third base.

To me...

It was just another baseball game.

To Jack...

Apparently it was something more.

After the game he walked over and introduced himself.

Simple.

Professional.

No big speech.

No dramatic movie moment.

Just an old baseball man introducing himself to a kid.

Looking back...

Neither one of us knew where that introduction would eventually lead.

---

Jack invited me to play with one of the San Francisco Giants' semi-professional teams.

Now...

When you're a high school baseball player...

Those words get your attention.

Suddenly you're putting on a Giants uniform.

You're standing beside older players.

Better players.

Players chasing the same dream you're chasing.

You quickly learn whether you belong.

Fortunately...

I did.

---

That's where I met George Genovese.

George was unlike anybody I'd ever met.

He had spent his life around baseball.

Not just watching it.

Living it.

He understood hitters.

He understood players.

More importantly...

He understood people.

---

George threw batting practice to me many, many times.

If you've never faced professional batting practice...

It isn't just somebody throwing baseballs.

Every pitch has purpose.

Every swing gets evaluated.

Every habit gets noticed.

George noticed everything.

---

Then there was his famous phrase.

I don't know how many times I heard it.

Hundreds maybe.

Probably more.

Some hitter would try to hit the cover off the baseball.

George would immediately yell,

> "Quit swinging from the ass!"

The first time you hear it...

You laugh.

Eventually...

You realize he's teaching something much bigger.

Stop trying to manufacture power.

Hit the baseball.

Square it up.

Trust yourself.

The power will happen.

Funny enough...

That advice applies to life too.

Don't force greatness.

Do the fundamentals well.

Results usually follow.

---

George believed in me.

I knew that.

You can tell when someone believes in you.

They invest time.

George invested time.

Not because he had to.

Because he wanted to.

That means more than people realize.

---

Eventually...

Draft conversations became serious.

Really serious.

The Giants drafted me.

Then came contract discussions.

George kept working on my behalf.

Matter of fact...

He believed enough that he called the General Manager.

The General Manager flew down to Southern California.

Imagine that for a minute.

You're eighteen years old.

The General Manager of the San Francisco Giants flies down specifically to watch you.

That's surreal.

---

He watched batting practice.

He watched infield.

He watched my first at-bat.

Then...

I struck out.

Perfect timing.

I still laugh about that.

Baseball has a funny sense of humor.

Of course I struck out right then.

---

The General Manager left.

Later...

George came back with another offer.

Twenty thousand dollars.

Dad had always said forty thousand would be enough to seriously consider giving up college.

Twenty wasn't forty.

George had done everything he could.

I knew it.

Dad knew it.

George knew it.

Sometimes life simply lands where it lands.

---

People have asked me over the years if I was disappointed.

Honestly...

Not really.

I was grateful.

Think about it.

How many kids grow up dreaming about professional baseball?

Millions.

How many have scouts invest years in them?

Very few.

How many have a General Manager fly in to watch them personally?

Even fewer.

Whether I signed or not...

Those men believed in me.

Nobody can ever take that away.

---

I also learned something important from George.

Baseball people have a way of seeing through excuses.

George didn't care how good you were yesterday.

He cared about today's swing.

Today's attitude.

Today's effort.

Looking back...

That's exactly how I've tried to lead people throughout my career.

Yesterday's success is wonderful.

Today's effort still matters.

---

When I think about Jack...

I think about opportunity.

When I think about George...

I think about development.

Jack opened the door.

George taught me how to walk through it.

Both men changed my life.

Neither one probably realized just how much.

Years later...

When I hear someone ask,

"Who believed in you?"

Their names immediately come to mind.

Every young person needs someone who sees something in them before they fully see it themselves.

I was blessed enough to have two.

Jack French.

George Genovese.

I'll be grateful to both of them for the rest of my life.
````
