# Chapter 29
# Choosing Alabama

Every young athlete dreams about getting to choose.

Most never get the opportunity.

They're simply hoping someone wants them.

I was blessed enough to have a choice.

Professional baseball.

Or college.

At eighteen years old...

That felt like the biggest decision in the world.

Looking back...

Maybe it was.

---

The San Francisco Giants had drafted me.

That wasn't a dream anymore.

It was reality.

There was a contract sitting in front of me.

There was money attached to it.

There was a chance to begin chasing the Major Leagues immediately.

For a kid who had spent his entire childhood dreaming about baseball...

It was everything I'd worked toward.

At least...

That's what I thought.

---

Then there was Alabama.

People sometimes ask why Alabama.

The answer is simple.

Because I wanted to play for Alabama.

Not because they were the only school interested.

Not because it was convenient.

Because when I pictured myself playing college baseball...

I pictured myself wearing Alabama across my chest.

There are dreams you slowly develop.

Then there are dreams that somehow quietly become part of who you are.

Alabama had become one of those dreams.

---

Dad and I talked a lot.

Probably more than either one of us realized.

Sometimes we'd sit quietly.

Sometimes we'd go over numbers.

Sometimes we'd simply think.

One thing I appreciated about Dad...

He never ordered me to do anything.

He gave me his opinion.

Then...

He trusted me enough to make the decision.

Looking back...

That's a tremendous gift.

Parents don't always know when to let go.

Dad somehow did.

---

The money mattered.

Let's not pretend it didn't.

I was eighteen years old.

Ten thousand dollars sounded like a fortune.

Twenty thousand sounded even better.

I'd never seen that kind of money.

Most kids my age hadn't either.

But Dad wasn't looking at eighteen-year-old Danny.

He was looking at forty-year-old Danny.

He'd spent his entire life building houses.

Working with men whose dreams sometimes didn't work out.

He understood something I didn't.

Professional baseball is a business.

A hard business.

Very few players make it.

Even fewer stay there.

He wasn't trying to keep me from my dream.

He was trying to make sure I still had a future if the dream didn't work out.

---

One conversation has stayed with me all these years.

Dad said something like,

"If they're willing to invest in you...

They'll still be willing after college."

That made sense to me.

If I got better...

If I got stronger...

If I matured...

Wouldn't my value increase?

That seemed logical.

Sometimes it works that way.

Sometimes it doesn't.

Life rarely gives you guarantees.

---

I also thought about something else.

Education.

People sometimes assume I chose Alabama because of the education.

That certainly mattered.

But if I'm being honest...

Baseball was driving the decision.

I wanted to compete against the best players in the country.

I wanted to find out how good I could become.

College wasn't the backup plan.

It was another step toward the same dream.

---

Eventually...

The decision became clear.

I wasn't signing.

I was going to Alabama.

I remember calling people.

Sharing the news.

Most were excited.

Some thought I was crazy.

That's okay.

Sometimes the right decision doesn't make sense to everyone else.

It only has to make sense to you.

---

Looking back now...

I've asked myself the question everyone asks.

"What if?"

What if I'd signed?

Would I have reached the Major Leagues?

Maybe.

Maybe not.

Nobody knows.

Would I have eventually gotten hurt?

Maybe.

Would I have spent years riding buses through the minor leagues?

Possibly.

Would I have become one of the tiny percentage who actually made it?

We'll never know.

And honestly...

I'm okay with that.

---

People often assume that because I didn't make the Major Leagues...

The decision somehow didn't work out.

I completely disagree.

The decision gave me Alabama.

It gave me Jerry Stubbs.

It eventually gave me Heather.

It gave me experiences that shaped who I became.

Looking back...

I don't evaluate that decision by asking,

"Did I make the Major Leagues?"

I evaluate it by asking,

"Would I choose this life again?"

Without hesitation...

Yes.

Absolutely yes.

---

Years later...

After Heather and Haley became part of my life...

That question became even easier.

Would I trade Heather for a chance at the Major Leagues?

No.

Would I trade Haley?

Not for anything.

Would I trade the life God eventually built for me?

Never.

Not once.

Not even for a childhood dream.

---

Dreams are funny.

Sometimes God fulfills them exactly the way we imagined.

Sometimes...

He fulfills something much bigger.

At eighteen...

I couldn't see that.

At fifty-five...

I can.

The dream wasn't really baseball.

The dream was becoming the man God intended me to become.

Baseball simply happened to be one of the roads He used to get me there.

Looking back now...

I wouldn't change a thing.
````

# Chapter 30
# Alabama Baseball

When I finally walked onto the baseball field at the University of Alabama...

I remember taking a deep breath.

Not because I was nervous.

Because I'd dreamed about that moment for a long time.

Dreams are funny.

You spend years imagining them.

Then one day...

They become ordinary.

You still have to show up.

Still have to work.

Still have to earn your place.

Dreams don't remove the work.

They simply change the address where the work happens.

---

One thing became obvious almost immediately.

Everybody was good.

Not good compared to high school.

Good.

Period.

Every pitcher had been the ace somewhere.

Every hitter had been the cleanup hitter somewhere.

Every infielder had been the best player on somebody's team.

You quickly realize...

You're not special anymore.

And strangely enough...

I liked that.

I've always enjoyed environments where I have to earn respect.

---

Practice was different than anything I'd experienced.

The pace.

The expectations.

The attention to detail.

Everything mattered.

A routine ground ball mattered.

Backing up a throw mattered.

Running out every fly ball mattered.

There weren't many free passes.

Not because the coaches were mean.

Because excellence lives in the details.

That's a lesson I've carried into every leadership position I've ever held.

---

One thing that surprised me was how much I enjoyed simply being around baseball people.

If you've never spent time around a college baseball program...

It's hard to explain.

There are baseball conversations everywhere.

At breakfast.

In the locker room.

Walking across campus.

Someone's always talking about a swing.

A pitcher.

A play from yesterday.

A game from ten years ago.

Baseball isn't just something you do.

It's a language.

And I loved speaking it.

---

I also learned something about pressure.

Most people think pressure happens during games.

That's actually the easy part.

The real pressure happens every single day.

Because somebody is always trying to take your spot.

College baseball is brutally competitive.

If you're not improving...

Somebody else is.

That doesn't create fear.

It creates urgency.

I never wanted to wake up one day and realize somebody had outworked me.

That thought bothered me far more than losing a game.

---

Looking back...

I realize Alabama also exposed me to something else.

Perspective.

Some of the players around me eventually played in the Major Leagues.

Some stayed there a long time.

Some never got out of the minors.

Some never played professionally at all.

The difference between those groups was often incredibly small.

People think success is separated by miles.

Sometimes it's separated by inches.

Or one injury.

Or one opportunity.

Or one organization believing in you.

That's humbling.

---

One thing I loved about Alabama baseball...

Nobody cared what you'd done before you arrived.

You could've hit .500 in high school.

Nobody cared.

You could've been drafted.

Nobody cared.

Every day started at zero.

Looking back...

That's one of the healthiest environments I've ever been part of.

Respect wasn't inherited.

It was earned.

Again.

And again.

And again.

---

I've often thought about the friendships that formed during those years.

There's something unique about teammates.

Not acquaintances.

Teammates.

You sweat together.

Condition together.

Lose together.

Win together.

Travel together.

Eat together.

Laugh together.

You learn who people really are.

Some friendships fade after graduation.

Others become permanent.

Jerry was one of those.

There were others too.

Men I still think about when someone mentions Alabama baseball.

Not because we talk every week.

Because we shared something that only teammates truly understand.

---

People sometimes ask me if Alabama was everything I hoped it would be.

Yes.

And no.

Yes...

Because the baseball was incredible.

The people were incredible.

The experience changed my life.

No...

Because dreams never unfold exactly the way we imagine.

That's okay.

Life usually gives us something different than we planned.

Sometimes...

It gives us something better.

---

I also began realizing something about myself.

I wasn't just an athlete anymore.

I was becoming a man.

That transition doesn't happen overnight.

Nobody announces it.

It quietly sneaks up on you.

One day you're worried about making the lineup.

The next you're thinking about careers.

Marriage.

Purpose.

The future.

College has a way of doing that.

If you let it.

---

When I think about Alabama today...

The first things that come to mind aren't championships.

Or statistics.

Or awards.

I remember teammates laughing in the locker room.

Long bus rides.

Batting practice.

The smell of fresh-cut grass.

The sound of aluminum bats echoing across Sewell-Thomas Stadium.

I remember believing...

For a while...

That I was exactly where I was supposed to be.

Looking back...

I still believe that.

Because whether Alabama was the destination...

Or simply another stop along the journey...

It prepared me for everything that came afterward.

Sometimes that's the greatest gift a season of life can give you.

It doesn't just prepare you for tomorrow.

It prepares you for the rest of your life.
````

# Chapter 31
# Becoming an Adult

People think adulthood begins the day you graduate.

Or the day you get married.

Or the day you have children.

I don't think that's true.

Looking back...

Adulthood happened much more quietly.

It happened one responsibility at a time.

One difficult decision at a time.

One mistake at a time.

One lesson at a time.

Before I realized it...

The little boy riding motorcycles around Gorman...

Had become a man.

I just didn't notice it happening.

---

College has a funny way of forcing you to grow up.

Nobody reminds you to get out of bed.

Nobody checks to see if you're studying.

Nobody makes you go to class.

Nobody tells you to do your laundry.

Trust me...

That became obvious pretty quickly.

If you don't wash clothes...

You eventually run out of clothes.

Life has a way of teaching practical lessons.

Sometimes they're funny.

Sometimes they're expensive.

Usually...

They're memorable.

---

One thing I appreciated about Alabama was that nobody cared about excuses.

The professors didn't.

The coaches didn't.

Life certainly didn't.

If you overslept...

That was your problem.

If you forgot an assignment...

That was your problem.

If you were late...

That was your problem.

Looking back...

I think that's healthy.

Responsibility isn't something someone gives you.

It's something you accept.

---

I also started paying attention to people.

Really paying attention.

Not just who they were.

How they lived.

How they treated others.

How they handled disappointment.

How they celebrated success.

Baseball had always taught me to observe.

Now I found myself observing life.

Without realizing it...

I was collecting lessons.

Some from coaches.

Some from professors.

Some from teammates.

Some from complete strangers.

I've always believed wisdom is available almost everywhere...

If you're paying attention.

---

One thing I noticed early in adulthood...

People often separate work from character.

I've never been able to do that.

How you work says something about who you are.

If someone consistently cuts corners...

That usually shows up somewhere else too.

If someone always keeps their word...

That usually shows up everywhere.

Integrity isn't something you turn on at work.

It's who you are.

I didn't have those words back then.

I lived them long before I could explain them.

---

Money also became real.

Growing up...

Money just sort of existed.

Bills got paid.

Food appeared.

Gas somehow found its way into the car.

As a young adult...

You suddenly realize...

None of that happens by accident.

Everything costs something.

Some lessons come through success.

Others arrive in your checking account.

Usually when the balance is lower than you'd hoped.

---

I've laughed over the years because people sometimes assume I had everything figured out.

Not even close.

I made plenty of mistakes.

Bought things I shouldn't have.

Waited too long to do things.

Acted before thinking.

Thought before acting.

Pretty much every mistake young adults make...

I probably made a version of it.

The important part wasn't avoiding mistakes.

It was learning from them.

---

One lesson Dad taught me kept coming back.

He used to say,

> "A man's word ought to mean something."

Simple.

Short.

Powerful.

As I got older...

I realized how rare that had become.

People promise things all the time.

Then quietly back away.

Dad didn't.

If he told you he'd be there...

He showed up.

If he gave his word...

You could count on it.

I wanted to become that kind of man.

I'm still working on it.

---

Somewhere during those college years...

I also started thinking differently about success.

As a kid...

Success looked like baseball.

By my early twenties...

It started looking like something bigger.

Character.

Faith.

Marriage.

Purpose.

I didn't have all the answers.

I still don't.

But I started asking better questions.

Sometimes that's more important.

---

Looking back...

Those years weren't simply preparing me for a career.

They were preparing me for Heather.

For Haley.

For leadership.

For taking care of Dad after his stroke.

For discovering my biological family.

For everything that followed.

At the time...

I thought I was simply becoming an adult.

Now I realize...

God was quietly shaping the man I would eventually become.

One ordinary day at a time.

And that's usually how He works.

Not through dramatic moments.

Through faithful ones.
````

# Chapter 32
# The Pinnacle Group

When I graduated from Alabama, I had two things.

A degree.

And absolutely no idea what I wanted to do for the rest of my life.

Funny how that works.

You spend years preparing for adulthood...

Then somebody hands you a diploma and says,

"Good luck."

---

Like a lot of young graduates, I wasn't chasing a lifelong career.

I was chasing an opportunity.

The opportunity that found me was a consulting company called The Pinnacle Group.

Looking back, I don't think I appreciated how much that job would shape the rest of my professional life.

It wasn't because of the work itself.

It was because of the people.

And because consulting teaches you something almost no other profession can.

It teaches you to solve problems.

---

One week you might be in one city.

The next week...

Somewhere completely different.

Different company.

Different personalities.

Different systems.

Different problems.

You learn very quickly that every organization thinks its problems are unique.

They're usually not.

People are people.

Processes are processes.

Leadership is leadership.

The names change.

The principles rarely do.

---

Consulting also taught me how to walk into a room full of strangers.

That's an underrated skill.

Imagine walking into a conference room where nobody knows you.

Half the people don't want you there.

The other half hope you can fix something.

You have about five minutes to establish credibility.

Not because you know everything.

Because you ask good questions.

That lesson has stayed with me my entire career.

You don't earn trust by pretending to have every answer.

You earn trust by helping people solve problems.

---

Travel became part of life.

Hotels.

Rental cars.

Airports.

Restaurant meals.

Packing.

Unpacking.

Packing again.

At first...

It felt exciting.

Then it simply became normal.

People sometimes ask if I enjoyed traveling.

I enjoyed seeing new places.

I didn't particularly enjoy living out of a suitcase.

There's a difference.

---

One of the best things Pinnacle gave me was perspective.

Working with different companies allowed me to see how differently people approached the exact same problems.

One company would make something incredibly complicated.

Another would solve it with a conversation.

One manager inspired people.

Another managed by fear.

Watching all of that quietly built my leadership philosophy long before I became a leader myself.

I didn't know it then.

I see it now.

---

It was also during my time with Pinnacle that life became much more interesting.

Not because of work.

Because of Heather.

She had become part of my life.

And now I had a job that wanted me traveling all over the country.

That created challenges.

Long-distance relationships aren't easy.

Long-distance engagement isn't easy either.

But somehow...

We made it work.

Looking back...

I think those miles actually strengthened us.

They forced us to communicate.

Really communicate.

When you can't simply drive across town...

Conversations matter more.

We learned that early.

---

One of my favorite memories from Pinnacle had nothing to do with consulting.

It had everything to do with a cruise.

Every year the company rewarded employees with a company trip.

One year...

It was a cruise.

That cruise eventually became the setting for one of the biggest moments of my life.

Actually...

Almost.

Originally...

My plan was to propose to Heather while we were on that cruise.

I thought it would be perfect.

Ocean.

Sunset.

Romantic.

Only...

Word got out.

Coworkers started congratulating us before I'd even asked.

Apparently I wasn't nearly as good at keeping secrets as I thought.

So instead...

The proposal happened before we ever boarded the ship.

Looking back...

I'm glad it did.

It became our story.

Not someone else's idea of romance.

Ours.

---

One thing Pinnacle also taught me was confidence in business.

Up until then...

Most of my confidence had come from athletics.

Now I was learning I could compete professionally too.

Not with a bat.

Not with a football.

With ideas.

With preparation.

With work ethic.

That realization quietly changed my life.

Because eventually...

Sports would end.

Work wouldn't.

I needed somewhere else to compete.

Consulting became that place.

---

People sometimes ask if I ever imagined I'd end up leading HRIS, Payroll, and Compensation.

Not even a little.

At that point in my life...

I didn't know what HRIS was.

I certainly didn't know what payroll systems looked like.

God has a funny way of preparing us for futures we can't yet imagine.

Consulting wasn't the destination.

It was training.

I just didn't know what I was training for.

Not yet.

But He did.
````

# Chapter 33
# The First Time I Saw Her

I've thought a lot over the years about first impressions.

Sometimes they're wrong.

Sometimes they're incomplete.

Every once in a while...

They're absolutely right.

Mine was.

---

I don't remember every detail about the first time I saw Heather.

I wish I did.

Memory doesn't always work that way.

What I remember isn't a conversation.

Or what she was wearing.

Or what anybody else said.

I remember thinking...

"She's different."

Now...

If you'd asked me that day what I meant...

I couldn't have answered.

She was beautiful.

That was obvious.

But beautiful women weren't exactly rare on a college campus.

This was something else.

Something quieter.

Something deeper.

Something I couldn't explain.

---

God has a funny way of preparing you for people before you realize they're important.

I had dated enough by then.

Enough to know what I didn't want.

Enough to recognize that excitement and compatibility aren't always the same thing.

Enough to realize that attraction alone doesn't build a life.

Heather wasn't just someone I wanted to date.

Without realizing it...

She was someone I wanted to know.

Really know.

There's a difference.

---

I've often wondered why God doesn't show us more of the future.

Then I think about Heather.

If someone had told me that first day,

"That's the woman you'll spend the rest of your life with."

I probably would've panicked.

Instead...

God simply let us meet.

Then become friends.

Then slowly fall in love.

Looking back...

That was much wiser.

---

One thing I noticed almost immediately...

Heather was comfortable being herself.

She didn't seem interested in impressing people.

She wasn't loud.

She wasn't trying to be the center of attention.

She didn't have to be.

She had a quiet confidence about her.

The older I get...

The more I admire quiet confidence.

It doesn't need applause.

It doesn't need recognition.

It simply exists.

Heather has always been that way.

---

There's something else I remember.

Laughter.

Heather laughed easily.

Not the fake laugh people sometimes use to be polite.

The real one.

The one that starts in your stomach and escapes before you can stop it.

I've always loved making people laugh.

When Heather laughed...

I found myself wanting to hear it again.

Not because it made me feel important.

Because it made me happy.

That's a pretty good sign you're heading in the right direction.

---

One thing people probably didn't know about me then...

I wasn't nearly as confident in relationships as I appeared.

Sports?

Absolutely.

Put me on a baseball field.

Give me a football.

Ask me to compete.

No problem.

Relationships were different.

Those mattered.

You can recover from striking out.

Hurting someone...

Or getting hurt...

Feels different.

Maybe that's why I approached Heather differently than anyone before her.

I slowed down.

I listened more.

I talked less.

That's unusual for me.

I like to talk.

Heather somehow made me want to listen.

---

As we spent more time together...

I noticed little things.

The way she treated waitresses.

The way she talked about her parents.

The way she listened when someone else was speaking.

The way she laughed.

The way she cared about people who couldn't do anything for her.

Character reveals itself through little things.

Not grand gestures.

Little things.

Heather's little things kept impressing me.

---

One evening after we'd been dating for a while...

I caught myself thinking about the future.

Not tomorrow.

Not next weekend.

The future.

That's when I realized something had changed.

I wasn't wondering if we'd keep dating.

I was wondering what our life might look like.

There's a huge difference between those two questions.

The first asks,

"Is this relationship working?"

The second asks,

"What could we build together?"

Without realizing it...

I had already started dreaming about forever.

---

Years later...

People have asked me,

"When did you know?"

I don't have an exact answer.

It wasn't lightning.

It wasn't fireworks.

It wasn't some movie moment.

It was quieter than that.

More peaceful.

One day I simply realized...

Life made more sense when Heather was in it.

I smiled more.

Laughed more.

Dreamed bigger.

Prayed differently.

She didn't complete me.

Only God can do that.

But she certainly made me a better version of myself.

And I think that's one of the greatest gifts one person can give another.

---

If I could go back today...

I'd find that young man standing there meeting Heather for the first time.

I'd smile.

Then I'd whisper,

"You have absolutely no idea what God is about to do."

Then I'd walk away.

Because part of the beauty of the journey...

Was getting to discover it one day at a time.
````

# Chapter 34
# Learning to Love Her Family

When you marry someone...

You don't just marry the person.

You marry the family.

I don't think I understood that when Heather and I first started dating.

Looking back...

I'm thankful I didn't.

If I had known how much her family would eventually mean to me...

I probably would've appreciated those early days even more.

---

The Pullers were different than my family.

Not better.

Not worse.

Different.

Families have personalities just like people do.

Mine did.

Theirs did.

One of the things I noticed almost immediately was how much they genuinely enjoyed spending time together.

Nobody seemed to be pretending.

Nobody seemed to be performing.

They simply enjoyed being a family.

I liked that.

A lot.

---

Linda Gail Puller...

Heather's mom...

Quickly became one of my favorite people.

I don't know that I appreciated her enough while she was alive.

I certainly do now.

Linda was one of those people who made you feel comfortable almost immediately.

She didn't have to impress you.

She didn't have to dominate a room.

She simply loved people.

You could feel it.

---

One of my favorite stories happened very early while Heather and I were dating.

I was over at their house.

Heather and I were standing in the kitchen.

I leaned in to kiss her.

She immediately backed away.

"No."

"My mom's in the next room."

I remember laughing.

"Seriously?"

"She's in the next room."

"So?"

Heather still wasn't convinced.

Finally...

She let me kiss her.

About halfway through the kiss...

Linda walked right into the kitchen.

She stopped.

Started giggling.

Looked at both of us.

Then smiled and said,

"Oh...

Excuse me."

She turned around...

Still laughing...

And walked back out of the room.

That's Linda.

No lecture.

No embarrassment.

Just laughter.

Heather was mortified.

I was trying not to laugh.

Looking back...

I still laugh every time I think about it.

---

Larry was different.

Quiet.

Steady.

The kind of man who didn't waste many words.

He worked hard.

Loved his family.

Provided.

There wasn't much drama with Larry.

You always knew where you stood.

I've always respected people like that.

---

The more time I spent around the Pullers...

The more I understood Heather.

Children don't become their parents.

But they certainly carry pieces of them.

Heather had Linda's kindness.

Larry's steadiness.

Both of those qualities have served her well.

And they've certainly blessed me.

---

One thing I appreciated about Heather's family was how they accepted me.

Not because I played baseball.

Not because of what I might become.

Simply because I loved Heather.

Looking back...

That's exactly how it should be.

---

I don't think I realized then how many holidays we'd eventually spend together.

Christmases.

Thanksgivings.

Birthdays.

Ordinary Sunday afternoons.

Life has a way of quietly weaving families together.

One meal at a time.

One conversation at a time.

Before you know it...

You stop saying,

"Heather's family."

You simply say,

"Our family."

---

Years later...

Linda became "Nana" to Haley.

Watching those two together became one of the great joys of my life.

Linda adored Haley.

Haley adored Nana.

That relationship became something very special.

When Linda eventually passed away...

It left a hole in all of our hearts.

Especially Heather's.

And Haley's.

Mine too.

I didn't lose a mother-in-law.

I lost someone I genuinely loved.

---

Sometimes people joke about in-laws.

I've never really understood those jokes.

I've been blessed.

The Pullers didn't just welcome me.

They loved me.

And over time...

I loved them too.

Looking back now...

One of the greatest gifts Heather ever gave me...

Wasn't simply becoming my wife.

It was inviting me into a family that would become part of my own.

For that...

I'll always be grateful.
````

# Chapter 35
# June 7, 1997

June 7, 1997.

People ask me if I remember my wedding day.

The answer usually surprises them.

Not very well.

At least...

Not the details.

I remember moments.

Feelings.

Pictures.

Pieces.

Almost like someone handed me a stack of photographs and removed everything in between.

That's how my memory works for that day.

---

I remember standing in that little chapel.

I remember sweating.

Actually...

I remember sweating more than almost anything else.

The air conditioning was turned down into the low sixties.

The bridesmaids were freezing.

Guests were reaching for jackets.

Meanwhile...

Sweat was literally dripping down my face.

If you look at some of our wedding pictures...

You can actually see it.

People probably assumed it was hot.

It wasn't.

I was.

I've never been that nervous before.

Or since.

---

People find that hard to believe.

After all...

I'd played quarterback in front of packed stadiums.

I'd played baseball in front of professional scouts.

I'd been drafted by the San Francisco Giants.

Pressure wasn't exactly new to me.

This was different.

This wasn't about making a play.

This wasn't about striking out.

This wasn't about winning or losing.

This was forever.

At least...

That was my intention.

Standing there waiting for Heather...

Forever suddenly became very real.

---

One thing I remember vividly...

Watching her walk toward me.

She was beautiful.

Absolutely beautiful.

People ask what I remember most from our wedding.

That's it.

Her.

The dress.

Her smile.

The way she looked at me.

I honestly don't remember many decorations.

Or flowers.

Or table arrangements.

I remember Heather.

Everything else faded into the background.

---

Then...

There were the vows.

I've laughed about this story for years.

I was supposed to say,

> "God's holy ordinance."

Instead...

I confidently announced,

> "God's holy orbits."

Orbits.

As in planets.

As in the solar system.

As in absolutely not the right word.

I don't even remember realizing I'd said it.

Apparently everyone else did.

Fortunately...

Heather married me anyway.

I've always appreciated that.

---

Then came the sermon.

Now...

This part still makes both of us laugh.

The pastor somehow decided that our wedding ceremony was the perfect place to tell the story of a prostitute who had been saved by Jesus.

To this day...

Neither one of us knows why.

We didn't request it.

Nobody expected it.

It simply...

Happened.

People still bring it up.

I guess every wedding needs something memorable.

That certainly qualified.

---

One of my favorite wedding photographs has puzzled us for years.

Heather has "the look."

You know the one.

The,

"You better stop."

look.

People assume we were arguing.

Not a chance.

Heather and I have talked about that picture many times.

Neither one of us remembers what was happening.

I know this much...

We weren't upset.

There wasn't an argument.

Knowing me...

I'm almost certain I made some completely inappropriate joke.

Probably about streaking.

Or getting naked.

Or something we were going to do later.

Something that probably shouldn't have been said in front of grandparents.

Heather's expression basically says,

"Would you please behave for five more minutes?"

Looking back...

She was probably right.

---

One of my favorite stories from that day doesn't involve Heather or me.

It involves Vance.

Vance Traffanstedt.

One of my closest friends.

Vance was one of my groomsmen.

A wonderful guy.

Funny.

Talkative.

Full of life.

The kind of friend you could trust.

I can still hear him laughing.

Matter of fact...

One of my favorite memories of Vance happened long before the wedding.

I took him out one night.

Let's just say...

He had a little too much to drink.

When we got back to his apartment...

His girlfriend, Darlene, had her boss over.

She looked at me and said,

"Take him to bed."

Reasonable request.

I got him headed toward the bedroom.

A few seconds later...

CRASH.

I ran into the bathroom.

There was Vance.

Completely naked.

Lying on the floor.

He had somehow managed to pull the entire shower curtain down with him.

So...

Being the good friend I was...

I helped him up.

Still completely naked.

Got him back into bed.

Went back into the bathroom to rehang the shower curtain.

Then I heard Darlene scream.

I ran into the living room.

There stood Vance.

Still completely naked.

Standing in front of Darlene...

And her boss.

To this day...

I don't know whether to laugh or apologize.

Actually...

I usually laugh.

Eventually...

Darlene forgave me.

I think.

---

That's the thing about weddings.

They're really collections of stories.

Some are beautiful.

Some are embarrassing.

Some become family legends.

All of them become part of who you are.

---

People often spend years planning a wedding.

Looking back...

Heather and I were much more excited about the marriage.

The wedding was important.

The marriage was the goal.

I think that's one of the reasons we've been blessed the way we have.

We weren't chasing one perfect day.

We were beginning a lifetime together.

The day mattered.

The promise mattered more.

---

When I look back now...

I don't think about the decorations.

I don't think about the flowers.

I don't think about the cake.

I think about standing there...

Sweating through my tuxedo...

Looking at the most beautiful woman I'd ever seen...

And realizing...

Somehow...

God had allowed me to marry her.

Nearly three decades later...

I still feel exactly the same way.
````

# Chapter 36
# The People in Our Wedding Pictures

One of the things I've discovered while writing this book is that photographs become more valuable as the people in them become fewer.

When I was twenty-six years old, I looked at my wedding album and saw pictures.

Today...

I see people.

Real people.

People with stories.

People who helped shape my life.

Some are gone now.

Some I still talk to.

Some I haven't seen in years.

But every one of them mattered enough to stand beside Heather and me on one of the most important days of our lives.

Looking back...

That means something.

---

Let's start with my dad.

Marvin.

If you look closely at our wedding pictures, you'll notice something.

He isn't the center of attention.

That would've made him uncomfortable.

Dad wasn't interested in attention.

He wanted to see me happy.

That's who he was.

I remember being excited that my friends finally got to spend time around him.

Most of them liked him almost immediately.

That wasn't unusual.

Dad had a way with people.

He could talk to almost anyone.

More importantly...

He genuinely liked people.

That tends to come through.

One of the greatest lessons Dad ever taught me had nothing to do with baseball or motorcycles.

He used to say,

> "I can't pick your friends for you, but I can damn sure limit your activities with them."

At the time...

It sounded funny.

Looking back...

It was brilliant.

He couldn't control my choices.

But he could influence them.

It worked.

I naturally gravitated toward people Dad respected.

Not because he forced me.

Because I wanted the freedom that came with choosing good friends.

Looking back over my life...

That simple lesson probably changed my future more than either one of us realized.

---

Then there was Granny.

Mary Elizabeth Nail.

Born September 19, 1919.

When people see her in our wedding photographs, they naturally assume I grew up with her.

I didn't.

Not really.

Growing up in California while most of Dad's family lived in Tennessee meant we rarely saw one another.

Phone calls were expensive back then.

Birthdays.

Christmas.

Thirty seconds.

Maybe a minute.

That was about it.

We'd see each other when family made the trip west.

Maybe two or three times.

I only remember going back to Tennessee once as a little boy.

So while she was always my Granny...

I didn't really know her.

That didn't happen until I was around twenty years old and we moved back to Tennessee.

That's when everything changed.

I got to know her as an adult.

And I'm so thankful I did.

She was sharp.

Independent.

A tough Southern country woman.

One of my favorite memories still makes me laugh.

I'd go over to her house and help mop the floors or do little jobs around the house.

One afternoon the telephone rang.

I said,

"I'll get it."

Without missing a beat she looked at me and said,

"Say hello."

I just stood there.

"What did you think I was going to say?"

We both started laughing so hard I almost couldn't answer the phone.

That joke never died.

To this day...

When a phone rings...

Heather or I will sometimes look at the other and simply say,

"Say hello."

Granny's been gone a long time.

That little phrase keeps bringing her back.

That's the power of family.

Sometimes an entire life gets wrapped up in two words.

---

My college friends were there too.

Russ Brockman.

Vance Traffanstedt.

Debra Johnson.

Jamie Tinker.

All of us had graduated from Alabama together.

Those friendships meant the world to me.

Russ and Vance stood beside me as groomsmen.

Debra stood beside Heather.

Looking back...

I smile because I realize those weren't just wedding attendants.

Those were people who had walked through some of the most important years of my life.

College.

Baseball.

Growing up.

Dreaming.

Figuring life out.

That's who I wanted standing beside me.

---

Russ has always made me smile.

He's about six-foot-six.

Towering over almost everybody.

His favorite word in college wasn't a cuss word.

It was,

"Freakin'."

"No freakin' way."

He probably said it a hundred times a week.

I still hear it when I think about him.

---

Then there was Vance.

Good friend.

Talkative.

Funny.

A wonderful husband and father today.

We've shared more laughs than I can count.

One of the reasons I trusted Vance so much was because I never felt like I had to pretend around him.

He accepted me exactly as I was.

Those kinds of friendships don't happen every day.

You hold onto them.

---

One thing I didn't realize until years later...

The people standing in our wedding pictures represented every major chapter of my life up to that point.

Family.

College.

Baseball.

Faith.

Friendship.

The people who had built me were all standing there together.

I don't think I appreciated that then.

I certainly do now.

---

There's one person missing from every wedding photograph.

Jerry Stubbs.

People have asked why.

The answer is simple.

Professional baseball.

Jerry had signed with the Montreal Expos organization.

He was in West Palm Beach playing minor league baseball.

The season didn't stop because I was getting married.

He couldn't be there.

I missed him.

A lot.

But I also understood.

His heart was with us.

Mine was with him too.

Dreams sometimes ask us to miss important moments.

Neither one of us held that against the other.

Real friendship doesn't work that way.

---

Looking back today...

I don't see a wedding party.

I see a snapshot of my life.

A father.

A grandmother.

Friends.

Family.

College teammates.

People who had quietly invested in me long before I understood how valuable they were.

That's why those photographs mean so much now.

They don't simply remind me of getting married.

They remind me of everyone who helped me become the man standing at that altar.
````

# Chapter 37
# Ride Bitch

If you ride motorcycles long enough...

You'll eventually collect stories.

Some are exciting.

Some are terrifying.

Some become family legends.

This one...

Is definitely the last category.

---

By this point in my life I had owned quite a few motorcycles.

I started on a little Honda Mini Trail 50.

Graduated to my MR50.

Then an XR75.

Dad's TT500.

His TT600.

A Suzuki Katana.

The Honda VTX1800.

Eventually Harleys.

Motorcycles had simply become part of who I was.

Not because I wanted to impress anybody.

Because I genuinely loved riding.

There is something peaceful about sitting on a motorcycle with nothing between you and the world.

No windshield.

No roof.

Just you...

The road...

And God.

---

One of my favorite motorcycles I've ever owned was my Honda VTX1800.

Now...

If you're a Harley rider...

You're probably already smiling.

Or rolling your eyes.

Maybe both.

Because for years Harley riders loved teasing Honda riders.

The jokes were endless.

"Real motorcycles."

"American made."

"You should've bought a Harley."

I'd hear it all the time.

The funny part?

My Honda almost never broke.

It was an absolute beast.

Eighteen hundred cubic centimeters.

Plenty of power.

Beautiful motorcycle.

Reliable.

Everything I wanted.

Except...

It didn't say Harley-Davidson on the tank.

Apparently that mattered to some people.

Not to me.

---

My brother Buddy...

Owned a Harley.

It was a beautiful motorcycle.

It was also...

Let's just say...

Mechanically gifted.

Which is a nice way of saying...

It broke down.

More than once.

We teased each other constantly.

He'd make fun of my Honda.

I'd remind him mine actually ran.

It became our running joke.

Neither one of us took it seriously.

That's just what brothers do.

---

Then one day...

My phone rang.

It was Buddy.

"Danny..."

"My Harley broke down."

"Can you come get me?"

Absolutely.

No problem.

The funny thing was...

Buddy assumed I was at work in my truck.

He expected me to pull up...

Throw his gear in the bed...

Drive him wherever he needed to go.

Instead...

A few minutes later...

He heard a motorcycle.

He looked up.

There I came...

Riding my Honda VTX.

I wish someone had taken a picture of his face.

It was priceless.

He looked at me like,

"What in the world are you doing?"

I shut the bike off.

Took my helmet off.

Looked at him.

Looked at the Harley.

Then smiled.

"Well..."

"You've got two choices."

"You can walk..."

"Or..."

"You can ride bitch."

---

Now...

If you've never spent much time around motorcycles...

You probably need a little explanation.

"Ride bitch" is old motorcycle slang.

It simply means riding as the passenger.

Usually...

Behind the rider.

Traditionally...

The girlfriend.

Or wife.

Or whoever happened to be riding along.

So here stood my older brother...

With his broken Harley...

Being told he had to climb on the back of my Honda.

The irony was absolutely beautiful.

---

He didn't have much choice.

Walking wasn't exactly practical.

So...

Up he climbed.

Behind me.

I don't think either one of us stopped laughing the entire ride.

Actually...

He probably wasn't laughing quite as hard as I was.

Every stoplight...

I'd glance back.

Smile.

Then pull away.

Thinking,

"You spent years making fun of my Honda..."

"And today..."

"My Honda is taking your Harley rider home."

Sometimes life writes jokes better than we ever could.

---

We finally arrived.

Buddy climbed off.

Shook his head.

"You are never going to let me forget this."

"Nope."

I haven't.

---

Matter of fact...

Years later...

We still laugh about it.

If motorcycles ever come up...

Somebody eventually mentions,

"Ride bitch."

It's become part of family history.

---

Looking back...

That story has almost nothing to do with motorcycles.

It's really about my brother.

That's the thing about memories.

The older you get...

The object matters less.

The people matter more.

I don't really remember where we were headed that day.

I don't remember exactly how his Harley broke down.

I remember laughing.

I remember seeing my brother climbing onto the back of my Honda.

I remember knowing...

This story was going to live for a very long time.

I was right.

---

People often ask me whether I like Hondas or Harleys better.

Honestly...

Both.

Each one belonged to a different season of my life.

The Honda represented power.

Reliability.

Adventure.

The Harley eventually became something different.

Slowing down.

Enjoying the journey.

Seeing America.

Neither one was better.

They were simply chapters.

Just like the motorcycles before them.

Just like the ones after.

But if I'm being completely honest...

The Honda VTX1800 gave me one thing no other motorcycle ever did.

The opportunity...

To make my older brother...

Ride bitch.

And that...

Was worth every penny I paid for that motorcycle.
````

# Chapter 38
# The Motorcycles

If baseball tells the story of my competitive life...

Motorcycles tell the story of almost everything else.

I don't think I ever realized that until I started writing this book.

When I look back over the different motorcycles I've owned...

I don't just see machines.

I see chapters.

Each one represents a season of my life.

A different version of Danny.

A different adventure.

A different lesson.

---

My first motorcycle was a Honda Mini Trail 50.

I was around four years old.

Think about that for a second.

Four.

People hear that today and usually react one of two ways.

"Your parents were crazy."

Or...

"Man, I wish I had that kind of childhood."

Honestly...

I do too.

Dad taught me to ride.

Patiently.

Looking back, I don't remember learning.

I just remember riding.

Motorcycles became part of life so early that I honestly can't remember life without them.

---

Not long afterward came my Honda MR50.

That motorcycle still lives in my garage today.

It's probably worth more to me than almost anything else I own.

Not because it's rare.

Not because it's valuable.

Because it's mine.

Because when I look at it...

I don't see an old motorcycle.

I see a little blond-haired kid who couldn't wait for Saturday morning.

I see Dad loading the truck.

I see Gorman.

I see freedom.

People ask why I don't restore it.

Why would I?

Every scratch tells a story.

Every faded decal reminds me of somewhere we went.

It's perfect exactly the way it is.

---

After the MR50 came my XR75.

Then...

Everything changed.

Dad bought a Yamaha TT500.

That motorcycle was legendary.

Not because it was fast.

Because it was hard to start.

Dad made me a deal.

He looked at me one day and said,

"When you're big enough to start it...

You can ride it."

Simple enough.

Except...

Starting a TT500 wasn't simple.

Not even a little.

You had to bring the piston up to top dead center.

Use the compression release.

Then kick it.

Hard.

If you got lazy...

That motorcycle kicked back.

Violently.

It hurt.

Matter of fact...

It made me cry more than once.

Not because I wanted to quit.

Because that motorcycle flat-out hurt you when you got it wrong.

I stayed with it.

Eventually...

I learned.

Then one day...

I started it.

Dad smiled.

Kept his promise.

The TT500 became mine.

Looking back...

I don't think he was teaching me to ride.

I think he was teaching perseverance.

---

Later...

Dad bought a TT600.

Eventually...

Just like the TT500...

It became mine.

That's how Dad did things.

He rarely handed me something.

He let me grow into it.

There's wisdom in that.

I've tried to remember it throughout my own life.

---

Years later...

While living in Atlanta...

I bought something completely different.

A Suzuki Katana.

Six hundred.

Maybe six-fifty.

I honestly can't remember which.

I absolutely loved that motorcycle.

Too much.

Living in Atlanta traffic...

With a sport bike...

Was probably one of the more dangerous combinations I ever created.

There's a reason they call them crotch rockets.

I pushed it.

Hard.

Looking back...

I had enough maturity to realize something.

The motorcycle wasn't the problem.

I was.

I loved speed.

I loved acceleration.

I loved seeing what it could do.

Eventually I sold it.

Not because I stopped loving sport bikes.

Because I finally admitted they brought out something in me that wasn't particularly wise.

I'd still enjoy owning one today.

I'm simply old enough now to know better.

That's growth.

---

Then came one of my all-time favorites.

The Honda VTX1800.

What a motorcycle.

Reliable.

Powerful.

Comfortable.

Beautiful.

Harley guys gave me grief constantly.

"It's not a Harley."

Nope.

It wasn't.

It also didn't spend much time in the repair shop.

I loved teasing them back.

Especially Buddy.

His Harley had a habit of breaking down.

Mine didn't.

Eventually...

That led to the famous Ride Bitch story.

I still smile every time I think about it.

---

After moving to 707 Briar Road...

Motorcycles took on another role.

Competition.

I bought a Honda XR650R.

Built a practice track in the woods behind Dad's house.

Complete with a jump.

Of course there was a jump.

I practiced constantly.

Then came the KTM 450 MXC.

Now things got serious.

Hare scrambles.

Eight-mile loops through the woods.

Trees so close together that we actually cut the handlebars down about three-quarters of an inch on each side just so they would fit.

I'm broad-shouldered.

Sometimes my shoulder pads would actually brush trees on both sides as I flew through the woods.

If you've never raced through tight Tennessee woods...

It's hard to explain.

You're constantly making decisions.

Roots.

Rocks.

Mud.

Trees.

Other riders.

Everything happens at once.

I loved it.

---

The KTM eventually wore number seven.

That number followed me everywhere.

Football.

Motorcycles.

Life.

I never really planned that.

It simply became part of who I was.

---

I started racing at around thirty-five years old.

Most people probably thought I was crazy.

They were probably right.

I didn't care.

I loved every second of it.

Until...

The second ACL.

That one ended things.

I finally admitted my racing days were over.

Not because I stopped loving motorcycles.

Because my body had finally voted.

Sometimes wisdom means listening.

---

Then came the Harley.

A 2016 Ultra Limited.

Crimson.

Not burgundy.

Crimson.

Alabama Crimson.

Let's get that straight.

I actually bought that motorcycle because of relationships.

I was getting ready to buy a used Harley.

My friend Brent Carter found out.

Brent and I had coached volleyball together.

He called and said,

"My parents own Three Rivers Harley-Davidson in Paducah."

A few phone calls later...

Instead of buying used...

I was buying new.

That's another lesson life has taught me.

Relationships matter.

They open doors.

Sometimes...

They put you on motorcycles you never expected to own.

---

When I look back over all those motorcycles now...

I realize they weren't transportation.

They were markers.

The Mini Trail 50.

Freedom.

The MR50.

Childhood.

The TT500.

Perseverance.

The Katana.

Youth.

The VTX.

Brotherhood.

The XR650R.

Rediscovery.

The KTM.

Competition.

The Harley.

Contentment.

Each motorcycle tells me where I was in life.

Each one reminds me who I was becoming.

People sometimes ask me which one was my favorite.

That's like asking me to pick my favorite chapter of life.

I can't.

Because every one of them helped carry me to the next one.

Looking back...

I don't think I've collected motorcycles.

I think...

I've collected stories.
````

# Chapter 39
# The Day I Became My Dad's Dad

I don't think anyone prepares you for the day your parents become your children.

It doesn't happen all at once.

It happens slowly.

A little more help.

A few more doctor appointments.

Another pill to remember.

Another thing they can no longer do for themselves.

One day...

You realize the roles have quietly reversed.

That realization hit me harder than almost anything else in my life.

---

Growing up...

Dad could fix anything.

Anything.

If the truck broke...

Dad fixed it.

If the motorcycle quit running...

Dad fixed it.

If the house needed work...

Dad built it.

If something heavy needed lifting...

Dad carried it.

That was just who he was.

Solid.

Capable.

Dependable.

He wasn't Superman.

But to a little boy...

He was pretty close.

---

Then came the stroke.

Overnight...

Everything changed.

The strongest man I'd ever known suddenly needed help standing up.

Buttoning a shirt.

Walking.

Remembering things.

Holding onto his balance.

I don't know if there's anything harder for a son to watch.

Not because your father becomes weak.

Because you suddenly realize...

He's human.

---

There were moments that broke my heart.

Dad would get frustrated.

Really frustrated.

His brain knew exactly what he wanted to do.

His body simply refused to cooperate.

Imagine that.

Imagine reaching for a coffee cup you've picked up ten thousand times...

And suddenly...

Your own hand won't listen.

That's humbling.

For anyone.

Especially a man who had spent his life building things with his hands.

---

One afternoon I watched him trying to button a shirt.

It should have taken maybe thirty seconds.

Instead...

It took several minutes.

His left hand wouldn't cooperate.

His fingers wouldn't do what his brain was asking them to do.

I stood there.

Watching.

Every part of me wanted to jump in and help.

I didn't.

Not right away.

I knew something.

If I took that moment away from him...

I was taking away one more piece of his independence.

So I waited.

Finally...

He looked up.

Our eyes met.

Without saying a word...

He nodded.

That was permission.

Only then did I help.

I've never forgotten that.

Sometimes helping too quickly actually hurts.

People deserve the dignity of trying.

Dad taught me that.

Even after the stroke.

---

Living together also meant we saw each other every day.

Not holiday visits.

Not Sunday dinners.

Every day.

That changes a relationship.

We weren't making appointments to see one another.

Life just happened.

Sometimes we'd sit on the porch talking.

Sometimes we'd watch television.

Sometimes we'd simply sit in the same room without saying much at all.

Looking back...

Those quiet moments became some of my favorites.

Funny...

When you're young you think memories come from exciting events.

As you get older...

You realize they usually come from ordinary afternoons.

---

One thing I noticed after the stroke...

Dad smiled more.

That may sound strange.

Life had become harder.

Much harder.

Yet somehow...

He seemed softer.

More patient.

More appreciative.

The things that used to frustrate him before...

Didn't seem nearly as important anymore.

I think suffering has a way of refining people.

Not always.

But sometimes.

It certainly did with Dad.

---

People have complimented me over the years.

"You took such good care of your dad."

I appreciate that.

But I don't really see it that way.

I wasn't paying him back.

You can't repay your parents.

How do you repay someone for teaching you to ride a bicycle?

To throw a baseball?

To work?

To be honest?

To choose good friends?

You can't.

You simply love them when it's your turn.

That's all I was trying to do.

Love Dad the way he'd loved me.

---

Heather deserves far more credit than I do.

She never once acted like Dad was in the way.

Never.

She treated him with dignity.

Respect.

Kindness.

The same man who had welcomed her into our family years earlier...

Was now living under our roof.

She quietly cared for him without asking for recognition.

That's one of the reasons I love her so deeply.

Service isn't something she talks about.

It's simply who she is.

---

Then there was Haley.

Watching Dad become Papa might be one of the greatest gifts God ever gave me.

She didn't see a stroke survivor.

She saw Papa.

The man who loved her.

Played with her.

Smiled at her.

She climbed into his lap without thinking about what he'd lost.

Children have a beautiful way of seeing people for who they are instead of what they can do.

I learned a lot from watching those two together.

---

Every once in a while...

Dad and I would talk about life.

Not deep philosophical conversations.

Just...

Life.

He'd tell stories I'd never heard before.

Stories about growing up.

Stories about construction.

Stories about family.

Sometimes we'd laugh so hard we'd both have tears in our eyes.

I didn't know then...

Those conversations were becoming my inheritance.

Not money.

Not property.

Stories.

---

When Dad eventually passed away...

People asked if I was glad I'd spent those years caring for him.

I remember thinking,

"Glad?"

That's the wrong word.

Grateful.

That's the word.

God gave me nine extra years.

Nine years I wasn't guaranteed.

Nine years many sons never receive.

How could I be anything but grateful?

---

If I could tell anyone reading this one thing...

It would be this.

If you're blessed enough to have your parents grow old...

Spend the time.

Ask the questions.

Listen to the stories.

Take the pictures.

Write things down.

Because one day...

You'll discover something.

The stories become far more valuable than anything they leave behind.

I know.

Because that's exactly what happened to me.
````

# Chapter 40
# Discovering My Real Mom

People have asked me over the years what it was like to finally learn about Barbara Jean.

The honest answer?

Complicated.

Not because of who she was.

Because of who she wasn't.

She wasn't the woman who raised me.

She wasn't the woman who kissed scraped knees.

She wasn't the woman who cheered from the stands.

She wasn't the woman who stayed up when I was sick.

She wasn't Mom.

Gloria had already earned that title.

Nobody was ever going to take it away from her.

---

That's important.

Really important.

Because people sometimes assume discovering your biological family somehow replaces the family who raised you.

It doesn't.

At least...

It didn't for me.

My heart didn't divide.

It expanded.

There's a huge difference.

---

The first time I saw Barbara Jean's photograph...

I stared at it for a long time.

Longer than I expected.

I wasn't looking for resemblance.

I was looking for answers.

Questions you've never had to ask suddenly become very important.

Do I have her eyes?

Her smile?

Do I laugh like her?

Does my personality come from her?

What parts of me belonged to someone I'd never known?

It was strange.

Really strange.

You're looking at your own history...

And at the same time...

Looking at a complete stranger.

---

One thing surprised me.

I wasn't angry.

I'd expected anger.

People probably expected anger.

Instead...

I mostly felt sadness.

Not sadness for me.

Sadness for everyone.

Somewhere along the way...

A whole lot of people got hurt.

Dad.

Mom.

Barbara Jean.

My biological sisters.

My Jenkins family.

There really weren't winners.

Just people trying to survive the consequences of decisions made many years earlier.

Life is rarely as simple as we'd like it to be.

---

As I learned more about Barbara Jean...

I also learned more about addiction.

About alcoholism.

About pain.

About brokenness.

It's easy to judge people when you only know the ending of the story.

It's much harder when you begin understanding the beginning.

I found myself asking different questions.

Not...

"What was wrong with her?"

But...

"What happened to her?"

Those are very different questions.

---

Dad had carried fear for years.

He'd worried I might inherit addiction.

That concern suddenly made sense.

He wasn't judging Barbara Jean.

He was trying to protect me.

That's a father's job.

Looking back...

I understand his fear.

I also understand why he didn't know how to talk about it.

Some conversations simply don't have easy words.

---

People have asked whether I ever blamed Barbara Jean.

Honestly...

No.

I've certainly wondered.

I've certainly wished some things had been different.

But blame?

Not really.

Without her...

There is no me.

Without her decisions...

There is no Haley.

No Heather.

No story.

Some of life's greatest blessings grow out of circumstances we never would've chosen.

I believe mine did.

---

One thing I wish I could tell her...

If she were sitting across the table from me today...

Is thank you.

Not because everything went perfectly.

It certainly didn't.

But because somewhere inside all of that brokenness...

She made one decision that changed my life.

She let me go.

I don't know how difficult that decision was.

I can't imagine it was easy.

I also know it allowed me to become part of the Jenkins family.

For that...

I'll always be grateful.

---

I've often thought about what would've happened if she'd made a different decision.

What if she'd kept me?

What if she'd never shown up at Dad's front door?

What if Gloria had said no?

Everything changes.

Everything.

There would be no Kathryn Avenue.

No baseball at TABB.

No Gorman.

No Dad teaching me motorcycles.

No Alabama.

No Heather.

No Haley.

The life I love today disappears.

That's hard to wrap your mind around.

---

As strange as it sounds...

Discovering Barbara Jean actually made me appreciate Gloria even more.

People sometimes ask who my real mother is.

I smile.

Then I answer.

"I have two."

One gave me life.

The other gave me a life.

Both matter.

But only one raised me.

Only one tucked me into bed.

Only one stayed through every scraped knee, every baseball game, every report card, every heartbreak, every victory.

That's Mom.

That's Gloria.

Always has been.

Always will be.

---

Looking back now...

I don't think discovering Barbara Jean answered all my questions.

It did something better.

It gave me peace.

Not because every mystery disappeared.

Because I finally understood that my story wasn't divided between two mothers.

It had been blessed by both.

One gave me birth.

The other gave me home.

I have room in my heart to honor both truths.

And I think that's exactly where God wanted me to arrive.
````

---

# Chapter 41
# The Day Everything Made Sense

Have you ever spent years trying to understand something...

Only to have one conversation suddenly explain everything?

That's what happened to me.

Not everything.

But enough.

Enough that the hurt I'd carried for years finally started making sense.

---

For almost eight years I believed something that wasn't true.

I believed my mom hadn't fought for me during the divorce.

I didn't say it out loud very often.

I didn't even know how to explain it.

It was just there.

Quietly sitting in the background.

Waiting.

Every time I thought about the divorce...

Those two words came back.

"I know."

Those words had become a wound.

One that never completely healed.

Until...

Dad told me the truth.

---

The strange thing about truth is...

It doesn't always erase the pain.

Sometimes...

It changes the meaning of the pain.

That's what happened to me.

Suddenly...

I wasn't looking at the same memory anymore.

I was looking at it through completely different eyes.

Mom hadn't abandoned me.

Mom hadn't failed to fight.

Mom couldn't fight.

Legally...

Biologically...

There wasn't a fight to have.

But emotionally...

She had already fought years earlier.

The day she decided to become my mother.

---

I remember sitting by myself afterward.

Just thinking.

Not crying.

Not angry.

Thinking.

Every memory suddenly had another layer.

Every photograph.

Every holiday.

Every birthday.

Every baseball game.

Everything looked different.

Yet somehow...

Nothing had changed.

Mom was still Mom.

Dad was still Dad.

The only thing that changed...

Was my understanding.

---

One of the hardest things to accept was this.

They had all carried that secret for me.

Not from me.

For me.

There's a difference.

For years I thought...

"Why didn't anyone tell me?"

Today...

I ask a different question.

"How hard must that have been?"

Imagine carrying that secret for twenty-two years.

Watching your son grow up.

Wondering when to tell him.

Wondering if telling him would hurt him.

Wondering if not telling him would hurt him.

There probably wasn't a perfect answer.

Dad did the best he knew how.

Mom did too.

Looking back...

I have a lot more grace for both of them than I did when I was twenty-two.

---

I also started realizing something else.

My life had been protected in ways I never understood.

People had sacrificed for me without expecting recognition.

Mom.

Dad.

Even my biological family.

Everybody had made difficult decisions.

Some right.

Some wrong.

Some impossible.

Life isn't nearly as neat as we'd like it to be.

---

One thing I've noticed over the years...

People often want simple answers.

Who's the hero?

Who's the villain?

Who's right?

Who's wrong?

Life almost never works that way.

At least mine didn't.

Every person in my story has strengths.

Every person has weaknesses.

Every person made decisions they wish they could take back.

Including me.

That's what makes us human.

---

The older I've become...

The more thankful I am that I didn't learn the truth as a child.

That might surprise some people.

Would it have answered questions?

Absolutely.

Would I have understood it?

Probably not.

Children don't process those things the way adults do.

Instead...

I got to spend my childhood simply being loved.

I think that's one of the greatest gifts Mom and Dad ever gave me.

They protected my childhood.

Even though protecting it came at a cost to them.

---

One of the greatest lessons I've learned from my story is this.

Love isn't defined by biology.

It's defined by sacrifice.

Biology explains where you came from.

Sacrifice explains who your family is.

Gloria sacrificed.

Over.

And over.

And over again.

How could I ever call anyone else Mom?

---

I don't think about this story very often anymore.

Not because it isn't important.

Because it no longer hurts.

Healing has a funny way of doing that.

The story stays.

The pain slowly leaves.

What's left...

Is gratitude.

I'm grateful Dad eventually told me.

I'm grateful Mom chose me.

I'm grateful Barbara Jean let me go.

I'm grateful my biological sisters welcomed me.

I'm grateful God somehow took a broken situation...

And built a beautiful life from it.

Only He could do that.

---

If someone asked me today...

"So who are you really?"

My answer is pretty simple.

I'm Danny Jenkins.

I always have been.

I always will be.

Not because of a birth certificate.

Not because of DNA.

Because that's the family who raised me.

Loved me.

Corrected me.

Cheered for me.

Believed in me.

The truth added another chapter to my story.

It never changed who I was.

And honestly...

I'm thankful for that.
````

# Chapter 42
# Looking Back

One of the unexpected blessings of writing this book has been discovering how differently I see my own life now.

When you're living life...

You're mostly looking forward.

You're trying to get through school.

Win the game.

Get the job.

Pay the bills.

Raise your kids.

Take care of your parents.

You don't spend much time looking backward.

Life keeps pulling you forward.

Writing this book forced me to stop.

To look.

To remember.

To think.

And sometimes...

To understand things I never understood while they were happening.

---

Take my dad, for example.

As a little boy...

Dad was just Dad.

The man who taught me to throw a baseball.

The man who took me motorcycle riding.

The man who nicknamed me Stump.

The man who expected me to work hard.

Then I became a teenager.

Suddenly...

Dad became the guy with rules.

The guy who didn't understand.

The guy who said no when I wanted him to say yes.

Looking back now...

I smile.

Because somewhere along the way...

I became Dad.

Not exactly like him.

But close enough to understand him.

That's one of the gifts of getting older.

You stop judging your parents by what they prevented.

You start appreciating what they protected.

---

The same thing happened with Mom.

As a child...

Mom was simply Mom.

The person who loved me.

The person who made things better.

The person who somehow always knew when something wasn't right.

Then I learned my story.

For a little while...

Everything became confusing.

Now...

Years later...

All I see is love.

I honestly believe she loved me every bit as much as if she'd given birth to me herself.

Maybe more.

Because every single day she made a choice.

She chose me again.

And again.

And again.

Not because she had to.

Because she wanted to.

---

I've also looked differently at sports.

When I was younger...

Everything felt like a competition.

Every game mattered.

Every at-bat mattered.

Every race mattered.

Winning mattered.

Looking back...

The victories aren't what I remember most.

I remember the people.

George.

Jack.

Jerry.

Johnnie.

Russ.

Vance.

Teammates.

Coaches.

Friends.

Funny...

The older I get...

The score matters less.

The people matter more.

---

I think about motorcycles differently now too.

For years I thought motorcycles were simply something I enjoyed.

Now I realize they marked the seasons of my life.

The Mini Trail 50.

Childhood.

The TT500.

Dad.

The Katana.

Youth.

The VTX.

Brotherhood.

The KTM.

Competition.

The Harley.

Contentment.

Each one became a chapter.

Not because of the motorcycle itself.

Because of who I was while riding it.

---

One of the biggest surprises has been discovering how much ordinary moments matter.

When I was young...

I assumed the important memories would be championships.

Graduation.

Marriage.

Haley being born.

Those are certainly important.

But as I've looked through old photographs...

I've noticed something.

The stories I tell the longest are rarely about the biggest events.

They're about pizza boxes stacked outside an apartment.

A naked roommate.

A little shovel in a creek.

My brother riding on the back of my Honda.

Granny saying,

"Say hello."

Those are the stories that make me smile.

Life isn't built on highlights.

It's built on ordinary Tuesdays.

We just don't realize it until much later.

---

People have asked me if writing this book has been emotional.

Absolutely.

There have been moments where I laughed so hard I had to stop typing.

Other moments...

I simply sat quietly.

Thinking.

Sometimes crying.

Not because I was sad.

Because I was thankful.

Thankful I got to live this life.

Thankful I had these people.

Thankful God gave me memories worth remembering.

---

I've also realized something about forgiveness.

When you're young...

You want answers.

As you get older...

You begin wanting understanding.

Those aren't the same thing.

Understanding has a way of making forgiveness much easier.

I've stopped asking,

"Why did they do that?"

Instead I find myself asking,

"What were they carrying?"

Everybody carries something.

The older I get...

The more grace I find myself extending.

Not because people earned it.

Because I've needed plenty of grace myself.

---

One thing I hope you discover while reading this book...

I'm still learning.

Just because I'm writing about my life doesn't mean I've figured life out.

Far from it.

Matter of fact...

Some of the biggest lessons in this book are lessons I'm still trying to live.

Maybe that's what growing older really is.

Not arriving.

Continuing to grow.

---

If you've made it this far...

You've probably noticed something.

This book really isn't about me.

Not completely.

It's about the people who built me.

That's become more obvious with every chapter.

Every story eventually leads back to someone else.

Mom.

Dad.

Heather.

Haley.

George.

Jack.

Granny.

Jerry.

The list keeps growing.

That's exactly how I hope my life is remembered.

Not because of what I accomplished.

Because of who I loved.

And who loved me.

Looking back...

I think that's a life worth being thankful for.
````

# Chapter 43
# Success

If you'd asked me when I was eighteen years old what success looked like...

The answer would've been easy.

Play Major League Baseball.

That was it.

Simple.

Clear.

Everything pointed in that direction.

If I made it...

I'd be successful.

If I didn't...

Well...

I honestly hadn't thought much beyond that.

Funny how life works.

Sometimes God answers your prayers.

Sometimes...

He changes the question.

---

Today...

At fifty-five years old...

If you ask me what success looks like...

My answer is completely different.

Success has a name.

Heather.

Success has another name.

Haley.

Success looks like sitting around a dinner table laughing with people you love.

Success looks like friends who still answer your phone calls decades later.

Success looks like your daughter actually wanting to spend time with you after she's grown.

Success looks like your wife still reaching for your hand after almost thirty years of marriage.

That's success.

Everything else...

Is just icing.

---

I don't mean that baseball wasn't important.

It absolutely was.

Baseball shaped me.

It introduced me to incredible people.

It taught me discipline.

It taught me leadership.

It opened doors.

It gave me dreams.

I'd never want to erase that part of my life.

But baseball was never the destination.

It was preparation.

I just didn't know it.

---

One of the greatest blessings of getting older is perspective.

When I was younger...

I measured life by achievements.

Starting quarterback.

Drafted by the Giants.

University of Alabama.

Those things mattered.

They still matter.

They're just no longer the things I'm proudest of.

I'm much prouder of hearing Haley call me Dad.

Much prouder of hearing Heather laugh in the next room.

Much prouder of knowing people trust me.

Those are accomplishments nobody puts on a résumé.

They're also the ones that matter most.

---

I've also learned something about ambition.

There's nothing wrong with wanting to accomplish great things.

Matter of fact...

I think God places dreams inside us for a reason.

The danger comes when we allow achievement to define our identity.

I came close to doing that.

Baseball was becoming my identity.

God, in His wisdom, gave me something better.

He gave me purpose.

Purpose lasts longer than careers.

---

People sometimes ask if I miss baseball.

Of course I do.

I miss competing.

I miss the smell of the field.

I miss batting practice.

I miss the clubhouse.

I miss everything about it.

But here's the interesting part.

I don't wish I were still playing.

I simply appreciate that I got to.

That's contentment.

There's a huge difference between missing something...

And wishing your life had turned out differently.

I don't.

I genuinely love the life God gave me.

---

Sometimes people ask if I would've changed anything.

Honestly...

Very little.

Sure...

There are mistakes I'd avoid.

Words I'd take back.

Moments I'd handle differently.

But the major events?

No.

Because changing one thing changes everything.

Take away Alabama...

Maybe I never meet Heather.

Take away Heather...

There's no Haley.

Take away Haley...

The world loses one of my favorite people.

No thank you.

I'll take the life I actually received.

Every single time.

---

Whole Life Journey has become another chapter in that story.

People sometimes ask why I'm building it.

The answer has very little to do with technology.

I'm trying to help people live intentionally.

I'm trying to help people remember what actually matters.

Funny enough...

Writing this book has reminded me that I'm trying to do exactly the same thing here.

Preserve what matters.

Not what impresses people.

What matters.

---

As I've looked through old photographs...

One thought keeps coming back.

The people in those pictures had no idea they were creating memories.

They were just living.

Dad wasn't thinking,

"This will become a story."

Neither was Mom.

Or Granny.

Or George.

Or Jerry.

Or Heather.

They were simply living faithful ordinary lives.

Years later...

Those ordinary moments became extraordinary memories.

That's encouraging.

It means you don't have to chase significance.

Sometimes significance quietly grows out of faithfulness.

---

One day...

Somebody reading this book may wonder what I'd want them to take away from my life.

That's actually pretty easy.

Love God.

Love your family.

Choose good friends.

Work hard.

Keep your word.

Laugh often.

Forgive quickly.

Never stop learning.

And don't wait until someone's gone to tell them you love them.

That's about it.

Everything else is details.

---

When I was a little boy...

Success looked like hitting a home run.

Today...

Success looks like walking through the front door after work...

Hearing Heather say,

"Hey, Honey."

Watching Haley smile.

Talking to friends I've had for decades.

Remembering Dad.

Missing Mom.

Thanking God.

Looking back...

I think He knew what success really looked like all along.

It just took me a while to catch up.
