# Chapter 44
# Whole Life Journey

If someone had told twenty-year-old Danny that one day he'd spend his life building software...

I'd have laughed.

Probably pretty hard.

Computers?

Sure.

Technology?

Interesting.

Building an entire platform designed to help people live better lives?

Never would've crossed my mind.

Not once.

And yet...

Looking back...

I can now see God preparing me for it all along.

I just couldn't see it while I was living it.

---

Whole Life Journey didn't begin as software.

It began as frustration.

Not frustration with technology.

Frustration with life.

More specifically...

How disconnected life had become.

I noticed something over the years.

Everybody had pieces.

One app tracked health.

Another tracked finances.

Another tracked calendars.

Another tracked habits.

Faith lived somewhere else.

Goals lived somewhere else.

Relationships...

Usually nowhere at all.

Everything existed in pieces.

Nobody was putting the pieces together.

That bothered me.

A lot.

---

The more I thought about it...

The more I realized something.

Human beings don't live compartmentalized lives.

Everything affects everything else.

If I don't sleep...

I'm a worse husband.

A worse employee.

A worse Christian.

A worse leader.

If my health suffers...

My energy suffers.

If my energy suffers...

My patience suffers.

If my patience suffers...

Relationships suffer.

Life is connected.

Why wasn't technology?

---

That's where Whole Life Journey was born.

Not from code.

From a question.

What if one system actually understood the whole person?

Not just their calendar.

Not just their blood sugar.

Not just their finances.

The whole person.

That question wouldn't leave me alone.

It followed me everywhere.

Driving.

Working.

Going to bed.

Getting up.

It was always there.

---

The funny thing is...

People assume I'm building software.

I'm really not.

I'm trying to build wisdom.

Software is simply the delivery mechanism.

If Whole Life Journey succeeds...

It won't be because it has the best interface.

Or the prettiest charts.

Or the newest AI.

It'll succeed because people finally feel understood.

That's the real goal.

Understanding.

---

One of the biggest inspirations for the project wasn't technology at all.

It was Dad.

Mom.

Heather.

Haley.

Watching people I loved struggle.

Watching them forget things.

Watching them lose stories.

Watching health affect everything else.

Watching life become increasingly complicated.

I kept thinking...

There has to be a better way.

Maybe...

Just maybe...

God had been preparing me to help build one.

---

People often ask where the idea came from.

I honestly don't know anymore.

It didn't arrive one afternoon.

It slowly grew.

Every experience added another piece.

Baseball taught me discipline.

Motorcycles taught me adventure.

Leadership taught me systems.

Faith taught me purpose.

Dad taught me work ethic.

Mom taught me compassion.

Heather taught me partnership.

Haley taught me legacy.

Whole Life Journey is really all of those things...

Woven together.

---

One thing became obvious pretty quickly.

This project was much bigger than me.

There was no way one person could build something like this alone.

That's when artificial intelligence entered the picture.

Not because AI is exciting.

Because it gave me another teammate.

People sometimes ask if AI scares me.

No.

People scare me.

AI is just a tool.

Like a hammer.

A hammer can build a house.

Or hurt someone.

The hammer isn't the problem.

The person holding it is.

I've always believed the same thing about technology.

---

Eventually...

The project grew large enough that it needed a name.

Beth.

People ask me why Beth.

The answer isn't nearly as interesting as people expect.

I wanted the system to feel personal.

Helpful.

Trustworthy.

Not robotic.

Not cold.

Beth became that personality.

Not because I wanted another gadget.

Because I wanted people to feel like someone genuinely cared about helping them live well.

---

Writing this book has actually changed how I think about Whole Life Journey.

At first...

I thought I was building software to help people remember.

Now...

I think I'm building software to help people preserve who they are.

Those aren't the same thing.

Memories matter.

Identity matters more.

That's exactly what this book has become.

Not a timeline.

A preservation of a person.

Maybe Whole Life Journey has been trying to accomplish the same thing all along.

I just hadn't recognized it yet.

---

If someone asks me years from now what I'm most proud of...

Maybe they'll expect me to say baseball.

Or my career.

Or some promotion.

Maybe even Whole Life Journey.

Honestly...

I hope my answer is much simpler.

I hope I can say...

"I loved my family well."

"I helped some people."

"I left the world a little better than I found it."

If Whole Life Journey helps me do those three things...

Then every late night...

Every line of code...

Every difficult conversation...

Every setback...

Will have been worth it.

Because at the end of the day...

Technology isn't the legacy.

People are.

Always have been.

Always will be.
````

# Chapter 45
# Legacy

The older I get...

The less I think about accomplishments.

I think about legacy.

When I was younger, legacy sounded like something famous people worried about.

Presidents.

Professional athletes.

Business leaders.

People whose names ended up in history books.

I don't think that anymore.

I think every parent leaves one.

Every grandparent leaves one.

Every coach.

Every teacher.

Every ordinary person who loves someone else leaves something behind.

The only question is...

What?

---

When I was younger, I assumed legacy meant leaving money.

Or property.

Or maybe a successful career.

Now I know better.

Money gets spent.

Houses get sold.

Cars wear out.

Even trophies eventually end up in boxes.

Stories...

Stories live much longer.

If someone still tells your stories...

Part of you is still here.

That's one of the reasons this book exists.

---

One afternoon, while Heather and I were going through old photographs, something hit me.

There were pictures of people Haley would never really know.

She knew their names.

She knew who they were.

But she didn't know *them*.

She didn't know that Granny answered the telephone by saying,

"Say hello."

She didn't know George yelled,

"Quit swinging from the ass."

She didn't know Dad called me Stump because I looked like the stump of a tree.

She didn't know Vance had once stood completely naked in front of his girlfriend and her boss because I'd put him to bed drunk.

Those aren't facts.

Those are people.

That's what disappears first.

Not birthdays.

Not death dates.

Personalities.

Laughter.

Inside jokes.

That's the tragedy.

---

I've spent enough time at funerals to notice something.

People don't gather afterward to talk about somebody's résumé.

They tell stories.

Remember when...

Do you remember...

I'll never forget...

That's what people carry.

Not accomplishments.

Experiences.

---

If you've read this far, you've probably noticed something.

I don't spend much time talking about statistics.

I could.

I could tell you batting averages.

Touchdown passes.

Awards.

Promotions.

Job titles.

Most of that information exists somewhere already.

What doesn't exist...

At least not until now...

Is how those moments felt.

How they changed me.

Who was standing beside me.

Who believed in me.

Who laughed with me.

That's what I don't want to lose.

---

One of the things I admire most about my dad wasn't that he built houses.

It was that he built people.

He probably would've laughed hearing me say that.

He wasn't trying to become a philosopher.

He was just being Dad.

Teaching me to work.

Teaching me to keep my word.

Teaching me to choose good friends.

Teaching me to finish what I started.

He probably had no idea those lessons would still be shaping me decades later.

That's legacy.

---

Mom's legacy looks different.

Dad taught strength.

Mom taught grace.

Dad taught me to compete.

Mom taught me to care.

Dad prepared me to face the world.

Mom prepared me to love people in it.

I needed both.

I still do.

---

Heather's legacy is still being written.

I hope she knows how much she's changed me.

People sometimes tell me,

"You've become a good husband."

If that's true...

Most of the credit belongs to her.

She has loved me through every version of Danny.

The confident athlete.

The nervous fiancé.

The young husband.

The new father.

The son taking care of his father.

The executive.

The entrepreneur.

The dreamer building Whole Life Journey.

She never asked me to become somebody else.

She simply encouraged me to become the best version of who God created me to be.

That's a remarkable gift.

---

Then there's Haley.

I've often wondered what she'll remember most about me.

Will it be baseball?

Motorcycles?

Whole Life Journey?

I honestly hope not.

I hope she remembers laughter.

Conversations.

Road trips.

Encouragement.

Showing up.

Listening.

Being there.

If she remembers those things...

Then I think I did okay.

---

As I write this, I'm fifty-five years old.

I've lived long enough to understand something my younger self never would've believed.

People won't remember you nearly as much for what you achieved...

As they will for how you made them feel.

I've forgotten a lot of impressive people.

I've never forgotten kind people.

There's a lesson in that.

---

If one day my grandchildren pick this book up...

I hope they don't think,

"Grandpa did some interesting things."

I hope they think,

"I wish I'd known him."

Even better...

I hope they feel like they do.

That's really been the goal all along.

Not to write an autobiography.

To preserve a grandfather.

A husband.

A father.

A son.

A friend.

A teammate.

An ordinary man who was blessed with an extraordinary collection of people.

---

People sometimes ask me what I want written on my tombstone.

Honestly...

I don't care very much about that.

If I had one wish...

It would simply be this.

That long after I'm gone...

Somebody would still smile...

Tell one of my stories...

And say,

"That sounds exactly like Danny."

If that happens...

Then I think I'll have left behind exactly the legacy I was hoping for.
````

# Chapter 46
# Why I'm Writing This

If you've made it this far...

You probably know me a little better than when we started.

Maybe you've laughed a few times.

Maybe you've cried once or twice.

Maybe you shook your head and thought,

"Only Danny..."

That's okay.

I probably would've done the same thing.

---

As I've been writing these stories, something unexpected happened.

I thought I was writing a book.

Instead...

I found myself having conversations with people who aren't here anymore.

I'd start writing about Dad...

And before long I'd hear his voice.

Not literally.

But clearly enough that I knew exactly what he would've said.

The same thing happened with Mom.

With Granny.

With George.

With Jerry.

With Linda.

With so many others.

It's amazing how memories work.

People leave this world.

Their voices don't have to.

---

That's become the real purpose of this book.

Not to preserve events.

To preserve voices.

I don't want future generations to simply know that Marvin Jenkins existed.

I want them to hear him saying,

> "When you're big enough to start it...

> You can ride it."

I don't want them to simply know Granny answered the phone.

I want them smiling every time a phone rings because they remember,

> "Say hello."

Those little moments...

That's where people actually live.

---

I've also realized something while writing.

I don't remember my life in chronological order.

Nobody does.

Memory doesn't work that way.

I'll be writing about baseball...

Then suddenly remember a motorcycle.

I'll think about Heather...

Then remember Linda.

I'll write about Dad...

Then suddenly remember something Buddy said twenty years later.

That's okay.

That's how memory works.

It's more like walking through a forest than following a road.

You never know what you'll discover around the next bend.

---

One of the things I've always loved about photographs is that they don't argue.

They simply wait.

Patiently.

Quietly.

You can walk past the same photograph a hundred times.

Then one day...

It suddenly reminds you of something you'd forgotten for forty years.

That's happened over and over while writing this book.

Matter of fact...

Some of my favorite stories only came back because I happened to notice one tiny detail in an old picture.

A look on Heather's face.

The way Dad was standing.

A little shovel.

A motorcycle.

The expression on Buddy's face.

Photographs are remarkable that way.

They patiently hold memories until we're ready for them.

---

I hope this book becomes something our family adds to.

I really do.

Maybe one day Haley remembers a story I forgot.

Maybe one day my grandchildren add stories about me.

Maybe this becomes less of a book...

And more of a living family history.

I'd love that.

Families shouldn't lose their stories every generation.

They should grow them.

---

I've spent most of my professional life building systems.

Payroll systems.

HR systems.

Technology.

Processes.

Eventually...

Whole Life Journey.

I've always enjoyed creating things that outlive me.

This book is no different.

Except...

Instead of preserving information...

It's preserving people.

That feels much more important.

---

One thing I hope nobody misunderstands.

This isn't about me.

Really.

It's about everyone who invested in me.

Every chapter eventually points somewhere else.

To Dad.

To Mom.

To Heather.

To Haley.

To coaches.

Friends.

Teachers.

Neighbors.

Family.

I'm simply the thread tying those stories together.

If you finish this book loving those people...

Then I've accomplished something worthwhile.

---

Sometimes people ask what I hope God says when I finally meet Him.

I don't have a complicated answer.

I simply hope He says,

"Well done."

Not because I was famous.

Not because I accomplished extraordinary things.

Because I tried.

Because I loved people.

Because I kept getting back up when I fell down.

Because I pointed people toward Him more often than toward myself.

That's enough.

More than enough.

---

If you've read every page...

Thank you.

Not for reading about me.

For taking the time to meet the people who made me who I am.

They deserve to be remembered.

Far more than I do.

If this book helps even one future member of our family feel connected to those who came before them...

Then every hour spent writing it will have been worth it.

Now...

Let's close the photo album.

Not because the stories are over.

Because I have a feeling we'll be opening it again before too long.

There are always more stories.

There always will be.

Relationally.

Jerry.

Vance.

Russ.

Dad.

Really do last a lifetime.

# Chapter 49
# If I Could Go Back

People ask that question a lot.

"If you could go back..."

"If you knew then what you know now..."

"What would you change?"

It's a fair question.

I've thought about it quite a bit.

The older I get...

The more complicated the answer becomes.

---

When I was younger...

I could've given you a long list.

I'd have played that at-bat differently.

Thrown a different pitch.

Taken a different job.

Bought different stock.

Said yes here.

Said no there.

Stayed longer.

Left sooner.

There would've been hundreds of little changes.

Now...

Most of them don't seem to matter much anymore.

---

Would I like another conversation with Dad?

Absolutely.

I'd ask more questions.

A lot more.

Not about baseball.

Not about construction.

About him.

What scared him?

What did he regret?

Who was he before he became my dad?

Those are the questions I wish I'd asked.

When you're young...

You assume your parents have always been parents.

You forget they were once young too.

I wish I'd known that sooner.

---

I'd ask Mom more questions too.

Not about me.

About her.

What was she thinking the day Barbara Jean knocked on the door?

What did she pray that night?

Was she scared?

Angry?

Hopeful?

Did she ever think about leaving?

Did she know, in that moment, she was about to become my mother?

I've heard parts of that story.

I wish I had heard all of it.

---

I'd tell Buddy something too.

I'd probably tell him I looked up to him more than he realized.

Growing up ten years apart meant we didn't spend our childhood the same way.

But that didn't mean he wasn't important.

He was.

He still is.

Sometimes brothers don't say those things.

Maybe we should.

---

I'd hug Granny a little longer.

Then I'd probably wait for the phone to ring.

Just so she could remind me to,

"Say hello."

Some moments deserve to be relived forever.

That one's on the list.

---

I'd spend more afternoons just sitting with Dad after the stroke.

Not talking.

Just sitting.

Some of the best conversations we ever had happened when neither one of us felt the need to fill the silence.

I wish I'd recognized how valuable those quiet moments really were.

Sometimes presence is enough.

Actually...

Most of the time it is.

---

People often assume I'd choose professional baseball if I got another chance.

That's probably the biggest surprise in this chapter.

I wouldn't.

Not because I stopped loving baseball.

I never did.

Because changing that decision changes everything.

No Alabama.

No Heather.

No Haley.

No life I have today.

No thank you.

I wouldn't trade my family for a Major League uniform.

Not for all the World Series rings in existence.

Twenty-year-old Danny wouldn't understand that.

Fifty-five-year-old Danny does.

---

I'd probably worry less too.

Funny...

Most of the things I worried about never actually happened.

The things that did happen...

I couldn't have predicted anyway.

I've learned that worry is one of the poorest investments you'll ever make.

It costs a lot.

Returns almost nothing.

---

I'd also spend less time trying to impress people.

That's something age has taught me.

When you're young...

You think everybody's watching.

They're not.

They're worried about their own lives.

The people who truly matter...

Already love you.

The rest...

Probably aren't thinking about you nearly as much as you imagine.

That's actually pretty freeing.

---

If I could go back...

I'd still buy the motorcycles.

Every one of them.

I'd still build the practice track.

I'd still ride with Haley.

I'd still laugh at Buddy on the back of my Honda.

I'd still marry Heather.

I'd still move Dad into our home.

I'd still spend those nine years with him.

I'd still write this book.

Matter of fact...

I'd probably start writing it sooner.

---

You know what I wouldn't change?

The mistakes.

Not all of them.

Some, absolutely.

But many of them taught me lessons success never could.

Failure has been one of my greatest teachers.

Embarrassment too.

Humility.

Disappointment.

They've all shaped me.

If I erase those...

I erase part of the man I've become.

I don't want to do that.

---

So...

If someone asked me one final time,

"If you could go back..."

I think my answer would simply be this.

I'd go back...

Not to change my life.

To appreciate it.

To notice the ordinary moments a little more.

To ask a few more questions.

To hug people a little longer.

To laugh a little harder.

To say,

"I love you,"

a little more often.

Everything else...

I think God handled just fine.

001 - The Boy on the Porch.md

# The Boy on the Porch

This is where my story begins.

Not in a hospital.

Not on my birthday.

Not on my birth certificate.

My story begins on a front porch.

Long before I understood what family meant...

Someone made a decision that changed the rest of my life.

Actually...

Several people made decisions.

Some good.

Some bad.

Some painful.

All of them led to me.

---

Everything I'm about to tell you happened before I was old enough to remember it.

I've pieced it together over the years through conversations with Dad, Mom, Aunt Janice, my biological sisters, Uncle Danny, and others.

Not everyone remembers every detail exactly the same way.

That's okay.

People remember moments differently.

What matters is the truth underneath the details.

---

I was born Danny Ray Dodge.

Very few people have ever known that name.

The world has always known me as Danny Jenkins.

Matter of fact...

Growing up in California almost everyone outside my family simply called me Dan.

When I moved to Tennessee I somehow became Danny again.

Funny how geography changes names.

Around home...

Dad usually called me Stump.

We'll get to that story later.

---

My biological parents were Marvin Jenkins and Barbara Jean Dorff.

Their relationship was an affair.

I don't tell you that because I'm embarrassed by it.

I'm certainly not proud of it.

It's simply part of the truth.

The older I've gotten...

The less interested I am in deciding who the villain was.

Life isn't that simple.

People make mistakes.

Sometimes terrible ones.

Sometimes life grows out of those mistakes.

I'm living proof.

---

From everything I've learned...

Dad knew about me almost from the beginning.

He visited me regularly.

Helped support me.

Brought diapers.

Food.

Money.

Whatever he could.

Over time he became increasingly concerned about how I was being cared for.

He repeatedly asked Barbara Jean to let me come live with him and Gloria.

She refused.

Again.

And again.

Until one day...

Everything changed.

---

Dad was sitting in his recliner.

Just another ordinary day.

Mom was home.

Three children were already part of the family.

Buddy.

Lindsey.

Julie.

Then there was a knock at the front door.

Mom answered it.

Standing there...

Was Barbara Jean.

Holding a little blond-haired boy.

Me.

Without much conversation she simply stretched out her arms toward Gloria and said,

> "Here.
> He belongs to your husband."

Then she turned around...

And walked away.

Just like that.

---

I've replayed that scene in my mind a thousand times.

Imagine opening your front door.

You expect the mailman.

Or a neighbor.

Instead...

Another woman hands you your husband's son.

How do you process something like that?

How do you breathe?

How do you think?

I honestly don't know.

---

Dad immediately jumped out of his recliner.

He told Mom to hold me.

Then he ran after Barbara Jean.

Not because he didn't want me.

Quite the opposite.

He'd wanted me for months.

He was furious because of how it happened.

He believed there had to have been a better way.

I imagine there probably was.

Life doesn't always give us better ways.

Sometimes it simply gives us reality.

---

When Dad came back into the house...

Everything had changed.

Not just for him.

For everyone.

Mom was now holding a baby she had never seen before.

A baby that represented one of the most painful moments of her marriage.

Yet...

She was holding me.

Not pushing me away.

Holding me.

That picture has become more meaningful to me every year.

---

A few weeks later...

Barbara Jean came back.

She wanted me.

Dad had already warned Mom.

"If she comes...

Don't let her leave with him.

Call me."

So she did.

While waiting for Dad to arrive...

Mom and Barbara Jean sat in the kitchen.

Me between them.

Barbara Jean smiled.

Reached toward me.

Held out her arms.

And said,

> "Come to Mommy."

According to Mom...

I looked at her.

Then turned away.

I crawled into Gloria's lap.

I've heard that story many times.

Every time...

It affects me differently.

---

Years later Mom told me something I've never forgotten.

She said,

> "Any baby that won't go to his own mother needs somebody to love him."

I've thought about that sentence hundreds of times.

She wasn't criticizing Barbara Jean.

She wasn't making herself look like the hero.

She simply saw a little boy who needed someone.

She decided...

That someone would be her.

---

That decision became the foundation of my entire life.

Everything else came later.

The tree.

Baseball.

Motorcycles.

Football.

College.

Heather.

Haley.

My career.

Whole Life Journey.

Every blessing I can point to traces back to that one decision.

One woman...

Choosing love over bitterness.

Grace over resentment.

Family over pain.

---

Here's something I've realized as an adult.

People often ask,

"Who is your real mother?"

I've never struggled with that question.

Not once.

Barbara Jean gave me life.

For that...

I'll always be grateful.

Gloria gave me a life.

She raised me.

Loved me.

Corrected me.

Encouraged me.

Cheered at my games.

Worried about me.

Prayed for me.

Held me accountable.

Celebrated my victories.

Comforted my failures.

That's Mom.

Always has been.

Always will be.

---

One of the hardest things for me to accept later in life was realizing what Mom must have carried.

For twenty-two years...

She never told me.

Not because she wanted to deceive me.

Because she wanted me to have a childhood.

A normal one.

Looking back...

I think she succeeded.

I never questioned whether I belonged.

Never.

I simply knew I was a Jenkins.

That may have been the greatest gift she ever gave me.

---

People sometimes ask whether I wish I'd known the truth sooner.

I've gone back and forth on that.

As a young man...

I would've said yes.

Today...

I'm not so sure.

Because my childhood wasn't built on confusion.

It was built on love.

Would knowing the truth earlier have answered some questions?

Absolutely.

Would it have robbed me of the security Mom worked so hard to give me?

Maybe.

I'll never know.

What I do know is this.

When I think about childhood...

I don't remember secrets.

I remember baseball.

Motorcycles.

The tree.

Mom.

Dad.

Buddy.

Lindsey.

Julie.

Laughter.

Safety.

Love.

That's a pretty wonderful childhood.

---

If I had one opportunity to speak to Gloria today...

I'd probably say something simple.

Thank you.

Not for raising me.

Although I'm certainly thankful for that.

I'd thank her for choosing me.

Every single day.

Because that's what she did.

People think adoption is one decision.

It isn't.

It's thousands.

She chose me when I was sick.

She chose me when I was difficult.

She chose me when I was a teenager.

# Childhood

## Introduction

When I think back on my childhood, I don't think in dates.

I don't remember thinking,

"That happened in 1976."

Or...

"That was second grade."

My mind doesn't work that way.

My childhood comes back to me in places.

People.

Smells.

Motorcycles.

Baseball fields.

Old photographs.

The tree in the front yard.

The sound of Dad's truck.

The smell of eucalyptus trees.

The sound of motorcycles echoing across Gorman.

Those are the things that bring my childhood back.

Writing this section has reminded me that childhood isn't really a collection of years.

It's a collection of moments.

Some lasted only seconds.

Others lasted my entire life.

---

## The Boy on the Porch

My story doesn't really begin with my birth.

It begins with a decision.

Actually...

Several decisions.

Some good.

Some painful.

Some courageous.

Every one of them eventually led to me.

I don't remember any of it.

Everything I'm about to tell you happened before I was old enough to form memories.

I've pieced it together through conversations with Dad, Mom, Aunt Janice, Uncle Danny, my biological sisters, and others over many years.

Different people remember different details.

That's okay.

Life isn't remembered like court testimony.

It's remembered through hearts.

The facts may vary around the edges.

The truth usually doesn't.

---

I was born Danny Ray Dodge.

Almost nobody knows that.

The world has always known me as Danny Jenkins.

Growing up in Southern California, almost everyone simply called me Dan.

When I moved to Tennessee years later, I somehow became Danny again.

Around the house...

Dad usually called me Stump.

We'll get to that story later.

---

My biological parents were Marvin Jenkins and Barbara Jean Dorff.

Their relationship was an affair.

That isn't something I celebrate.

It isn't something I hide either.

It's simply part of my story.

The older I've become, the less interested I am in deciding who deserves blame.

Life is usually far more complicated than that.

People make decisions.

Some good.

Some terrible.

Sometimes beautiful things grow out of broken places.

My life certainly did.

---

Dad knew about me almost immediately.

He visited me.

Supported me financially.

Checked on me.

As time passed he became increasingly concerned about the conditions I was living in.

He repeatedly asked Barbara Jean if I could come live with him and Gloria.

Every time...

The answer was no.

Until one ordinary day...

It became yes.

---

Dad was sitting in his recliner.

Mom was home.

Buddy.

Lindsey.

Julie.

Life was moving along like every other day.

Then someone knocked on the front door.

Mom answered it.

Standing there...

Was Barbara Jean.

Holding a little blond-haired boy.

Me.

Without much conversation...

She held me out toward Gloria and simply said,

> "Here.
> He belongs to your husband."

Then she turned around...

And walked away.

I have replayed that moment in my mind hundreds of times.

I can't imagine what Mom must have felt.

Shock.

Confusion.

Pain.

Anger.

Maybe all of them.

Yet the only thing she did...

Was hold me.

---

Dad immediately ran after Barbara Jean.

He wasn't angry because she brought me.

He had wanted me for months.

He was angry because of how she brought me.

He believed there had to have been a better way.

Maybe there was.

Life rarely asks us whether we like the circumstances.

It simply hands them to us.

---

Dad eventually came back inside.

Nothing in that house would ever be the same.

One marriage.

Three children.

One unexpected little boy.

One impossible conversation.

One extraordinary woman.

Looking back...

That's where my childhood really begins.

Not because of what Barbara Jean did.

Because of what Gloria chose to do next.

---

A few weeks later...

Barbara Jean returned.

This time...

She wanted me back.

Dad had already warned Mom.

"If she comes...

Don't let her leave with him.

Call me."

While waiting for Dad to get home...

The three of us sat in the kitchen.

Barbara Jean reached toward me.

Smiled.

Held out her arms.

And said,

> "Come to Mommy."

According to Mom...

I looked at her.

Turned away.

Then crawled into Gloria's lap.

Years later Mom told me something that has stayed with me ever since.

She said,

> "Any baby that won't go to his own mother needs somebody to love him."

Then she added something else.

She knew...

At that moment...

She wasn't letting me go.

That was the day she became my mother.

Not biologically.

Not legally.

Spiritually.

Emotionally.

In every way that truly matters.

---

I didn't know any of this.

Not as a child.

Not as a teenager.

Not even after high school.

I simply knew Mom.

Dad.

Buddy.

Lindsey.

Julie.

That was my family.

I never questioned it.

Looking back...

I think that's one of the greatest gifts Mom ever gave me.

She protected my childhood.

She let me simply be a little boy.

---

## Growing Up a Jenkins

One thing I've realized while writing this book is that I had a wonderful childhood.

Not a perfect childhood.

There's no such thing.

But a wonderful one.

I grew up feeling safe.

Loved.

Protected.

Encouraged.

I never spent one day wondering whether I belonged.

I belonged.

Completely.

That's an incredible gift.

One many children never experience.

I did.

And I will spend the rest of my life being grateful for it.

---

Buddy was ten years older than I was.

That meant we didn't grow up like most brothers.

By the time I was making memories...

Buddy was already becoming an adult.

He wasn't another kid running through the neighborhood with me.

He was my older brother.

Someone I admired.

Someone I watched.

Someone who seemed much older and much wiser than I could imagine becoming.

Looking back...

I wish I'd told him that more often.

---

Lindsey had a gentle spirit.

She accepted people.

She accepted me.

She never seemed interested in changing who I was.

Julie loved me too.

She just expressed it differently.

Julie believed in accountability.

If I was wrong...

Julie let me know.

Usually immediately.

Sometimes loudly.

Looking back...

I needed both of them.

One taught encouragement.

The other taught responsibility.

Together...

They made me better.

---

Dad was the disciplinarian.

Mom was the comforter.

Dad pushed.

Mom encouraged.

Dad expected.

Mom believed.

Looking back...

Neither approach would've been enough by itself.

Together...

They gave me exactly what I needed.

I didn't understand that then.

I certainly do now.

Neither sister tried to become the other.

Neither one was right.

Neither one was wrong.

They simply loved differently.

That taught me something I'll carry forever.

People don't all express love the same way.

Some encourage.

Some challenge.

Both can be acts of love.

---

## California

When people hear "Southern California" today...

They picture traffic.

Movie stars.

Freeways.

Crowds.

Politics.

That's not the California I remember.

The California I remember was neighborhood kids.

Bicycles.

Little League.

Motorcycles.

Sunshine.

Walking to school.

Playing outside until dark.

Parents standing on front porches calling kids home for dinner.

It felt like childhood.

---

One of the greatest blessings of growing up there was simply being outside.

Almost every day.

Year-round.

There wasn't much reason to stay inside.

If the sun was up...

Kids were outside.

We didn't need somebody entertaining us every minute.

We entertained ourselves.

That's something I think we've lost a little.

Imagination needs room.

We had plenty of it.

---

When I think back now...

I don't remember expensive vacations.

I don't remember fancy toys.

I remember freedom.

Freedom to ride.

Freedom to explore.

Freedom to imagine.

Freedom to simply be a little boy.

That's a gift.

One I don't think I appreciated until much later.

---

## Looking Back

As I sit here writing all of this...

One thought keeps coming back.

I really did have a wonderful childhood.

Not because nothing bad ever happened.

It did.

Not because my family was perfect.

It wasn't.

Not because life was easy.

It wasn't.

I had a wonderful childhood because I never doubted I was loved.

Looking back...

That's probably the greatest gift parents can ever give a child.

Mom and Dad gave me that.

Every single day.

Long before I knew my story...

They were already helping me write it.
````

01 - Childhood.md (Part 5 of 8)

## Gorman

If I had to choose one place that represents my childhood more than anywhere else...

It would probably be Gorman, California.

To most people...

It's just another place on a map.

To me...

It was adventure.

Every trip felt like Christmas morning.

Not because of presents.

Because I knew something exciting was waiting.

---

The excitement usually started the night before.

Dad would begin loading the truck.

I can still picture it.

The Ford F-150.

The camper already mounted on the bed.

The box trailer sitting behind it.

Fuel cans.

Helmets.

Sleeping bags.

Food.

Coolers.

Tools.

Motorcycles.

Sometimes...

The gold dredging equipment instead.

Sometimes...

Both.

Dad checked everything.

Twice.

He was methodical.

Nothing happened by accident.

Looking back...

I realize he wasn't just packing.

He was preparing.

Another lesson I didn't appreciate until years later.

---

I never slept very well the night before those trips.

Not because anything was wrong.

Because I was too excited.

I'd lay there imagining the next day.

The motorcycles.

The campfire.

The creek.

The hills.

The dust.

As a kid...

Anticipation is almost as much fun as the event itself.

Maybe even more.

---

The drive itself seemed to take forever.

Kids don't measure distance in miles.

They measure it in,

"Are we there yet?"

Every hill looked like it should be the last one.

Every turn felt like we had to be getting close.

Eventually...

We'd arrive.

The camper would be backed into place.

Everybody would start unloading.

Within minutes...

The grownups had become campers.

The kids had become explorers.

---

One thing I loved about those trips was that they weren't just our family.

Several families camped together.

The campers usually formed a big circle.

Almost like pioneers circling wagons.

Looking back...

There were probably twenty or thirty kids.

Maybe more.

Nobody seemed worried.

Parents watched everybody.

Not just their own children.

Everybody belonged.

If somebody got hurt...

The closest adult handled it.

If somebody needed help...

Whoever was nearest helped.

That's just the way life worked.

I wish more of the world still worked that way.

---

## Gold Dredging

Eventually Dad became fascinated with gold dredging.

Now...

Most people have never seen one.

Imagine two pontoons floating in a creek.

A gasoline engine mounted on top.

A giant suction hose reaching into the water.

The dredge sucked rocks...

Gravel...

Sand...

Everything off the creek bottom.

Then the material traveled across a sluice box.

The heavy gold stayed.

Everything else washed away.

It looked like the greatest machine ever invented.

At least to a little boy.

---

Dad gave me my own little shovel.

People laugh when they see the old photographs.

They think,

"What a tiny shovel."

Well...

It was.

Because I was tiny.

It wasn't a toy.

It was my shovel.

Dad wanted me involved.

I wasn't just watching.

I was helping.

Maybe I wasn't moving much dirt.

Didn't matter.

I was part of the crew.

That meant everything to me.

Dad had a wonderful way of making me feel like I contributed.

Even when I probably wasn't contributing very much.

---

At the end of the day...

Dad would clean the concentrates.

Then we'd get out the gold pan.

Slowly...

Patiently...

Wash away the black sand.

Eventually...

Tiny flakes of gold started appearing.

Every single time...

It felt like magic.

Real gold.

Something we'd actually found ourselves.

I don't remember how much we ever recovered.

I don't care.

Finding treasure with Dad was the reward.

Not the gold.

---

One of my favorite childhood memories happened at school.

The teacher wanted everyone to give a presentation.

Normally...

That would've terrified me.

Standing in front of the class wasn't exactly my favorite thing.

Unless...

I actually knew the subject.

Dad let me take my gold pan to school.

I stood in front of the class explaining how gold dredging worked.

How black sand collected.

Why gold stayed behind.

What the dredge did.

For the first time...

I wasn't nervous.

Because I wasn't giving a report.

I was telling my story.

I've thought about that many times since.

Speaking becomes much easier when you're talking about something you've actually lived.

---

Many years later...

That little gold pan came back into my life.

Not literally.

The memories did.

When Haley got married...

I wanted to give her something meaningful.

Not just jewelry.

Something connected to our family.

I remembered the gold Dad and I had recovered together.

I had some of it melted down and placed inside a bead that became part of a beautiful rose bracelet.

Most people saw jewelry.

I saw Dad.

I saw Gorman.

I saw a little shovel.

I saw a little blond-haired boy standing beside his father.

That's what made the gift valuable.

Not the gold.

The memories.

---

## My First Motorcycle

My first motorcycle was a Honda Mini Trail 50.

I was around four years old.

Today...

People hear that and usually say one of two things.

"Your parents were crazy."

Or...

"I wish I'd grown up like that."

Honestly...

So do I.

Dad taught me to ride.

Patiently.

I don't actually remember learning.

I just remember riding.

Motorcycles became so normal that I can't remember a time before them.

They're woven into my childhood memories the same way bicycles are for most kids.

---

The Mini Trail wasn't fast.

It wasn't supposed to be.

It was freedom.

My first taste of independence.

My first experience controlling something bigger than myself.

Looking back...

Dad wasn't just teaching me throttle and brakes.

He was teaching responsibility.

Trust.

Confidence.

Those lessons would stay with me long after the little Honda was gone.

---

I wish I still had that motorcycle.

I don't.

It's probably the only motorcycle I truly wish I'd never sold.

Not because of its value.

Because of what it represents.

The beginning.

Everybody remembers their first.

I certainly do.

````

## The MR50

Not long after the Mini Trail...

Dad bought me my second motorcycle.

A Honda MR50.

To this day...

I still own it.

Matter of fact...

It's sitting in my garage as I write this.

People have asked me over the years,

"Why don't you sell it?"

Sell it?

I can't imagine doing that.

That motorcycle isn't transportation.

It's part of my childhood.

Every scratch has a story.

Every faded decal reminds me of somewhere we rode.

Every time I look at it...

I'm six years old again.

Standing beside Dad.

Helmet in my hand.

Waiting for him to say,

"Let's go."

---

The funny thing is...

It still ran the last time I parked it.

I haven't started it in years.

Life gets busy.

Projects happen.

Careers happen.

Families happen.

One day becomes another.

But every time I walk past it...

I smile.

Because I know it's still there.

Waiting.

Almost like it's been patiently holding my childhood until I had time to come back.

---

If my house were on fire...

Obviously I'd grab Heather first.

Then Haley.

After that...

There aren't many possessions I'd worry about.

That little MR50 would probably be one of them.

Not because it's valuable.

Because it's irreplaceable.

You can buy another motorcycle.

You can't buy your childhood back.

---

## Learning from Dad

Looking back...

I don't think Dad realized how much I was watching him.

Kids are always watching.

Even when they don't seem interested.

Especially then.

I'd watch him hook up trailers.

Tie down motorcycles.

Check oil.

Load fuel.

Organize tools.

Fix broken parts.

He rarely explained what he was doing.

He simply did it.

I learned by watching.

That's still how I learn best today.

---

Dad had an incredible mechanical mind.

He could look at something broken...

And almost immediately begin figuring out how to fix it.

I admired that.

I still do.

People often ask me where my systems thinking comes from.

Whole Life Journey.

Payroll.

Technology.

I honestly think part of it came from watching Dad troubleshoot mechanical problems.

You learn to ask,

"Why?"

Instead of simply replacing parts.

That mindset eventually moved from engines...

To organizations.

From motorcycles...

To people.

---

One thing Dad never seemed afraid of...

Work.

If something needed doing...

He did it.

Didn't complain much.

Didn't wait for somebody else.

Just...

Worked.

As a kid...

I assumed everybody's dad was like that.

As an adult...

I realized they weren't.

I'm thankful mine was.

---

## Little League Begins

Somewhere during all those motorcycle years...

Baseball entered my life.

Looking back...

I don't really remember choosing baseball.

It simply became part of life.

Almost as naturally as motorcycles had.

The difference was...

Motorcycles belonged mostly to Dad and me.

Baseball belonged to the entire family.

Everybody became involved.

Mom.

Dad.

Buddy.

Lindsey.

Julie.

Eventually...

Baseball would become the center of our family calendar.

We just didn't know it yet.

---

Before organized baseball...

There was backyard baseball.

Neighborhood baseball.

Imaginary baseball.

If I had a baseball...

I was happy.

If I had somebody to throw with...

Even better.

If nobody was around...

I'd throw against the garage.

Or a wall.

Or anything else that would throw the ball back.

People sometimes think practice has to be organized.

It doesn't.

The best practice usually isn't.

It's just repetition.

Over.

And over.

And over.

Until something becomes part of you.

---

Looking back...

I don't remember anyone forcing me to practice.

Matter of fact...

Dad usually had the opposite problem.

Getting me to stop.

I'd stay outside until it got too dark to see.

Eventually Mom would call me in.

Sometimes twice.

Maybe three times.

She had incredible patience.

---

## California Summers

One of the greatest gifts of growing up in Southern California was the weather.

People who haven't lived there probably won't fully understand this.

The weather wasn't something you thought about.

It simply cooperated.

Almost every day.

You could play baseball.

Ride motorcycles.

Ride bicycles.

Climb trees.

Without worrying much about seasons.

That meant childhood happened outdoors.

Constantly.

---

Summer felt endless.

School would finally end.

Then...

Freedom.

No alarms.

No homework.

Just...

Outside.

Those summers seemed to last forever.

Looking back...

They probably didn't.

Childhood simply stretches time.

A single summer feels like several years.

An adult summer seems to disappear in a few weeks.

I've often wished adulthood borrowed a little more from childhood.

Slow down.

Notice things.

Stay outside a little longer.

---

## What Childhood Really Gave Me

People have asked me many times what my childhood was like.

The older I get...

The simpler my answer becomes.

I felt loved.

I felt safe.

I felt free.

Everything else grew out of those three things.

Baseball.

Motorcycles.

Confidence.

Faith.

Friendships.

Leadership.

Dreams.

You can't build those things very easily if you're constantly wondering whether you're safe.

Mom and Dad gave me that foundation.

Not perfectly.

No parents do.

But consistently.

Looking back...

I think that's one of the greatest gifts parents can ever give a child.

The confidence to simply go be a kid.

I was blessed with that.

More than I realized.

Much more.
````

## My First Taste of Competition

I don't know if I was born competitive...

Or if it was something that slowly developed.

Either way...

By the time I was a little boy...

It was already there.

Not in an unhealthy way.

I didn't have to beat everybody at everything.

I simply wanted to know...

"How good can I become?"

Looking back...

That's a very different question.

I wasn't chasing people.

I was chasing improvement.

That mindset has stayed with me my entire life.

---

One of the first places I noticed it was with my cousins.

Chris and Jon Aycock.

They were older than me.

Taller than me.

Excellent athletes.

Whenever they came to visit California...

Or whenever we were together...

We found a basketball.

It didn't matter where.

A driveway.

A school playground.

Seaside Elementary.

Anywhere.

We played.

For hours.

---

Now...

Common sense says they should've dominated me.

They were bigger.

Older.

More experienced.

Sometimes they did.

But a surprising number of times...

I held my own.

Looking back...

I understand why.

I wasn't stronger.

I wasn't taller.

I simply anticipated.

Before the rebound came off the rim...

I was already moving.

Before a pass happened...

I could often see it coming.

I didn't know I was doing that.

It simply felt normal.

Years later...

I would recognize that same ability in baseball.

Football.

Leadership.

Even business.

God had wired my brain to anticipate.

It became one of the greatest gifts He ever gave me.

---

## Learning How I Learn

School and I had an interesting relationship.

I wasn't a bad student.

I wasn't a great student either.

What I eventually realized was...

I didn't learn the way schools generally teach.

Give me a textbook.

I'd struggle.

Stand me in front of a chalkboard.

You'd probably lose me.

Let me experience something...

I'd remember it forever.

---

Gold dredging.

Motorcycles.

Baseball.

Construction.

Those weren't just hobbies.

They became classrooms.

Dad probably never intended to homeschool me.

Yet...

He did.

Without ever realizing it.

He taught me by doing.

That's exactly how I still learn today.

Matter of fact...

It's one of the reasons Whole Life Journey eventually became what it did.

I don't want information.

I want understanding.

There's a huge difference.

---

## Friends

Dad taught me something about friendship long before I realized he was teaching it.

He used to say,

> "I can't pick your friends...
> but I can damn sure limit your activities with them."

At first...

That sounded like one of Dad's funny one-liners.

Looking back...

It was one of the smartest parenting principles I've ever heard.

He understood human nature.

If I wanted freedom...

I'd naturally choose friends he trusted.

He never had to forbid very many friendships.

He simply made me think.

---

Looking back over my entire life...

I think Dad was successful.

I've been blessed with incredible friends.

People like Jerry.

Russ.

Vance.

Johnnie.

People who made me better.

People who challenged me.

People who laughed with me.

People I trusted.

That didn't happen by accident.

Dad quietly shaped that.

I'm grateful.

---

## Looking Through Adult Eyes

One of the strange things about writing this archive is that I get to experience childhood twice.

Once...

As the little boy living it.

Again...

As the fifty-five-year-old man looking back.

Those two perspectives aren't always the same.

The little boy saw adventure.

The grown man sees sacrifice.

The little boy saw motorcycles.

The grown man sees a father creating memories.

The little boy saw camping.

The grown man sees parents investing time.

The little boy saw baseball.

The grown man sees confidence quietly being built.

It's fascinating.

---

I don't think I fully appreciated Mom until I became an adult.

I certainly didn't appreciate Dad the way I do now.

That's probably true for most children.

Parents spend decades making sacrifices their children never notice.

Then...

One day...

The children become parents.

Suddenly...

Everything makes sense.

I've experienced that.

Many times.

---

## The Foundation

People often ask why I've always seemed optimistic.

I think the answer starts here.

Childhood.

I began life believing the world was a safe place.

Not because the world actually is.

Because Mom and Dad made it feel that way.

They gave me roots.

Confidence.

Security.

They allowed me to become curious.

To dream.

To explore.

Without constantly wondering whether someone would catch me if I fell.

That's an incredible foundation.

---

Everything I've accomplished...

Everything I've attempted...

Everything I've built...

Stands on top of those early years.

People often look at adulthood and wonder where confidence comes from.

Confidence doesn't suddenly appear.

It's built.

Quietly.

One ordinary day at a time.

My parents built mine.

---

## Closing Thoughts on Childhood

If someone asked me today to summarize my childhood in one sentence...

I think I'd simply say this.

I was loved far more than I understood.

That's really it.

The motorcycles mattered.

The baseball mattered.

The camping mattered.

The tree mattered.

The neighborhood mattered.

But all of those things mattered because of the people I shared them with.

Without Mom...

They're just memories.

Without Dad...

They're just stories.

Without Buddy...

Lindsey...

Julie...

They're just photographs.

People gave childhood its meaning.

---

As I close this section...

One thought keeps coming back.

I had no idea how blessed I was.

As children...

We rarely do.

We're too busy living.

Looking back now...

I realize something.

Childhood wasn't preparing me for baseball.

Or football.

Or Alabama.

Or marriage.

Or my career.

Childhood was preparing me to become Danny Jenkins.

Every baseball.

Every motorcycle.

Every campfire.

Every hug.

Every correction.

Every laugh.

Every ordinary Tuesday.

God was quietly building a foundation that would support everything else He planned to do with my life.

I just thought I was being a little boy.

Turns out...

He was building a man.
````

01 - Childhood.md (Part 8 of 8)

## Things I Didn't Appreciate Until Later

One of the interesting things about getting older is realizing how much was happening around you that you never noticed.

As a little boy...

I thought life was simply...

Life.

Dad went to work.

Mom made dinner.

The bills somehow got paid.

The lights always came on.

Food magically appeared in the refrigerator.

Motorcycles somehow got fixed.

Camping trips somehow happened.

Christmas somehow arrived.

I never stopped to ask,

"How?"

Kids aren't supposed to.

Parents quietly carry those burdens so children don't have to.

Looking back now...

I see all the things I never saw.

Dad working long hours.

Mom stretching dollars.

Sacrifices that weren't announced.

Dreams that were probably postponed.

Arguments that happened after we went to bed.

Worries they kept to themselves.

That's what good parents do.

They protect childhood.

---

## My Childhood Wasn't Perfect

I want to be careful not to paint an unrealistic picture.

Our family wasn't perfect.

No family is.

Dad and Mom had struggles.

The marriage eventually ended.

There were arguments.

Disappointments.

Financial pressures.

Moments I didn't understand.

Life wasn't always easy.

It just always felt safe.

Those are two different things.

Safety isn't the absence of problems.

It's knowing somebody is there when problems arrive.

That's how childhood felt to me.

---

## The Seeds of Faith

Looking back...

Faith was present long before I understood theology.

It wasn't something we talked about every hour.

It was simply woven into life.

Church.

Prayer.

The understanding that God mattered.

I didn't yet know how deeply my faith would eventually shape my life.

That would come much later.

But the seeds were planted early.

I'm thankful for that.

---

## Curiosity

If I had to describe myself as a child in one word...

It might actually be...

Curious.

I wanted to know how things worked.

Why they worked.

Could they be improved?

Could I build one?

Could I fix one?

That curiosity eventually showed up everywhere.

Motorcycles.

Computers.

Payroll systems.

Artificial intelligence.

Whole Life Journey.

Looking back...

It's all the same curiosity.

Just different subjects.

---

## Competition

People often think competition is about beating someone else.

I don't think that's ever been true for me.

Competition has always been internal.

Can I become better?

Can I improve?

Can I figure this out?

Can I solve this problem?

That's why I enjoyed baseball so much.

There was always another level.

Always another challenge.

The same thing happened in business.

Then technology.

Then leadership.

I'm still competing today.

The opponent just happens to be yesterday's version of me.

---

## Why Childhood Matters

I've often heard people say,

"Don't live in the past."

I understand what they mean.

But I also think people misunderstand something.

Looking back isn't the same thing as living back there.

Looking back allows us to understand ourselves.

I know why I love motorcycles.

I know why I enjoy leadership.

I know why I love solving problems.

I know why I value loyalty.

I know why trust matters so much to me.

The answers all begin somewhere in childhood.

If I ignore childhood...

I ignore the foundation of who I became.

---

## The Pictures

One of the reasons this entire project started was photographs.

Boxes and boxes of photographs.

Some labeled.

Many not.

As I started scanning them...

Something incredible happened.

The pictures started talking.

Not literally.

They started waking up memories.

One picture became three stories.

Those three stories reminded me of five more.

Then another photograph connected to another person.

Suddenly...

A childhood I thought I remembered pretty well became incredibly rich.

That's why I don't ever want these photographs separated from the stories.

One without the other loses something.

Together...

They become history.

Family history.

---

## If I Could Talk to That Little Boy

Sometimes I imagine walking into one of those old photographs.

The little blond-haired boy is standing there holding a baseball.

Or sitting on his motorcycle.

Or climbing that tree.

If I could walk up beside him...

What would I say?

Honestly...

Probably not much.

I'd simply smile.

Because I know something he doesn't.

Everything is going to be okay.

Actually...

Better than okay.

You're going to experience heartbreak.

You'll lose people you love.

Dreams will change.

Plans won't always work out.

You'll cry more than you think.

You'll laugh even more.

One day you'll marry the woman God created for you.

You'll become the father of an incredible little girl.

You'll discover a family you never knew existed.

You'll take care of your dad.

You'll build a career you never imagined.

You'll create something called Whole Life Journey.

Most importantly...

You'll discover that God was with you every single step.

Even when you couldn't see Him.

So...

Relax.

Go ride your motorcycle.

Play another baseball game.

Climb the tree one more time.

Love Mom.

Listen to Dad.

Laugh with Buddy.

Spend time with Lindsey.

Let Julie get on your nerves once in a while.

You're going to miss all of it someday.

Not because you want to go back.

Because you'll finally understand how beautiful it really was.

---

## Closing Childhood

As I close this section, I realize something.

This isn't really the end of childhood.

It's simply the point where the world started getting bigger.

Baseball was about to become serious.

Football was about to enter my life.

Friends would become lifelong brothers.

California would eventually become Tennessee.

A little boy named Stump...

Was about to begin discovering the man God had always intended him to become.

But before all of that happened...

He got to be a kid.

And looking back...

I'm incredibly thankful he did.

**End of 01 - Childhood.md**

# Baseball

## Introduction

If you asked me to tell you my life story...

I'd probably end up talking about baseball.

Not because baseball was my entire life.

Because baseball became the backdrop for so much of it.

When I think about Dad...

I think about baseball.

When I think about confidence...

I think about baseball.

When I think about childhood...

I think about baseball.

When I think about friends...

I think about baseball.

When I think about learning to compete...

I think about baseball.

Baseball wasn't simply something I played.

It became one of the primary ways God shaped me.

Looking back now...

I don't think He was preparing me to become a baseball player.

I think He was using baseball to prepare me for life.

I just didn't know it.

---

## The First Time I Held a Baseball

I honestly don't remember the first baseball I ever held.

It feels like baseball has always been part of my life.

Some people remember getting their first glove.

Their first bat.

Their first game.

I don't.

I simply remember baseball always being there.

It was as normal as bicycles.

As normal as motorcycles.

As normal as eating dinner.

If there was daylight...

There was a pretty good chance there was a baseball nearby.

---

Dad loved baseball.

Not because he was trying to create the next Major Leaguer.

He genuinely loved the game.

He understood it.

He appreciated it.

He respected it.

I think I inherited that appreciation.

Baseball isn't just athletic ability.

It's thinking.

It's anticipation.

It's patience.

It's discipline.

It's failure.

It's resilience.

You can spend a lifetime learning baseball.

You never completely master it.

Maybe that's why I loved it so much.

---

## Why Baseball Was Different

I played other sports.

Football.

Basketball.

I enjoyed all of them.

But baseball was different.

Football felt exciting.

Basketball felt fast.

Baseball...

Felt peaceful.

That may sound strange.

People who haven't played probably won't understand.

Baseball has quiet moments.

Time to think.

Time to anticipate.

Time to notice things.

That's where I lived.

Most people watched the baseball.

I watched everything else.

The pitcher.

The hitter's feet.

The catcher's setup.

The infield.

The wind.

The shadows.

Without realizing it...

I was collecting information.

By the time the ball was hit...

I usually already knew where I needed to go.

I didn't consciously think through it.

It simply happened.

Looking back...

I think that was one of God's gifts.

---

## Backyard Baseball

Long before uniforms...

Long before umpires...

Long before scoreboards...

There was the backyard.

Or the driveway.

Or the garage.

Or the side yard.

If I had a baseball...

I was entertained.

I threw against the garage until Mom probably thought the house was going to fall apart.

Ground ball.

Throw.

Ground ball.

Throw.

Ground ball.

Throw.

Hour after hour.

Nobody made me.

Dad certainly didn't have to tell me to practice.

I wanted to.

Looking back...

That's probably the biggest reason I became as good as I did.

Practice never felt like work.

It felt like play.

---

I learned something during those hours that stayed with me my entire life.

Repetition matters.

People want shortcuts.

There usually aren't any.

You become good at something by doing it...

Again.

And again.

And again.

Until it becomes part of who you are.

That's true in baseball.

It's true in leadership.

It's true in marriage.

It's true in faith.

It's true in business.

Life rewards repetition.

---

## Dad's Batting Practice

Some of my favorite memories involve nothing more complicated than Dad throwing batting practice.

No crowds.

No trophies.

No coaches.

Just Dad.

A bucket of baseballs.

A bat.

And me.

Looking back...

Those were some of the most valuable hours we ever spent together.

Not because of baseball.

Because we were together.

---

Dad wasn't trying to become my coach.

He was simply my dad.

Sometimes he'd throw.

Sometimes he'd shag baseballs.

Sometimes he'd tell me to keep my front shoulder in.

Sometimes he'd simply smile after I squared one up.

I don't remember many long speeches.

Dad taught through repetition.

The lesson was almost always the same.

Again.

One more.

Again.

Eventually...

Good things happen.

That's how he lived his life too.

---

## Falling in Love with the Game

I don't know exactly when baseball stopped being a game...

And became a passion.

It happened gradually.

One day I realized I wasn't just looking forward to games.

I was thinking about baseball all the time.

I'd lie in bed imagining situations.

Bottom of the seventh.

Runner on second.

Two outs.

What pitch would I expect?

Where would I play this hitter?

I didn't even know I was studying.

I just thought I was daydreaming.

Looking back...

I was preparing.

That's what passion does.

Nobody has to force it.

---

## Confidence

People have often mistaken my confidence for arrogance.

I understand why.

Confidence makes some people uncomfortable.

Especially if they don't understand where it comes from.

Mine didn't come from compliments.

It came from preparation.

When you've fielded ten thousand ground balls...

You expect to field the next one.

Not because you're cocky.

Because you've done the work.

That's confidence.

It isn't believing you're better than someone else.

It's believing you've prepared honestly.

That lesson has stayed with me my entire life.

---

## The Gift

Looking back now...

I know God gave me a gift.

Not just athletic ability.

The ability to see.

To anticipate.

To process.

To compete.

To remain calm while everything around me sped up.

At the time...

I thought everybody experienced baseball that way.

Later...

I realized they didn't.

That gift would eventually leave the baseball field.

It would show up in leadership.

Technology.

Problem solving.

Building Whole Life Journey.

Different game.

Same gift.

I just didn't know it yet.
````

## TABB

If there is one place outside my home that helped shape me...

It was TABB.

Torrance American Boys Baseball.

To most people it was simply Little League.

To me...

It became home.

Not my house.

My second home.

---

I still remember driving into the parking lot.

The smell hit you before anything else.

Eucalyptus trees.

If you've never smelled eucalyptus after a warm California afternoon...

It's hard to describe.

It's one of those smells that permanently attaches itself to memory.

Even today...

If I smell eucalyptus...

I'm back at TABB.

Little League uniform.

Glove under my arm.

Waiting for practice.

Memory is funny that way.

---

The parking lot was alive.

Parents talking.

Kids running.

Somebody carrying bats.

Another family unloading lawn chairs.

Coaches already standing near the field.

The snack bar beginning to open.

Everything felt exciting.

Not rushed.

Exciting.

---

Looking back...

I don't remember ever dreading practice.

Ever.

Matter of fact...

If Dad had said,

"Practice is canceled."

I'd probably have been disappointed.

Who says that?

Kids who love the game.

I genuinely loved being there.

---

## The Reds

My first team was the Reds.

I've looked at those pictures hundreds of times.

Little uniform.

Little stirrup socks.

Little cleats.

Little Danny.

Standing there smiling.

Completely unaware that baseball was about to shape the next twenty years of his life.

Looking back...

I wish I could tell him.

Enjoy every minute.

Because one day you'll miss every one of them.

---

One thing I've noticed about those old pictures...

Everybody looked proud.

Parents.

Kids.

Coaches.

Nobody was thinking about scholarships.

Nobody was thinking about the Major Leagues.

They were simply excited to play baseball.

That's one thing I miss about youth sports.

Somewhere along the way...

Adults started taking it more seriously than the kids.

Back then...

It was still about baseball.

---

## Dad the Coach

One of the greatest blessings of my baseball career...

Was Dad.

Not because he pushed me.

Because he was there.

He coached.

Year after year.

Looking back...

That required an incredible commitment.

Work all day.

Come home.

Grab dinner.

Head to the ballpark.

Coach other people's kids.

Not just me.

Everybody.

I didn't appreciate that then.

I certainly do now.

---

Dad wasn't one of those coaches trying to live through his son.

He loved coaching every kid.

Matter of fact...

Some of the boys on my teams still remember him today.

That tells me everything I need to know.

People don't remember coaches because they won.

They remember coaches because they cared.

Dad cared.

---

Eventually...

Dad became President of TABB.

At the time...

I just thought,

"Well...

Dad's the president."

Looking back...

I realize how much work that involved.

Meetings.

Schedules.

Fields.

Volunteers.

Problems.

Parents.

Umpires.

Everything.

He wasn't simply coaching anymore.

He was serving an entire baseball community.

I don't think he ever looked at it that way.

He simply saw something that needed doing.

So he did it.

That's who Dad was.

---

## Mom at the Ballpark

Dad coached.

Mom watched.

Cheered.

Encouraged.

Supported.

Looking back...

Mom spent an incredible amount of her life sitting in bleachers.

Baseball.

Football.

Basketball.

She was there.

Not because she loved sports.

Because she loved me.

Parents do that.

They sit through things they'd never choose themselves...

Simply because somebody they love is participating.

I didn't appreciate that enough.

---

## Lindsey and Julie

Baseball became a family affair.

Lindsey eventually coached.

Julie worked in the concession stand.

Everybody had a role.

Looking back...

TABB wasn't just my baseball league.

It became part of our family culture.

Summer meant baseball.

Weekends meant baseball.

Conversations meant baseball.

Everything somehow connected back to baseball.

I loved it.

---

## The Snack Bar

Every kid remembers the snack bar.

Hot dogs.

Candy.

Soft drinks.

Snow cones.

It wasn't really about the food.

It was about freedom.

Winning usually tasted a little better.

Losing usually made the candy disappear a little faster.

Funny how that works.

---

The concession stand also became one of those places where families gathered.

Parents talked.

Kids traded baseball cards.

Coaches laughed about practices.

Nobody seemed in a hurry.

Life moved slower then.

Or maybe...

We simply weren't carrying smartphones around reminding us to leave.

---

## Pizza

If baseball ended...

Pizza usually began.

That became part of the routine.

Game.

Pizza.

Stories.

Laughter.

The game wasn't really over.

It simply moved to another location.

Those conversations probably did more to build friendships than the games themselves.

---

Looking back...

Nobody talked about statistics.

Nobody discussed batting averages.

We talked about funny plays.

Close calls.

Somebody's diving catch.

Somebody forgetting how many outs there were.

Baseball became the excuse.

Friendship became the result.

---

## Confidence Begins

People have asked me where my confidence came from.

It began here.

Not because somebody constantly told me I was good.

Because people trusted me.

There's a difference.

Coaches put me at shortstop.

They put me on the mound.

They handed me responsibility.

Responsibility quietly builds confidence.

Compliments usually don't.

Looking back...

TABB gave me confidence long before I realized I needed it.

That confidence eventually followed me everywhere.

Football.

College.

Business.

Leadership.

Whole Life Journey.

02 - Baseball.md (Part 3 of ?)

## All-Stars

If making your first Little League team is exciting...

Making the All-Star team is something different.

Every kid dreams about it.

At least...

Every kid who takes baseball seriously.

You don't talk about it much.

You don't want to sound arrogant.

But every one of us wondered.

"Am I good enough?"

"Will they pick me?"

"Did I do enough?"

Those thoughts quietly live inside every competitive athlete.

Mine certainly did.

---

One of my favorite stories about making the All-Star team is that I was probably the last person to know.

Dad already knew.

Mom knew.

People around the league probably knew.

Everybody managed to keep it from me.

Looking back...

That couldn't have been easy.

I'm pretty observant.

Eventually...

Someone told me.

I don't remember exactly who.

I don't remember exactly where.

I just remember the feeling.

Validation.

Not because I thought I was better than anyone else.

Because people I respected believed I belonged.

There's a difference.

---

Putting on that All-Star uniform felt different.

It wasn't just another jersey.

It represented trust.

The coaches had looked across an entire league and decided,

"We want him."

That meant something.

It still does.

---

Looking back at those pictures now...

I don't see a baseball player.

I see a little boy discovering confidence.

Real confidence.

Not loud confidence.

Quiet confidence.

The kind that whispers,

"You belong here."

---

## The Birth Certificate Story

One of the strangest stories from my baseball years is something I didn't even understand until I was an adult.

At the time...

It just seemed like grownups arguing about paperwork.

Looking back...

It had everything to do with my identity.

---

When All-Star selections came around one year...

Questions were raised about my eligibility.

Not because of where I lived.

Not because of anything I'd done.

Because of my birth certificate.

Only...

I didn't know that.

Remember...

At this point in my life...

I still had absolutely no idea I had been born Danny Ray Dodge.

As far as I knew...

I'd always been Danny Jenkins.

So when adults started discussing paperwork...

I couldn't understand what the big deal was.

---

Dad fought it.

Hard.

At the time...

I simply thought,

"That's Dad."

Standing up for me.

Years later...

After learning my story...

Everything finally made sense.

He wasn't fighting over a document.

He was fighting for his son.

That changes everything.

---

Looking back...

I can't imagine what that must have felt like for him.

Knowing the entire truth.

Watching people question my eligibility.

Trying to protect me.

Trying to protect the secret.

Trying to protect my childhood.

All at the same time.

That's a heavy burden for any father.

I don't think I appreciated it until decades later.

---

## Becoming a Student of the Game

Somewhere around this time...

Baseball stopped being just something I played.

I started studying it.

Not intentionally.

Naturally.

I'd watch older players.

Notice little things.

Footwork.

Throwing motions.

How infielders positioned themselves before the pitch.

How pitchers held runners.

How hitters adjusted.

I was fascinated.

---

One thing people don't always understand about baseball...

It's a thinking game.

Physical ability matters.

Absolutely.

But baseball rewards anticipation.

Preparation.

Observation.

The better I became...

The more I realized baseball wasn't slowing down.

I was seeing it faster.

That's a huge difference.

---

I loved standing at shortstop.

Not because I wanted attention.

Because every pitch became a puzzle.

What's the count?

Who's hitting?

Where's the runner?

What's the pitcher trying to do?

If the ball comes to me...

Where am I going?

Those thoughts happened almost instantly.

Eventually...

They stopped feeling like thoughts.

They became instinct.

---

## Learning to Fail

Baseball also introduced me to something incredibly valuable.

Failure.

Real failure.

Repeated failure.

The beautiful thing about baseball is that even the greatest players fail most of the time.

Think about that.

If you get a hit three times out of ten...

You're considered an excellent hitter.

That means failure isn't unusual.

It's expected.

---

As a little boy...

That lesson probably mattered more than any batting lesson I ever received.

You strike out.

You come back tomorrow.

You make an error.

You field the next ground ball.

You lose a game.

You play another one.

Life works that way too.

The people who succeed aren't usually the people who never fail.

They're the people who don't stay down.

Baseball taught me that before I even realized I was learning it.

---

## Falling Deeper in Love

By now...

Baseball wasn't simply something I did.

It had become part of my identity.

If someone asked what I wanted to do...

The answer usually involved baseball.

If someone asked what I was thinking about...

Probably baseball.

If there wasn't a game...

I wanted practice.

If there wasn't practice...

I wanted to throw.

If nobody else wanted to play...

I'd throw against the garage.

Or hit wiffle balls.

Or simply imagine situations.

Looking back...

The game had quietly become part of who I was.

Not because somebody pushed me toward it.

Because I genuinely loved every part of it.

And I was just getting started.
````
