````markdown id="h8m5qx"
02 - Baseball.md (Part 4 of ?)

## Pony League

Little League eventually gives way to something bigger.

For me...

That was Pony League.

The fields got bigger.

The players got stronger.

The pitching got faster.

Everything moved up another level.

Looking back...

I loved every bit of it.

Matter of fact...

I think I enjoyed getting challenged.

If something became too easy...

I usually got bored.

Pony League solved that problem.

---

One of the first things I noticed was that mistakes mattered more.

In Little League...

You could occasionally get away with a bad throw.

Or a poor decision.

The older we got...

The game punished mistakes more quickly.

I actually liked that.

It forced me to think.

It forced me to prepare.

It forced me to become a student of the game instead of simply an athlete.

---

By this point...

Shortstop had become home.

I loved everything about that position.

Every play seemed to involve me somehow.

If the ball wasn't hit to me...

I was backing somebody up.

Covering second.

Cutting off a throw.

Talking to the infield.

You were never standing around.

That's probably one of the reasons I loved it.

I've never enjoyed standing around.

---

## Seeing the Game

People have asked me over the years,

"What made you different?"

I don't think it was arm strength.

I don't think it was speed.

Those certainly helped.

The biggest difference...

I could see the game.

That probably sounds strange.

Let me explain.

---

Most people watch the baseball.

I watched people.

The hitter's feet.

The pitcher's balance.

The catcher's target.

The runner's lead.

The third-base coach.

The wind.

The count.

Everything.

By the time the pitch crossed home plate...

My brain had already processed several possible outcomes.

I didn't know I was doing it.

I just thought everyone did.

Apparently they didn't.

Looking back...

That gift eventually became one of the greatest strengths in my professional life too.

I still don't think in isolated events.

I think in systems.

Patterns.

Connections.

I learned that on a baseball field.

---

## Dad and Me

As I got older...

Baseball quietly became something Dad and I shared.

Not because we talked about emotions.

That wasn't really Dad's style.

We talked baseball.

Sometimes baseball was how we communicated.

One afternoon we'd be talking about a double play.

The next thing I knew...

Dad was teaching me about life.

Without ever announcing he was teaching me anything.

That's how he did it.

---

Looking back...

I think baseball became our language.

Some fathers fish with their sons.

Some hunt.

Some restore old cars.

Dad and I talked baseball.

We didn't always realize that baseball was simply carrying a much deeper conversation underneath it.

---

## Coaches

I've been blessed with a lot of coaches.

Some were excellent teachers.

Some were excellent motivators.

Some were simply good men.

One thing they all had in common...

They expected something from me.

I've thought about that many times.

Expectation is a powerful gift.

When someone expects something from you...

You usually rise toward it.

That's exactly what happened.

Coach after coach trusted me with responsibility.

I didn't want to let them down.

Looking back...

That probably accelerated my development more than natural ability ever could have.

---

## The Mental Side

By now...

I had stopped thinking about baseball as physical.

The game had become mental.

Every hitter had weaknesses.

Every pitcher had tendencies.

Every situation required thinking.

People often describe baseball as slow.

I never experienced it that way.

Inside my head...

Everything happened very quickly.

The game never slowed down.

My understanding sped up.

---

One thing I've tried to explain to people is that confidence isn't loud.

Real confidence is actually very quiet.

You simply expect yourself to perform.

Not because you're better than anyone else.

Because you've done the work.

That's exactly how baseball felt.

I wasn't hoping I'd make the play.

I expected to.

Not because I was arrogant.

Because I'd fielded that same ground ball thousands of times before.

---

## Learning Leadership

I didn't know it then...

But baseball was also teaching leadership.

Not through speeches.

Through consistency.

People notice consistency.

If you're the first one practicing...

People notice.

If you're the one diving for ground balls during warmups...

People notice.

If you hustle every play...

People notice.

Leadership isn't usually something people announce.

It's something they observe.

Looking back...

That's where I first learned it.

---

## Dreaming Bigger

As Pony League continued...

Something else quietly happened.

The dream got bigger.

Little League dreams become Pony dreams.

Pony dreams become high school dreams.

High school dreams become college dreams.

Nobody had to tell me to dream bigger.

Baseball naturally kept expanding the horizon.

I wasn't thinking about the Major Leagues every day.

But I was beginning to realize...

Maybe...

Just maybe...

I was capable of playing this game much longer than I'd ever imagined.

That thought was exciting.

Not because it guaranteed anything.

Because it made me curious.

How good could I actually become?

I don't think I've ever stopped asking that question.

It just isn't about baseball anymore.
````

````markdown id="n4q7kp"
02 - Baseball.md (Part 5 of ?)

## High School Baseball

There comes a point where baseball stops being something you do after school...

And starts becoming part of your future.

High school was that point for me.

Suddenly...

People weren't just watching games.

They were evaluating them.

Coaches.

Scouts.

Opposing teams.

Parents.

Everybody seemed to be paying a little more attention.

I tried not to think about it.

The game hadn't changed.

The audience had.

---

I attended South High School in Torrance.

Walking onto that field the first day felt different.

Nobody cared what I'd done in Little League.

Nobody cared about Pony League.

Everybody had been somebody before they got there.

Now...

We all started over.

I've always liked that.

One thing sports has taught me over and over again is this:

Yesterday's accomplishments don't play today's game.

You earn your place again.

Every season.

---

One thing became obvious pretty quickly.

The game had sped up.

Pitchers threw harder.

Hitters punished mistakes.

Coaches expected more.

The margin between success and failure got much smaller.

I loved that.

Pressure has never really bothered me.

Matter of fact...

I've often played better under pressure.

Looking back...

That probably says something about how God wired me.

---

## Third Base

By high school...

Third base had become home.

People often ask why I didn't stay at shortstop.

The answer is pretty simple.

Wherever the coach thought I could best help the team...

That's where I played.

I never really cared about positions.

I cared about competing.

Still do.

---

Third base requires anticipation.

The ball gets there fast.

Sometimes frighteningly fast.

You don't have time to react after the ball is hit.

You have to be moving before it's hit.

Again...

That gift of anticipation kept showing up.

Without realizing it...

I was seeing things before they happened.

That became one of my greatest strengths.

---

## Practice

I've always believed something.

Games reveal you.

Practice builds you.

I loved practice.

Not because it was easy.

Because I left every practice a little better than I arrived.

That excited me.

I wasn't trying to impress coaches.

I genuinely loved improving.

If we took batting practice...

I wanted one more round.

If we fielded ground balls...

Give me another bucket.

If conditioning started...

Let's go.

Not because I enjoyed running.

Nobody enjoys running.

Because I knew improvement lived on the other side of effort.

I've carried that philosophy into every area of my life.

---

## Confidence

By high school...

People began noticing my confidence.

Some interpreted it correctly.

Others called it cockiness.

I've smiled about that my entire life.

Confidence and arrogance aren't the same thing.

Confidence says,

"I've prepared."

Arrogance says,

"I'm better than you."

Those aren't remotely the same.

Did I occasionally cross that line as a teenager?

Probably.

Teenagers aren't exactly known for balance.

But deep down...

My confidence came from work.

Not compliments.

---

## Saturday Mornings

One of my favorite memories from high school had nothing to do with Friday night lights.

Or games.

It was Saturday mornings.

Johnnie Morton and I would get together and work out.

Nobody made us.

There weren't crowds.

No newspaper photographers.

No applause.

Just two athletes trying to become better.

Looking back...

That's what I remember most about Johnnie.

Not the NFL.

Not USC.

Not the celebrity.

The work.

People see greatness on Sunday afternoons.

I remember Saturday mornings.

That's where greatness is usually built.

---

## Johnnie

I've said this before, but I want to capture it correctly.

God gave me a tremendous athletic gift.

He gave Johnnie...

*the* gift.

There's a difference.

We both worked incredibly hard.

I never once felt like Johnnie outworked me.

He didn't.

We both paid the price.

The difference was...

God gave him a ceiling that almost didn't exist.

Mine was exceptionally high.

Just not that high.

I've never been bitter about that.

Matter of fact...

Standing beside someone like Johnnie taught me humility.

Sometimes you're standing next to greatness.

The appropriate response isn't jealousy.

It's appreciation.

I got to witness it firsthand.

That's a privilege.

---

## Senior Night

Of all the football and baseball pictures from high school...

One of my favorites isn't even an action shot.

It's Senior Night.

Standing there...

Me.

Mom.

Dad.

Johnnie.

His parents.

A simple photograph.

At the time...

It just felt like another school event.

Looking back...

It means much more.

Mom and Dad had already been divorced for several years.

Yet there they stood.

Together.

Supporting me.

People have asked if it felt awkward.

Honestly...

Not at all.

It felt normal.

It felt loved.

Looking back now...

I'm pretty sure that was one of the last public events they ever attended together.

If that's true...

I'm thankful it was for their son.

That picture has become one of my favorites because it reminds me that love sometimes quietly sets aside differences for someone else.

Mom and Dad did that for me.

I'll never forget it.

---

## The Dream Changes

Somewhere during high school...

The dream stopped being imaginary.

Professional baseball became possible.

Not guaranteed.

Possible.

That's a huge difference.

Coaches started talking differently.

Scouts started appearing.

Conversations changed.

People asked questions they'd never asked before.

"What are your plans?"

"What schools are recruiting you?"

"Who's been talking to you?"

It all felt exciting.

It also felt surprisingly normal.

I never walked around thinking,

"I'm going to the Major Leagues."

I simply thought,

"I'm going to become the best baseball player I can become."

I've always believed that's a healthier way to pursue dreams.

Control your effort.

Let God handle the outcome.
````

````markdown id="y8m3rv"
02 - Baseball.md (Part 6 of ?)

## Scouts

The first time you notice a scout at one of your games...

Everything changes.

Not because the game changes.

Because your imagination does.

Until then...

Professional baseball is just something you watch on television.

Suddenly...

Somebody from professional baseball is standing behind the backstop watching you.

That'll get your attention.

---

People sometimes assume I played differently because scouts were there.

Actually...

I tried very hard not to.

One thing Dad taught me early was,

"You don't change who you are because somebody important is watching."

Play your game.

Trust your preparation.

Everything else will take care of itself.

I've tried to live that way ever since.

---

The truth is...

Scouts weren't looking for one great game.

They were looking for consistency.

Anybody can have one good night.

Professional baseball isn't built on one night.

It's built on years.

I didn't fully understand that then.

I certainly do now.

---

## Jack French

One night changed everything.

I had a really good game.

If memory serves me correctly...

I hit a double.

Then a triple.

Played well at third base.

Made several difficult plays.

To me...

It was simply another baseball game.

To Jack French...

Apparently it was something more.

After the game...

He introduced himself.

Looking back...

That introduction quietly changed the direction of my life.

---

Jack wasn't flashy.

He wasn't loud.

He didn't try to impress anyone.

He'd spent his life around baseball.

He knew players.

He knew talent.

More importantly...

He knew character.

Looking back...

I'm thankful he saw something in me.

Even more thankful he took the time to invest in me.

---

People often think scouts simply evaluate players.

The really good ones become mentors.

Jack became much more than someone with a radar gun.

He opened a door.

One I had dreamed about for years.

---

## Wearing a Giants Uniform

Jack eventually invited me to play with one of the San Francisco Giants' semi-professional teams.

I still remember putting on that uniform.

It's funny...

Putting on a professional organization's uniform doesn't automatically make you a professional.

But it sure feels different.

There I was...

Still in high school.

Standing beside grown men.

Many of whom had the exact same dream I had.

Some would eventually make it.

Some wouldn't.

At the time...

We were all simply chasing the opportunity.

---

One thing those games taught me...

I belonged.

Not because I was the best player.

Because I could compete.

That realization meant more to me than almost anything else.

I wasn't overwhelmed.

I wasn't intimidated.

I simply played baseball.

That confidence would become incredibly important later.

---

## George Genovese

Playing with that team introduced me to another man who changed my life.

George Genovese.

People sometimes confuse George with Jack.

I've done it myself over the years.

Jack found me.

George developed me.

Those are two very different things.

Both mattered.

---

George had spent his life around baseball.

He could see things ordinary people couldn't.

A swing.

A stance.

A habit.

A weakness.

He noticed everything.

He threw batting practice to me countless times.

Those sessions became some of the greatest baseball education I ever received.

---

George also had one phrase that became legendary.

Whenever somebody tried to muscle the baseball...

He'd yell,

> "Quit swinging from the ass!"

The first time I heard it...

I laughed.

Eventually...

I understood it.

He wasn't saying don't swing hard.

He was saying,

"Trust your swing."

"Square the baseball up."

"Stop trying to manufacture power."

Funny enough...

I've realized that's good advice for life too.

Don't force greatness.

Master the fundamentals.

Power usually follows.

---

## Baseball People

One thing I've always loved about baseball people...

They're different.

There's almost an unspoken language.

You can sit beside someone you've never met.

Talk baseball for five minutes.

And suddenly...

You're friends.

The game has a way of doing that.

George was one of those people.

Jack too.

They loved baseball.

Not because it made them rich.

Because they genuinely loved the game.

I've always admired people who love something enough to spend their lives helping other people enjoy it.

That's exactly who they were.

---

## The Dream Gets Real

Somewhere during all of this...

Professional baseball quietly stopped being fantasy.

It became possible.

Scouts.

Conversations.

Evaluations.

Invitations.

The Giants.

George.

Jack.

It all started becoming real.

Not guaranteed.

Possible.

That distinction mattered.

Looking back...

I'm glad I never assumed anything.

Dreams are healthiest when they're pursued with gratitude instead of entitlement.

I never believed baseball owed me anything.

I simply wanted the opportunity to find out how good I could become.

That opportunity was finally arriving.
````

````markdown id="r5k8nm"
02 - Baseball.md (Part 7 of ?)

## Draft Day

Every baseball player dreams about draft day.

At least...

Every serious baseball player does.

Not because the draft means you've made it.

It doesn't.

The draft simply means someone believes you're worth investing in.

That's a pretty incredible feeling.

---

1989.

My senior year at South High School.

The San Francisco Giants selected me in the Major League Baseball Draft.

Thirty-fifth round.

Pick number 905.

I've had people over the years respond with,

"Only the thirty-fifth round?"

That always makes me smile.

Only?

Do you know how many high school baseball players dream about hearing their name called?

Almost all of them.

Do you know how many actually do?

Very few.

I never once thought,

"Only."

I thought,

"Thank you, God."

---

I wish I could tell you I jumped up and down.

I didn't.

It actually felt surprisingly peaceful.

There was excitement.

Absolutely.

There was also gratitude.

Somebody believed enough in me to spend a draft pick.

Nobody can ever take that away.

---

## The Contract

Not long after the draft...

The contract discussions began.

The Giants offered me a signing bonus.

If memory serves me correctly...

It was around ten thousand dollars.

Now...

To an eighteen-year-old...

Ten thousand dollars sounded enormous.

I'd never seen that kind of money.

Most kids my age hadn't.

For a little while...

It felt like everything I'd dreamed about was sitting right in front of me.

---

Then Dad and I started talking.

Real talking.

Not emotional.

Practical.

Dad looked at the situation differently than I did.

He wasn't thinking about eighteen-year-old Danny.

He was thinking about forty-year-old Danny.

He understood something I couldn't possibly understand yet.

Professional baseball is hard.

Really hard.

The vast majority of players never make the Major Leagues.

Even fewer stay there.

If I signed...

My college eligibility disappeared.

If baseball didn't work out...

I'd have to figure life out without college baseball.

Dad wasn't trying to keep me from my dream.

He was trying to protect my future.

---

## George Believed

George Genovese believed in me.

Really believed.

Enough that he picked up the telephone and called the General Manager of the San Francisco Giants.

Think about that.

One man cared enough about a kid from Torrance...

That he called the General Manager himself.

That's remarkable.

---

The General Manager flew down to Southern California.

He watched batting practice.

Watched me take infield.

Stayed long enough to watch my first at-bat.

Then...

I struck out.

I've laughed about that for years.

Of all the timing...

That was it.

Baseball has an incredible sense of humor.

---

Later...

George came back with another offer.

Twenty thousand dollars.

Double the original amount.

To me...

That sounded unbelievable.

To Dad...

It still wasn't enough.

Dad had always believed around forty thousand dollars would justify giving up college.

Twenty wasn't forty.

---

## The Decision

Eventually...

The decision became mine.

Not Dad's.

Mine.

People have asked whether Dad made the decision for me.

Absolutely not.

He gave advice.

Wise advice.

Then...

He trusted me.

That's one of the greatest gifts a father can give his son.

The freedom to choose.

---

I chose Alabama.

I've replayed that decision in my mind many times over the years.

Not because I regret it.

Because people ask about it.

"What if?"

It's a natural question.

What if I'd signed?

Would I have reached the Major Leagues?

Maybe.

Maybe not.

Nobody knows.

---

What I do know is this.

If I had signed...

There's a very good chance my entire life changes.

No Alabama.

No Jerry Stubbs.

No Heather.

No Haley.

No Tennessee.

No UT Medical Center.

No Whole Life Journey.

No life I'm living today.

---

People assume dreams always look the same at fifty-five as they did at eighteen.

They don't.

At eighteen...

Playing professional baseball felt like the greatest dream imaginable.

Today...

I wouldn't trade Heather for the Major Leagues.

I wouldn't trade Haley.

I wouldn't trade my life.

Not for anything.

That's perspective.

Only time gives you that.

---

## What Baseball Really Gave Me

Looking back...

Baseball gave me much more than a chance to play professionally.

It taught me discipline.

Failure.

Leadership.

Preparation.

Humility.

Friendship.

It introduced me to George.

Jack.

Jerry.

Johnnie.

Dozens of teammates.

Lifelong friendships.

It gave me confidence.

Not because of statistics.

Because of preparation.

---

I often say God gave me a gift.

That's true.

He absolutely did.

He just didn't give me *the* gift.

Standing beside athletes like Johnnie Morton taught me that.

Johnnie worked every bit as hard as I did.

Probably harder.

God simply gave him a ceiling that almost didn't exist.

Mine was exceptionally high.

Just not unlimited.

I've never been bitter about that.

Matter of fact...

I'm grateful I got to witness greatness up close.

That changes your perspective forever.

---

## Looking Back

When people ask whether baseball was worth it...

The answer comes instantly.

Absolutely.

Even if I'd never been drafted.

Even if I'd never gone to Alabama.

Even if professional baseball had never called.

It still would've been worth it.

Because baseball wasn't really preparing me for baseball.

It was preparing me for life.

Everything I became afterward...

Leader.

Husband.

Father.

Executive.

Entrepreneur.

Builder.

Much of that foundation was laid on a baseball field.

God simply used baseball as the classroom.

The lessons...

Lasted a lifetime.
````

````markdown id="w2n8qm"
02 - Baseball.md (Part 8 of ?)

## Baseball Was Never Really About Baseball

The older I get...

The more I realize baseball was never really about baseball.

At least not for me.

It became the classroom where God quietly taught me almost everything I would eventually use in the rest of my life.

At the time...

I thought I was learning how to hit a curveball.

How to turn a double play.

How to read a hitter.

Looking back...

I was learning discipline.

Leadership.

Humility.

Perseverance.

Preparation.

Those lessons followed me long after the uniform came off.

---

## Failure

People who don't know baseball often think it's a game of success.

It isn't.

It's a game of failure.

The greatest hitters who have ever lived failed seven out of every ten times they walked to the plate.

Think about that.

If you fail seventy percent of the time...

You're one of the greatest players in history.

That's incredible.

No other profession works that way.

Imagine a surgeon succeeding thirty percent of the time.

Nobody would let him operate.

Yet baseball teaches you to expect failure.

Accept it.

Learn from it.

Then step back into the batter's box anyway.

---

That lesson shaped me more than I realized.

When payroll projects failed...

I didn't panic.

When technology didn't work...

I didn't quit.

When Whole Life Journey hit obstacles...

I wasn't surprised.

I'd already learned something as a little boy.

Failure isn't final.

Failure is information.

Adjust.

Then step back into the batter's box.

---

## Leadership

Baseball also taught me something about leadership.

Leaders don't always talk the most.

Sometimes...

They're simply dependable.

If somebody hit a ground ball to shortstop...

I wanted my teammates thinking,

"Danny's got it."

Not because I wanted attention.

Because dependable people make everybody else better.

That lesson followed me into management.

Into payroll.

Into HRIS.

Into leadership.

People don't need perfect leaders.

They need dependable ones.

I've tried to become one.

---

## Preparation

I've often said confidence comes from preparation.

I still believe that.

When I stepped into the batter's box...

I wasn't hoping I'd hit the baseball.

I'd already hit thousands.

This was simply another one.

Preparation removes fear.

It doesn't guarantee success.

It simply allows you to compete without being controlled by anxiety.

I've lived my professional life exactly the same way.

Prepare.

Then trust the preparation.

---

## Teammates

Baseball also taught me that nobody succeeds alone.

Not one championship.

Not one great season.

Not one successful organization.

People love celebrating stars.

Championships usually belong to teams.

I've carried that into leadership too.

I don't enjoy winning by myself.

Matter of fact...

I don't think winning by yourself is really winning.

The greatest satisfaction comes from helping other people succeed.

That's exactly what good teammates do.

---

## The Dugout

Some of my favorite baseball memories didn't happen on the field.

They happened in the dugout.

The conversations.

The jokes.

The teasing.

The friendships.

Those moments are almost impossible to explain to someone who never played.

You spend so much time together...

You become family.

Not because somebody tells you to.

Because shared experiences naturally create connection.

---

I've often thought about Jerry.

Johnnie.

The teammates whose names never appeared in newspaper articles.

Some became successful professionally.

Some didn't.

None of that changed how I felt about them.

Baseball introduced me to remarkable people.

That alone made the journey worthwhile.

---

## Parents

As I've grown older...

I've also realized baseball wasn't simply my journey.

It belonged to Mom and Dad too.

Mom sat through countless games.

Dad coached countless practices.

Neither one of them ever asked for recognition.

They simply showed up.

Again.

And again.

And again.

I've often wondered how many hours they invested in my baseball career.

Thousands.

Without question.

Driving.

Practicing.

Watching.

Supporting.

Paying.

Encouraging.

Correcting.

They never complained.

At least not to me.

Looking back...

I hope they knew how grateful I eventually became.

---

## God's Gift

People have complimented me throughout my life for my athletic ability.

I appreciate that.

But I honestly believe something.

The gift wasn't mine.

It was God's.

He simply trusted me with it for a while.

That perspective changes everything.

When you believe your abilities belong entirely to you...

Pride comes naturally.

When you believe they're gifts...

Gratitude becomes much easier.

I've tried to remember that.

Not always perfectly.

But intentionally.

---

## The Lasting Impact

People sometimes ask me whether I miss baseball.

I do.

I miss the smell.

The sounds.

The competition.

The friendships.

The challenge.

I don't miss it because I wish I were still playing.

I miss it because it represented a wonderful season of life.

That's different.

I wouldn't go backward.

I simply smile when I look back.

---

If someone asked me what baseball ultimately gave me...

I don't think I'd say championships.

Or statistics.

Or being drafted.

I'd simply say...

It gave me the man I eventually became.

Everything afterward...

Marriage.

Fatherhood.

Leadership.

Technology.

Whole Life Journey.

All of it stands on lessons first learned while chasing a little white baseball around a dusty field in Southern California.

Looking back...

God knew exactly what He was doing.

I just thought I was playing baseball.

**End of 02 - Baseball.md**
````

````markdown id="r9m4kv"
03 - Football.md (Part 1 of ?)

# Football

## Introduction

If baseball was where I found peace...

Football was where I found adrenaline.

The two sports couldn't have been more different.

Baseball was quiet.

Football was loud.

Baseball gave you time to think.

Football demanded decisions in an instant.

Baseball rewarded patience.

Football rewarded commitment.

I loved both.

But I loved them differently.

---

People have asked me over the years,

"Which sport did you love more?"

That's like asking a parent which child they love more.

The answer depends on what you mean.

If you're asking which sport shaped my life the most...

Baseball wins.

If you're asking which sport gave me the greatest rush...

Football.

Without question.

There is nothing quite like Friday night lights.

Nothing.

---

## The First Time I Put on Football Pads

The first thing I remember wasn't the helmet.

It wasn't the jersey.

It wasn't the football.

It was the smell.

If you've ever played football...

You know exactly what I'm talking about.

Shoulder pads.

Fresh-cut grass.

Sweat.

Athletic tape.

There is a smell unique to football.

The moment I smell it today...

I'm seventeen again.

Standing in a locker room.

Getting ready to play.

Memory is funny that way.

---

The equipment felt enormous.

The shoulder pads made everybody look bigger than they actually were.

The helmet changed the way your voice sounded.

The chin strap always seemed just a little too tight.

Then...

You stepped onto the field.

Everything disappeared.

---

## Number Seven

Somewhere along the way...

I became Number Seven.

Looking back...

That number followed me almost my entire life.

Football.

Motorcycles.

Race numbers.

It became part of my identity.

I never intentionally made that happen.

It simply kept showing up.

Eventually...

It felt wrong wearing anything else.

---

People still remember me by that number.

Not because it was magical.

Because it represented a season of life.

Whenever I see an old picture...

If Number Seven is standing there...

I immediately know where I am.

Who I was.

How I felt.

It's funny how numbers can become memories.

---

## Quarterback

Quarterback wasn't simply another position.

It carried responsibility.

Every play started with you.

Every huddle looked toward you.

Every mistake became yours.

Every success belonged to the team.

Looking back...

I think that's one of the reasons I loved it.

Responsibility has never scared me.

Matter of fact...

I've usually moved toward it.

---

Standing in the huddle became one of my favorite places in sports.

People often imagine quarterbacks giving inspirational speeches.

Hollywood has done a wonderful job with that.

Real football usually sounds much less dramatic.

"Trips right."

"Blue 42."

"Watch the safety."

"Let's go."

Simple.

Direct.

Everybody knew their job.

Then...

We trusted each other.

---

## Leadership Begins

Looking back...

Football probably taught me leadership more than any other sport.

Baseball taught responsibility.

Football taught leadership.

Those aren't exactly the same thing.

As quarterback...

You couldn't hide.

If things were going badly...

Everybody looked at you.

If things were going well...

Everybody still looked at you.

You learn very quickly that leadership isn't about talking.

It's about earning trust.

---

I wasn't the loudest guy.

Matter of fact...

I don't think I've ever been the loudest guy.

My leadership style has always been pretty simple.

Prepare.

Work hard.

Show up.

Do what you said you'd do.

People eventually decide whether they trust you.

You can't demand it.

You earn it.

Football taught me that long before business ever did.

---

## Friday Nights

There are moments in life you never completely forget.

Friday night football is one of mine.

Walking out of the locker room.

Hearing the band.

Seeing the crowd.

Looking up at the lights.

There was electricity in the air.

Not fear.

Energy.

The kind that makes your heart beat a little faster.

The kind that reminds you you're alive.

---

I've played baseball in front of scouts.

I've spoken in front of executives.

I've led large organizations.

Very few experiences compare to walking onto a football field under Friday night lights.

It's difficult to explain unless you've experienced it.

For a few hours...

Nothing else exists.

Just teammates.

Opponents.

And one football.

---

## Preparation

One thing people rarely see...

Is everything that happens before Friday.

Monday.

Tuesday.

Wednesday.

Thursday.

Conditioning.

Film.

Practice.

More practice.

Then another practice.

Friday night is simply the final exam.

The work happened long before the crowd arrived.

I've carried that lesson into every part of my life.

People celebrate performances.

Very few people ever see preparation.

God does.

That has become enough for me.
````

````markdown id="q3w8mr"
03 - Football.md (Part 2 of ?)

## Summer Practice

People see Friday night.

They don't see July.

They don't see August.

They don't see two-a-days.

If you've never experienced football practice in the summer...

It's difficult to explain.

The heat.

The sweat.

The exhaustion.

The coaches.

The repetition.

You don't become a football team on Friday night.

You become one on hot afternoons when nobody's watching.

---

I actually liked practice.

That probably sounds strange.

Not because practice was fun.

Some days it absolutely wasn't.

I liked becoming better.

I liked solving problems.

I liked seeing the offense begin to click.

I liked watching eleven individuals slowly become one unit.

There's something incredibly satisfying about that.

---

One thing I learned early...

Football is impossible by yourself.

You can survive a baseball game with one superstar.

You cannot survive football that way.

Every single player matters.

One missed block.

One wrong route.

One missed assignment.

The play falls apart.

That's a tremendous lesson for life.

Organizations work exactly the same way.

---

## The Huddle

The huddle may have been my favorite place on the football field.

Think about it.

Eleven young men.

All breathing hard.

All looking toward one person.

Waiting.

Not because that person is better.

Because somebody has to lead.

As quarterback...

That happened to be me.

---

People often imagine quarterbacks giving dramatic speeches.

Truthfully...

Most huddles sound pretty boring.

"Trips Right."

"Blue 80."

"Watch the safety."

"Ready?"

"Break."

That was about it.

The speech had already happened all week.

Friday night wasn't for talking.

Friday night was for trusting.

---

I've thought about that a lot over the years.

Leadership usually isn't long speeches.

Leadership is preparation.

Leadership is credibility.

Leadership is consistency.

People follow someone they trust.

Not someone who talks the loudest.

Football taught me that before I ever managed another person.

---

## Johnnie Morton

It's impossible to tell my football story without talking about Johnnie Morton.

Today...

Most people know him because of the NFL.

USC.

Detroit.

Kansas City.

Thousands of receiving yards.

Professional football.

That's not who I remember.

---

I remember the kid.

The teammate.

The worker.

Saturday mornings.

Weight room.

Conditioning.

Running routes.

Trying to become better.

People saw Sundays.

I remember Saturdays.

That's where greatness is built.

When nobody's watching.

---

Johnnie and I weren't inseparable.

We weren't hanging out every weekend.

But we shared something important.

Mutual respect.

We both loved competition.

We both loved improvement.

We both understood that talent wasn't enough.

Work mattered.

---

I've said this before, but it's worth preserving correctly.

God gave me a tremendous athletic gift.

He gave Johnnie...

"The" gift.

There's a difference.

I don't say that because I think less of myself.

I say it because I stood beside greatness.

I watched it every day.

Johnnie worked.

Really worked.

People often assume gifted athletes don't have to.

They're wrong.

The truly great ones usually work harder than everyone else.

Johnnie did.

---

One thing I've always appreciated about him...

Success never changed how I viewed him.

He's still Johnnie.

The same guy I practiced beside.

The same teammate.

The same person.

I don't need anything from him.

Never have.

Friendship isn't built on somebody's accomplishments.

It's built on shared experiences.

We shared plenty.

---

## Senior Night

Of every football picture I own...

Senior Night has become one of my favorites.

Not because of me.

Because of Mom and Dad.

By that point...

They had already been divorced for several years.

Yet there they stood.

Together.

Beside me.

Smiling.

Supporting me.

---

People have asked if it felt awkward.

Honestly...

No.

I don't remember awkward.

I remember loved.

That's the word.

Loved.

Looking back now...

I realize how difficult that evening probably was for both of them.

They put everything aside.

Not for themselves.

For me.

That's one of the greatest gifts parents can ever give a child.

The willingness to make the day about them instead of themselves.

Mom and Dad did exactly that.

---

One of my favorite parts of those pictures is seeing Dad standing beside Johnnie's dad.

Two fathers.

Proud of their sons.

Probably talking football.

Looking back...

It's one of those ordinary moments that quietly became extraordinary.

---

I'm also pretty sure that was one of the last public events Mom and Dad ever attended together.

If that's true...

I'm thankful it happened on Senior Night.

I wouldn't trade those photographs for anything.

Not because they captured football.

Because they captured love.

---

## Friday Night Lights

People have asked me over the years whether I miss football.

I do.

Not because I wish I were still playing.

My body certainly doesn't.

I miss the atmosphere.

Walking out of the locker room.

The lights.

The band.

The crowd.

The sound of helmets clicking together.

The smell of fresh-cut grass.

The butterflies just before kickoff.

Those moments are difficult to recreate anywhere else.

---

Looking back...

Football wasn't preparing me to become a quarterback.

It was preparing me to become a leader.

I just thought I was learning plays.

God was teaching something much bigger.
````

````markdown id="v6t2qp"
03 - Football.md (Part 3 of ?)

## Learning to Lead

Looking back now...

Football taught me something I didn't fully understand until decades later.

Leadership isn't a position.

It's a responsibility.

There's a huge difference.

As quarterback...

I wasn't more important than anyone else.

Matter of fact...

Without the offensive line...

I wasn't anything.

Without receivers...

Nothing happened.

Without a center...

The play never even started.

Quarterbacks get far too much credit.

And far too much blame.

I learned that pretty quickly.

---

One thing I appreciated about football...

Everybody knew their job mattered.

The guy who made the tackle.

The guy who blocked.

The guy who kicked.

The guy who held.

Everybody contributed.

If one person quit doing his job...

Everybody noticed.

That's exactly how organizations work.

I didn't realize football was preparing me for executive leadership.

It absolutely was.

---

When I eventually became a director...

Then an executive...

People often complimented my leadership style.

I always smiled.

Most of it started on a football field.

Not in business school.

Not in management classes.

On Friday nights.

---

## Pressure

Pressure has always fascinated me.

People often ask,

"Were you nervous?"

Of course.

Everybody gets nervous.

The question isn't whether you feel pressure.

The question is what pressure does to you.

For some people...

Pressure creates panic.

For others...

Pressure creates focus.

I discovered pretty early that pressure sharpened me.

The bigger the moment...

The calmer I seemed to become.

I didn't understand why.

I still don't completely.

I simply know that's how God wired me.

---

That ability eventually followed me everywhere.

Payroll deadlines.

System conversions.

Executive meetings.

Whole Life Journey.

Pressure still exists.

Only the playing field changed.

---

## Losing

People love talking about winning.

I think losing teaches far more.

Some of the greatest lessons I ever learned came after losses.

Walking back into the locker room.

Everybody exhausted.

Nobody saying much.

Those are honest moments.

Nobody's pretending.

Nobody's celebrating.

Everybody's evaluating.

---

I learned something during those moments.

Good teammates don't disappear after losses.

Matter of fact...

That's when you discover who your teammates really are.

Winning usually reveals talent.

Losing reveals character.

I've carried that lesson with me ever since.

---

## Coaches

I've been blessed with tremendous coaches throughout my life.

Some taught football.

Some taught life.

The best ones understood the difference.

Looking back...

The coaches I remember most aren't necessarily the ones who won the most games.

They're the ones who believed in us.

Who expected something from us.

Who corrected us because they cared.

That's real coaching.

---

One thing I admired...

The best coaches weren't trying to create football players.

They were trying to create men.

At the time...

I didn't realize that.

Now I do.

I've tried to lead people exactly the same way.

Don't just solve today's problem.

Help build tomorrow's person.

---

## Confidence

Football gave me another kind of confidence than baseball.

Baseball confidence came from repetition.

Football confidence came from trust.

Trusting teammates.

Trusting preparation.

Trusting yourself.

As quarterback...

You eventually stop second-guessing every decision.

Not because you're always right.

Because hesitation usually creates bigger problems than mistakes.

That lesson has served me incredibly well.

Leadership often requires decisions with incomplete information.

Football taught me that before business ever did.

---

## The Brotherhood

One thing people who never played football probably don't fully understand...

Those teammates become brothers.

Not because somebody tells you they should.

Because shared hardship creates connection.

Summer conditioning.

Practices.

Games.

Injuries.

Victories.

Losses.

You go through enough together...

Eventually something changes.

You're no longer simply classmates.

You're brothers.

---

I don't remember every game.

I don't remember every score.

I certainly don't remember every statistic.

I remember locker room laughter.

Bus rides.

Practice jokes.

Standing shoulder-to-shoulder before kickoff.

Those memories have lasted far longer than any scoreboard.

---

## Looking Back

People have asked whether football or baseball prepared me more for life.

That's actually an impossible question.

Baseball taught me discipline.

Football taught me leadership.

Baseball taught patience.

Football taught courage.

Baseball taught consistency.

Football taught trust.

Together...

They became one education.

One classroom happened to have dirt.

The other happened to have grass.

God used both.

---

When I look back now...

Football wasn't really about touchdowns.

Or wins.

Or Friday nights.

It was about becoming the kind of man other people wanted to stand beside.

I hope I've continued becoming that man.

Not perfectly.

But intentionally.

Because long after the games ended...

Leadership remained.

And that's the lesson football gave me that I'll carry the rest of my life.
````

````markdown
03 - Football.md (Part 4 of ?)

## The Dream of Playing Two Sports

There was a time in my life when I honestly believed I could do both.

Football.

Baseball.

Not just in high school.

In college.

When you're young, you don't spend much time thinking about limitations.

You think about possibilities.

I loved both games.

I competed in both.

People encouraged me in both.

Why couldn't I continue doing both?

Eventually reality answered that question.

Not because I wasn't capable.

Because time isn't.

College athletics eventually demand everything.

There simply aren't enough hours in the day to give yourself completely to two Division I sports.

Looking back...

I understand why baseball eventually won.

Not because I loved football less.

Because baseball had become my future.

---

## Playing Hurt

Football teaches you something baseball never can.

You're going to get hit.

A lot.

Every single game.

Sometimes every single play.

You quickly learn the difference between being hurt...

And being injured.

Football players understand that language.

If you're hurt...

You keep playing.

If you're injured...

Someone else has to take over.

That's just part of the game.

---

Looking back, I probably played through things I shouldn't have.

Most football players do.

Not because they're trying to be heroes.

Because they don't want to let their teammates down.

There were bruises that lasted weeks.

Sprained fingers.

Twisted ankles.

Shoulders that hurt every time you lifted your arm.

Nobody talked much about it.

You taped it up.

Then you played.

That was football.

---

## The Locker Room

Some of my favorite football memories happened after the game.

Win or lose.

The locker room was honest.

If we won...

There was laughter.

Music.

Jokes.

Everybody reliving the big plays.

If we lost...

Nobody had to say much.

You could feel it.

Sometimes silence says everything.

---

One thing I always appreciated...

The locker room didn't care who you were outside football.

Didn't matter if your family had money.

Didn't matter what grades you made.

Didn't matter what kind of car you drove.

If you played hard...

You earned respect.

If you didn't...

Everybody knew it.

There was something refreshingly honest about that.

---

## Respect

One of the greatest gifts football gave me wasn't confidence.

It was respect.

Respect for teammates.

Respect for opponents.

Respect for coaches.

Respect for preparation.

I learned very quickly that talent earns attention.

Character earns respect.

Those are not the same thing.

---

There were players far more gifted than I was.

Some worked.

Some didn't.

The ones I respected most weren't necessarily the most talented.

They were the ones who showed up every day.

Worked.

Kept improving.

Encouraged teammates.

Accepted coaching.

Stayed humble.

Those were the guys I wanted beside me.

I've looked for those same qualities in coworkers ever since.

---

## Johnnie Again

When people hear me talk about Johnnie Morton, I want them to understand something.

I'm not talking about an NFL player.

I'm talking about my teammate.

There's a difference.

The world knows him because of Sundays.

I know him because of Saturdays.

Weight rooms.

Practice fields.

Conditioning.

Competition.

Mutual respect.

People often become impressed with celebrities.

I've never really been wired that way.

I'm impressed by character.

Johnnie had both.

Talent and character.

That's a rare combination.

---

Years later we're still connected on Facebook.

Every once in a while we'll interact.

He's become somewhat of a celebrity.

That comes with people constantly wanting something from you.

Autographs.

Pictures.

Recognition.

None of that interests me.

To me...

He's still Johnnie.

The teammate I worked beside.

The guy who earned everything he achieved.

I respect him for that.

Not because he played in the NFL.

---

## Looking Through Adult Eyes

As I write this section, I realize football gave me much more than memories.

It gave me perspective.

Standing beside athletes like Johnnie taught me humility.

Leading a huddle taught me responsibility.

Losing games taught me resilience.

Winning games taught me gratitude.

The older I get...

The more I realize every sport was simply another classroom.

God kept changing classrooms.

The lessons remained remarkably similar.

---

## Friday Nights Never Really Leave You

Even today...

If I drive past a high school football stadium on a Friday night...

I'll slow down.

Sometimes I'll roll the windows down.

I'll listen.

The band.

The whistles.

The crowd.

The announcer.

For just a moment...

I'm seventeen again.

Standing under those lights.

Looking into the huddle.

Waiting for the snap.

It's funny.

The older I get...

The less I miss playing.

The more I appreciate that I had the opportunity.

Very few people get to experience Friday nights from the middle of the field.

I did.

I'll always be thankful for that.

---

## Closing Football

Football taught me to lead.

It taught me to trust.

It taught me that preparation earns confidence.

It taught me that teammates matter more than individual recognition.

It taught me that pressure isn't something to fear.

It's simply another opportunity to become the person you've been preparing to be.

Looking back...

Football wasn't preparing me to become a better quarterback.

It was preparing me to become a better husband.

A better father.

A better leader.

A better man.

God simply used a football to teach those lessons.

And for that...

I'll always love the game.

**End of 03 - Football.md**
````

````markdown
04 - Alabama.md (Part 1 of ?)

# Alabama

## Introduction

There are places in life that change you.

Not because of the buildings.

Not because of the traditions.

Not even because of the opportunities.

They change you because of the people you meet there.

The University of Alabama became one of those places for me.

People often ask if I still consider myself an Alabama fan.

Absolutely.

Not because they have a great football team.

Although they certainly have.

Not because of championships.

Because that's where part of my life happened.

When you've worn the uniform...

Something inside you never really leaves.

---

## Why Alabama?

People have asked me many times,

"Why Alabama?"

The answer is actually pretty simple.

Because that's where I wanted to play.

It wasn't an accident.

It wasn't my backup plan.

It wasn't the only school interested.

Somewhere along the way...

Alabama became the dream.

Not Major League Baseball.

That was a different dream.

College baseball.

At Alabama.

Those are two different things.

---

Looking back...

I think Alabama represented something bigger.

It represented proving to myself that I belonged with the best players.

High school was one thing.

Division I baseball was something entirely different.

I wanted that challenge.

I've always been drawn toward challenges.

Comfort has never motivated me.

Growth has.

---

## Leaving California

One of the hardest parts wasn't baseball.

It was leaving California.

That was home.

Everything I'd ever known existed there.

The beaches.

The mountains.

The weather.

The friends.

The baseball fields.

The tree at Kathryn Avenue.

Gorman.

Everything.

People who grow up in one place often don't appreciate what it means to leave it.

I certainly didn't.

Not until I actually did.

---

Dad had already decided he wanted to move back to Tennessee.

His Tennessee.

The place where he grew up.

Where his brothers and sisters still lived.

To him...

He was going home.

To me...

I was leaving home.

Those are two very different perspectives.

Neither one is wrong.

---

I remember thinking,

"I wonder if I'll ever live in California again."

Life has a funny way of answering questions.

Sometimes...

The answer is no.

Not because something went wrong.

Because something better was waiting somewhere else.

I just couldn't see it yet.

---

## Arriving in Tuscaloosa

Driving into Tuscaloosa for the first time felt surreal.

I'd dreamed about this place.

Thought about it.

Imagined it.

Now...

I was actually there.

I wasn't visiting.

I was moving in.

That realization hit me pretty quickly.

This wasn't another baseball tournament.

This was life.

---

Everything felt different.

The campus.

The people.

The accents.

Even the humidity.

Southern California and Alabama are two completely different worlds.

I learned that pretty quickly.

The first time I walked outside in August...

I remember thinking,

"Who turned the shower on?"

Humidity was something California never really prepared me for.

---

## University Downs

I moved into University Downs.

That apartment would become one of the most important places in my young adult life.

Not because of the apartment itself.

Because of the people inside it.

That's where I met Jerry Stubbs.

A friendship that would last the rest of my life.

Neither one of us knew it then.

We were simply trying to figure out how to be adults.

---

Looking back...

University Downs wasn't where I learned baseball.

It was where I learned adulthood.

Paying bills.

Cleaning apartments.

Doing laundry.

Buying groceries.

Making mistakes.

Fixing those mistakes.

Nobody teaches you those things in high school.

Life does.

---

## My First Practice

I'll never forget my first official practice.

Walking into that locker room...

I suddenly realized something.

Everybody here had been the star somewhere.

Every pitcher.

Every catcher.

Every infielder.

Every outfielder.

Every one of us had been "the guy."

Now...

Nobody cared.

We all started over.

I loved that.

---

I've always appreciated environments where respect must be earned.

Not inherited.

Not assumed.

Earned.

Every ground ball.

Every batting practice.

Every sprint.

Every workout.

Every day.

You earned your place.

Again.

And again.

---

## Better Competition

The biggest difference wasn't talent.

It was consistency.

In high school...

Most teams had a few really good players.

College baseball was different.

Everybody could play.

Everybody.

There were no easy innings.

No easy at-bats.

No easy practices.

The standard moved up.

So did I.

---

One thing I noticed almost immediately...

I wasn't intimidated.

Respectful?

Absolutely.

Intimidated?

Not really.

I believed I belonged there.

Not because someone handed me a scholarship.

Because I'd worked for it.

That confidence mattered.

Without it...

College athletics will eat you alive.

---

## Starting Over

One thing Alabama taught me very quickly...

Nobody cares what you did yesterday.

Not high school.

Not the draft.

Not newspaper articles.

Not awards.

Today's practice.

Today's effort.

Today's attitude.

That's what mattered.

I've carried that philosophy into leadership ever since.

Your résumé might get you into the room.

Your effort determines whether you stay there.

---

## Looking Back

Looking back now...

I realize Alabama wasn't preparing me for professional baseball.

It was preparing me for professional life.

I simply thought baseball was still the destination.

God already knew it was becoming the classroom.

I just hadn't figured that out yet.
````

````markdown
## Jerry Stubbs

Meeting Jerry Stubbs turned out to be one of the greatest blessings of my college years.

At the time...

He was simply my roommate.

Today...

He's one of the first people I think about when someone mentions Alabama.

Funny how life works.

You have no idea you're meeting someone who will become part of your story forever.

You're just trying to figure out who's taking the top shelf in the kitchen.

---

Jerry was from Pennsylvania.

I was from Southern California.

Different backgrounds.

Different accents.

Different experiences.

Yet somehow...

We fit.

I think one of the reasons was that neither one of us knew how to be adults.

People assume college students suddenly become grown-ups.

That's one of the funniest myths in the world.

We weren't adults.

We were kids pretending to be adults.

Trying to figure everything out one mistake at a time.

---

Our apartment at University Downs became home.

Not because it was beautiful.

Because life happened there.

If those walls could talk...

Heather would probably tell them to keep quiet.

---

One of the first things we learned...

Was that we knew absolutely nothing about apartments.

One afternoon we decided to run the dishwasher.

Seems simple enough.

Except...

We didn't have dishwasher detergent.

We did have regular dish soap.

One of us...

I honestly don't remember which...

Said,

"I think you only use a little."

The other genius...

Probably me...

Thought,

"Why don't we just fill it up?"

So...

We did.

We completely filled the detergent compartment with regular dish soap.

Turned the dishwasher on.

Walked away.

Life was good.

For about twenty minutes.

Then Jerry yelled,

"DANNY!!"

I walked into the kitchen.

Foam.

Everywhere.

Not a few bubbles.

A mountain of bubbles.

They were rolling across the kitchen floor.

Making their way into the dining room.

It looked like we'd accidentally opened a bubble factory.

For about five seconds we just stood there.

Then...

We laughed so hard we could barely breathe.

Eventually we shut everything off and spent the next couple of hours cleaning up.

Neither one of us ever made that mistake again.

Some lessons only require one demonstration.

---

Cleaning the apartment wasn't exactly one of our strengths.

Actually...

That's probably being generous.

Jerry and I had developed a system.

A terrible system.

Neither one of us cleaned...

Until one of us couldn't stand it anymore.

Then...

Whoever finally broke first would simply start cleaning.

The amazing part was that the other one immediately joined in.

Within two hours...

The apartment looked fantastic.

Then...

We ignored it again for another month.

I don't recommend the system.

But it seemed perfectly reasonable at twenty years old.

---

Then there were the pizza boxes.

College students consume an unbelievable amount of pizza.

We certainly did.

Every empty box went onto the kitchen counter.

When the counter filled up...

We started stacking them beside the front door.

Then...

Outside the front door.

Eventually...

The stack became taller than either one of us.

No exaggeration.

Sometimes we'd have to throw the next box on top and then straighten the stack with a broom handle.

Looking back...

I'm amazed the apartment management didn't evict us.

Eventually the old crusts started smelling.

That's usually a clue you've waited too long.

---

Dad came to visit.

He walked upstairs.

Stopped.

Looked at the mountain of pizza boxes.

Then looked at us.

"What in the hell are y'all doing?"

Honestly...

Great question.

Neither one of us had a good answer.

The pizza mountain disappeared that afternoon.

Funny how parental visits improve housekeeping.

---

Another day...

Somebody decided it would be fun to throw darts.

That part wasn't unusual.

Then somebody had another idea.

Let's throw them into the wall near the vaulted ceiling...

Then jump up and grab them before they fell.

Perfectly reasonable.

At least to two college baseball players.

Eventually one dart stuck way up near the ceiling.

Jerry backed up.

Got a running start.

Jumped.

Missed.

As he landed he stumbled backward.

Trying to catch himself...

He threw his foot behind him.

Straight through the drywall.

Not into it.

Through it.

One size-twelve foot sticking out the other side.

We both just stared at the hole.

Then immediately started laughing.

Fortunately...

Dad had spent his life building houses.

I'd watched enough over the years to know how to repair drywall.

We patched it.

Sanded it.

Painted it.

To this day...

I don't know whether the apartment ever discovered what happened.

I'd like to think they didn't.

---

Then came the Blizzard of 1993.

If you weren't in Alabama...

You probably don't understand how unusual that was.

The entire state shut down.

Everybody went outside.

Snowball fights broke out everywhere.

Dad happened to be visiting.

He was standing on one of the upper balconies taking pictures.

Jerry looked over at me and said,

"I bet you can't hit him."

Now...

Let's pause.

I'm a baseball player.

That's not a dare.

That's an invitation.

I packed a snowball as tightly as I possibly could.

Honestly...

It was closer to a baseball made out of ice.

I stepped into it.

Let it fly.

At first...

I was impressed.

Then...

As it kept flying...

I became concerned.

Finally I yelled,

"LOOK OUT!"

Too late.

The snowball hit Dad's camera lens dead center.

It exploded all over his face.

Silence.

For maybe one second.

Then...

Rhonda started laughing.

Jerry collapsed on the ground laughing so hard he couldn't breathe.

I'm convinced that laughter saved my life.

Because Dad wasn't amused.

At least not immediately.

Years later...

It's one of our favorite stories.

At the time...

I wasn't entirely sure I was going to survive the afternoon.

---

That's what college was.

Not just classes.

Not just baseball.

Life.

Learning.

Friendship.

Growing up.

Looking back...

I don't think Jerry and I realized we were creating stories we'd still be laughing about thirty-five years later.

I'm glad we did.
````

````markdown id="v0g2hm"
## Learning to Live Together

Living with Jerry taught me something I didn't expect.

Friendship isn't built during the exciting moments.

It's built during ordinary Tuesdays.

Doing laundry.

Cooking terrible meals.

Watching television.

Studying.

Talking until two in the morning.

That's where real friendships grow.

Looking back...

Jerry wasn't simply my roommate.

He became family.

---

People sometimes ask why.

That's actually easy.

Jerry never pretended to be somebody else.

What you saw...

Was Jerry.

Good day.

Bad day.

Didn't matter.

He was authentic.

I've always been drawn toward authentic people.

I don't need perfection.

Never have.

I simply want real.

Jerry was real.

---

One thing people probably don't know about me...

I'm pretty loyal.

Once you're part of my circle...

You're there.

That's one reason I've had so many long-term friendships.

Jerry became one of those people.

The kind you don't have to talk to every week.

Years can pass.

Then you pick up exactly where you left off.

Those friendships are rare.

I've been blessed with several.

Jerry is one of them.

---

## Baseball at Alabama

Walking onto the baseball field at Alabama felt different than anything I'd experienced before.

Not because it was intimidating.

Because it was honest.

Nobody cared what I'd done in high school.

Nobody cared I'd been drafted.

Nobody cared about newspaper articles.

Today's practice.

Today's effort.

Today's attitude.

That's what mattered.

Looking back...

That's one of the healthiest environments I've ever experienced.

Every day started at zero.

I've tried to build teams that work exactly the same way.

Yesterday's success doesn't earn today's respect.

Today's effort does.

---

The pace of practice amazed me.

There wasn't much standing around.

Ground balls.

Throw.

Next.

Hit.

Run.

Again.

Everything happened quickly.

There was purpose behind every drill.

Purpose behind every repetition.

Purpose behind every correction.

Looking back...

That's where I began understanding intentional coaching.

The best coaches don't simply keep athletes busy.

They create deliberate improvement.

---

I also realized something else.

The gap between players had become much smaller.

Everybody could play.

Everybody.

The difference wasn't usually talent.

It was consistency.

Who prepared every day?

Who paid attention to details?

Who recovered from failure the fastest?

College baseball taught me that excellence isn't usually dramatic.

It's remarkably consistent.

---

## The Clubhouse

The clubhouse became another classroom.

Not because coaches were giving speeches.

Because players were always talking baseball.

Somebody discussing a pitcher.

Another guy breaking down a swing.

Somebody arguing over yesterday's game.

Baseball people speak a different language.

I loved being part of it.

Matter of fact...

I still do.

---

One thing I noticed...

Nobody spent much time talking about themselves.

They talked about the game.

That's one of the beautiful things about baseball.

The game becomes bigger than the player.

I've tried to remember that in leadership.

The mission has to become bigger than the leader.

Otherwise...

The organization eventually revolves around personality instead of purpose.

---

## Learning from Better Players

One of the smartest things I did at Alabama...

Was watch.

Constantly.

How did the older players prepare?

How did they stretch?

How did they take batting practice?

How did they carry themselves?

How did they respond after a strikeout?

People often think learning happens when you're talking.

I've learned just as much by watching.

Maybe more.

---

I discovered something.

Really good players are rarely flashy.

They're efficient.

Everything has purpose.

They don't waste movement.

They don't waste energy.

They don't waste words.

That observation stayed with me.

I've noticed the same thing among outstanding leaders.

The best ones rarely make everything about themselves.

They're quietly effective.

---

## Missing Home

There were moments I missed California.

Not because Alabama wasn't wonderful.

Because home was home.

I missed Dad.

Mom.

The familiar roads.

The ocean.

The smell of eucalyptus trees.

Gorman.

The weather.

Those feelings surprised me.

I'd been excited to leave.

I didn't expect homesickness.

Apparently...

You can love where you are...

And still miss where you've been.

Both can be true.

---

## Becoming Danny

College has a strange way of introducing you to yourself.

Nobody knows your history.

Nobody knows who you were in high school.

Nobody cares.

You're free to become whoever you're going to become.

Looking back...

That's exactly what happened.

I didn't become somebody different.

I became more completely myself.

That's one of the greatest gifts college gave me.

Not a degree.

Identity.

---

## Looking Back

When I think about Alabama today...

I don't first remember classes.

Or practices.

Or games.

I remember Jerry laughing.

The apartment.

The pizza boxes.

The bubbles.

The snowball.

Walking across campus.

Conversations that lasted until two in the morning.

Dreams that still felt possible.

Friendships that somehow survived decades.

Alabama wasn't simply where I played baseball.

It was where a California kid quietly became a man.

And looking back...

I don't think I appreciated that nearly enough while I was living it.
````
